name: Roma
subtitle: Eternal City
description: Rome from the Tarquin kings to Michelangelo: the walled city between the Vatican and the Lateran, drawn as an illustrated atlas plate. Positions are projected from real coordinates; the drawing is an illustration, not a survey.

water.name: Tiber
water.blurb: Rome's river, yellow with silt, navigable by barge to the Emporium and later Ripa Grande and Ripetta. Its floods regularly drowned the low city; floating mills turned beside Tiber Island.

hills.name: Capitoline
hills.blurb: Lowest but holiest of the seven hills: citadel, Temple of Jupiter and state archive. Goal of every triumph, seat of the medieval Senate; Michelangelo's piazza faces St Peter's.

hills.name: Palatine
hills.blurb: Rome's birthplace, between Forum and Circus. Aristocrats' houses under the Republic became one continuous imperial palace; the word 'palace' comes from its name. Later vineyards and Farnese gardens.

hills.name: Aventine
hills.blurb: The plebeian hill across the Circus from the Palatine, long outside the sacred boundary. Temples of Ceres and Diana, granaries below; later rich villas, then Santa Sabina and Santa Prisca.

hills.name: Caelian
hills.blurb: Long ridge south-east of the Forum, said to be named for the Etruscan Caelius Vibenna. Imperial mansions and the Temple of Claudius; later churches among vineyards.

hills.name: Esquiline
hills.blurb: Rome's biggest hill, with two spurs, the Oppian (and Fagutal) and Cispian. Once the paupers' cemetery, then Maecenas's gardens, Nero's Golden House, Trajan's Baths and Santa Maria Maggiore.

hills.name: Viminal
hills.blurb: The smallest and least remembered hill, between Quirinal and Esquiline, named for its osier willows. Diocletian's Baths covered its north end; the Praetorian camp stood beyond.

hills.name: Quirinal
hills.blurb: The northern ridge, home of the Sabine god Quirinus, later senators' houses, the Temple of Serapis and the Baths of Constantine. Popes built their summer palace there after 1583.

hills.name: Janiculum
hills.blurb: The high ridge west of the Tiber, not one of the seven. Janus's hill guarded the Etruscan side; water-mills worked its slopes. San Pietro in Montorio marks Peter's supposed crucifixion.

hills.name: Pincian
hills.blurb: The 'hill of gardens' north of the Campus Martius, with the villas of Lucullus, Sallust and the Pincii. Outside the Republican city, inside Aurelian's walls; later Trinità dei Monti.

hills.name: Vatican Hill
hills.blurb: Across the Tiber: an unhealthy slope with Nero's circus and cemeteries. Peter's tomb there became Constantine's basilica; by 1560 the papal palace and the half-built new St Peter's stood here.

hills.name: Monte Testaccio
hills.blurb: An artificial hill about 35 metres high of broken olive-oil amphorae dumped from the Emporium warehouses, mostly in the 2nd and 3rd centuries: roughly 53 million jars.

roads.name: Via Sacra
roads.blurb: The Forum's sacred way, down from the Velia past the Regia and the Temple of Castor towards the Capitol. Route of triumphs; lined with jewellers' and luxury shops.

roads.name: Clivus Capitolinus
roads.blurb: The paved ramp winding up from the Temple of Saturn to the Temple of Jupiter, the last stretch of every triumph. Its basalt paving partly survives.

roads.name: Argiletum
roads.blurb: From the Forum north-east into the Subura, past the Curia: shoemakers and booksellers, including Martial's bookseller Atrectus. Domitian's Forum Transitorium later swallowed its first stretch.

roads.name: Vicus Tuscus
roads.blurb: The 'Etruscan street' from the Forum past the Temple of Castor to the Velabrum and Circus. Shops of silk, perfume and incense dealers; a reputation for shady characters.

roads.name: Vicus Jugarius
roads.blurb: Skirting the Capitoline's southern foot from the Forum to the Forum Boarium and river. Named for yoke-makers or an altar of Juno Juga; carters and traders used it.

roads.name: Via Lata
roads.blurb: The Via Flaminia's straight run through the Campus Martius to the Capitoline, 'the broad street'. Imperial arches spanned it; from the 1460s it was the Corso, the Carnival racecourse.

roads.name: Via del Corso
roads.blurb: The old Via Lata, renamed for the carnival races (corse) of riderless horses, run along it from Paul II's time in the 1460s. Palaces slowly replaced tenements.

roads.name: Via Appia
roads.blurb: The queen of roads, begun 312 BCE by Appius Claudius to Capua, later Brindisi. Leaving by the Porta Capena between tombs; armies marched out, eastern goods came in.

roads.name: Via Ostiensis
roads.blurb: Along the Tiber's left bank 25 kilometres to Ostia, the grain port. Carts and towed barges shared the route; St Paul was buried beside it at the second milestone.

roads.name: Via Tiburtina
roads.blurb: East through the Esquiline gate 30 kilometres to Tivoli, whose travertine quarries supplied the Colosseum. Later pilgrims took it to San Lorenzo fuori le Mura.

roads.name: Via Labicana
roads.blurb: Twin roads out of the Porta Praenestina south-east to Labici and Palestrina. Helena's mausoleum and catacombs lay on the Labicana; aqueduct arcades marched beside the Praenestina.

roads.name: Via Nomentana
roads.blurb: North-east 23 kilometres to Nomentum through the Porta Collina, later the Porta Nomentana. Sant'Agnese and Constantina's mausoleum stand at its second mile; Pius IV built the Porta Pia.

roads.name: Via Salaria
roads.blurb: The ancient salt road north-east up the Tiber valley to the Sabine hills, older than Rome. The Gardens of Sallust lay beside it; Alaric's Goths entered its gate in 410.

roads.name: Via Aurelia
roads.blurb: West over the Tiber and the Janiculum to the Etruscan coast and Pisa, begun around 241 BCE. Travellers left through the Porta Aurelia, now the Porta San Pancrazio.

roads.name: Via Triumphalis
roads.blurb: From the Vatican plain across the Tiber towards the Campus Martius, probably the route of returning generals before Augustus. Its line later carried pilgrims down from Monte Mario.

roads.name: Alta Semita
roads.blurb: The 'high path' along the Quirinal ridge from the Capitoline towards the Porta Collina. Senators' houses and the Baths of Constantine lined it; Pius IV's Strada Pia followed its course.

roads.name: Clivus Palatinus
roads.blurb: The paved road climbing from the Arch of Titus onto the Palatine, main approach to the imperial palace. Basalt paving survives; petitioners and courtiers queued along it.

roads.name: Via Papalis
roads.blurb: The papal procession route from St Peter's through the abitato, past Pasquino and the Capitol, to the Lateran: every new pope rode it to take possession of his cathedral.

roads.name: Via Giulia
roads.blurb: Julius II's straight street along the Tiber, laid out by Bramante from 1508: a kilometre of palaces, bankers and the Florentines' church, Rome's first planned Renaissance avenue.

roads.name: Via del Pellegrino
roads.blurb: The pilgrims' street from Campo de' Fiori to the bankers' quarter, part of the Via Papalis; goldsmiths and rosary-sellers packed it, and papal corteges squeezed through.

roads.name: Via dei Banchi
roads.blurb: The bankers' street at the bridgehead, where Florentine and Genoese houses, the Chigi bank and the papal mint handled Jubilee cash and Church revenues. Printers followed the money.

roads.name: Via Recta
roads.blurb: A straight ancient street across the Campus Martius from the bridgehead towards the Via Lata. Its medieval successor, Via dei Coronari, was named for the rosary-sellers serving pilgrims.

bridges.name: Pons Sublicius
bridges.blurb: Rome's oldest bridge, a timber deck on wooden piles, built by tradition under King Ancus Marcius. Religious rule kept iron out of it; the priests who maintained it, the pontifices, took their name from bridge-making. Horatius Cocles held it against the Etruscans while it was cut down behind him.

bridges.name: Pons Aemilius
bridges.blurb: Rome's first stone bridge: piers of 179 BCE, arches finished in 142 BCE. It carried traffic from the cattle market to Trastevere for seventeen centuries; floods broke it in 1598 and one arch, the Ponte Rotto, still stands in the river.

bridges.name: Pons Fabricius
bridges.blurb: Two broad arches from the Campus Martius to the Tiber Island, built in 62 BCE by Lucius Fabricius, curator of roads, whose name is still cut on it. It is the oldest Roman bridge in Rome still in use as built.

bridges.name: Pons Cestius
bridges.blurb: The bridge from the Tiber Island to Trastevere, built in the 1st century BCE and rebuilt in 370 CE by the emperors Valentinian, Valens and Gratian with stone from the Theatre of Marcellus. A single main arch with two small flood arches.

bridges.name: Pons Aelius
bridges.blurb: Hadrian's bridge of 134 CE, leading straight to the gate of his mausoleum. Pilgrims later crossed it to St Peter's; in the Jubilee crush of 1450 its parapets gave way and nearly two hundred people died.

bridges.name: Pons Neronianus
bridges.blurb: A bridge to the imperial gardens and Nero's circus on the Vatican plain, probably built by Caligula or Nero. It was already in ruins by late antiquity; low piers still show in the river when the water is low.

bridges.name: Pons Agrippae
bridges.blurb: A crossing from the Campus Martius to Trastevere, attributed to Agrippa and known from an inscription; its piers were found in the riverbed in 1887. A later bridge near here, the Pons Aurelius, was rebuilt as the Ponte Sisto.

bridges.name: Ponte Sisto
bridges.blurb: Built for Pope Sixtus IV in 1473 to 1479 on the ruined piers of the ancient Pons Aurelius: the first new bridge over the Tiber since antiquity, with a round oculus in the central pier to let flood water through.

districts.name: Subura
districts.description: The crowded valley between the Esquiline, Viminal and Quirinal, reached via the Argiletum. Tall tenements, shops, taverns and brothels; Martial calls it loud; Juvenal would prefer a barren island. Caesar grew up here. Augustus's firewall shut it off from the marble centre.

districts.name: Campus Martius
districts.description: The floodplain north-west of the old city, where the army drilled and citizens voted. Mostly open fields under the kings and early Republic; Pompey, Agrippa and the emperors filled it with theatres, baths, porticoes and the Pantheon. By 400 CE it was Rome's monumental showpiece.

districts.name: Velabrum
districts.description: Low ground between the Palatine and Capitoline, the old marsh drained by the Cloaca Maxima. A busy commercial quarter of oil, wine, perfume and food dealers; Plautus and Horace mention its shops. The Vicus Tuscus crossed it from the Forum to the cattle market.

districts.name: Forum Boarium
districts.description: The cattle market beside the Tiber's first landing place, Rome's oldest trading quarter and site of the Ara Maxima of Hercules. Temples round and rectangular, the river port and warehouses lined it; under the Empire the money-changers' guild raised the Arch of the Argentarii here.

districts.name: Aventine
districts.description: The plebeian hill south of the Circus, outside the sacred boundary until Claudius. Temples of Ceres, Diana and Mercury guarded the commoners' interests; granaries and the port lay below. Under the Empire rich houses climbed it; the baths of Sura and Decius stood on top.

districts.name: Trans Tiberim (Trastevere)
districts.description: Across the river: a working quarter of boatmen, tanners, potters and millers, many of them immigrants, Jews and Syrians, beside Caesar's gardens and the naval barracks. In the Middle Ages a dense, proudly separate neighbourhood around Santa Maria in Trastevere, inside the Aurelian Walls' loop.

districts.name: Esquiline
districts.description: Rome's largest hill: once the paupers' burial ground outside the Servian Wall, which Maecenas turned into gardens. Mansions and imperial parks spread over the top; crowded streets filled the slopes below, then Nero's Golden House and Trajan's Baths. Later Santa Maria Maggiore crowned it.

districts.name: Caelian
districts.description: The long ridge south-east of the Colosseum: in the Republic ordinary houses and tufa quarries, under the Empire a quiet quarter of senators' mansions, the Castra Peregrina and the vast Temple of Claudius. Churches like Santi Giovanni e Paolo rose on their ruins.

districts.name: Emporium district
districts.description: The river port south of the Aventine, laid out from 193 BCE: the Emporium quay, the Porticus Aemilia and warehouses for grain, wine and oil. Dockers, clerks and mule drivers worked here. Discarded oil amphorae piled up into Monte Testaccio, a hill of sherds.

districts.name: Borgo (the Leonine City)
districts.description: The pilgrim suburb between Castel Sant'Angelo and St Peter's, walled by Leo IV in the 850s after a Saracen raid. Hostels of the Saxons, Frisians and Lombards, relic-sellers, money-changers and taverns lined its streets. By the 16th century the papal palace ruled it.

districts.name: The abitato (inhabited city)
districts.description: The crowded Tiber bend where medieval and Renaissance Romans actually lived: the old Campus Martius, with narrow lanes, baronial towers, markets at Campo de' Fiori and the Pantheon, and the bankers' street by the bridge. Floods, mud and cardinals' palaces side by side.

districts.name: The disabitato
districts.description: The empty two-thirds inside the Aurelian Walls: vineyards, ruins, pasture, marsh and scattered churches and monasteries. The Forum was the Campo Vaccino, cow pasture; the Baths of Caracalla a quarry. Pilgrims crossed it on foot to reach the Lateran and San Lorenzo. Wolves were reported.

districts.name: Ghetto
districts.description: The walled Jewish enclosure beside the Tiber, a few flood-prone hectares around the Portico d'Ottavia, locked nightly from 1555. Some 3,000 people crammed into houses that grew upwards; rag trade, tailoring and pawnbroking were the permitted trades. One building, the Cinque Scole, held five synagogues.

districts.name: Palatine
districts.description: The hill of Rome's founding legend, where visitors were shown the hut of Romulus. In the Republic an aristocratic address: Cicero, Clodius, Hortensius and Catulus had houses here beside the temples of Magna Mater and Victoria. Augustus's house began its total takeover by palaces.

districts.name: Capitoline
districts.description: A small, steep hill and the state's religious heart: the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus on one summit, the Arx and Juno Moneta on the other, the Tabularium between. The medieval Senators' Palace sat on the Tabularium; Michelangelo's piazza remade it as civic Rome.

periods.label: Regal Rome
periods.summary: Hill villages fusing into a town under Etruscan-style kings. The Forum marsh is being drained by the Cloaca, huts of wattle and thatch give way to houses on tufa footings with terracotta roofs, and the Capitoline temple is rising. Timber, thatch, tufa and clay; a wooden bridge; salt and bronze traded at the river ford.
periods.feel: Smoke from thatched roofs, the smell of the marsh, a bronze-smith's hammer ringing under the Palatine.

periods.label: Middle Republic
periods.summary: Rome just after Hannibal: a crowded, muddy city of tufa, timber and terracotta ruled by the Senate and annual magistrates. Stone temples, the first basilicas and porticoes in the Forum, the Emporium and stone quays on the river, two aqueducts, streets only now being paved. Greek loot, Greek plays and Greek ideas begin to arrive.
periods.feel: Grain barges on the river, Plautus in a wooden theatre, the Forum packed with litigants, bankers and soldiers home from Greece.

periods.label: Late Republic
periods.summary: Capital of the Mediterranean, bursting its old walls: citizens, freedmen and slaves packed into tenements, the first marble temples, Pompey's stone theatre in the Campus Martius, Caesar's new Forum under construction. Politics is fought in the streets by gangs; aqueducts, the river port and the free grain dole keep the city alive.
periods.feel: Election mobs, street gangs, Cicero's voice from the Rostra; carts banned by day, the Subura burning somewhere every week.

periods.label: High Empire
periods.summary: Trajan's Rome at its peak: marble over brick-faced concrete, fourteen regions, the Colosseum, the imperial fora, great baths, nine aqueducts and tenements six storeys high. The emperor rules from the Palatine; the Senate meets and obeys. Free grain, games and water for a million people fed by sea from Egypt and Africa.
periods.feel: Marble glare at noon, tens of thousands of tenements, the roar of the amphitheatre and the clatter of carts all night.

periods.label: Severan Rome
periods.summary: The Severan city: Caracalla's enormous baths, the Septizodium, a marble plan of every street displayed in the Temple of Peace. Still a million people on the dole, now with free oil too; soldier-emperors from Africa and Syria, gilded brick and coloured marble. The Aurelian Walls (271–275) will soon enclose a city that has begun to fear the north.
periods.feel: Soldiers everywhere, the biggest baths yet, the brick city at its most crowded and most confident.

periods.label: Late Antiquity
periods.summary: A Christian capital without an emperor, inside the Aurelian Walls: basilicas at the Lateran, St Peter's and across the city; temples closed since 391 and stripped of bronze. Senators still rich, the population shrinking; Alaric's Goths sack the city in 410. Old marble reused, tenements decaying, the dole continuing, the games fading away.
periods.feel: Chant from new basilicas, bronze torn from old roofs, a thinning crowd in a city built for a million.

periods.label: Medieval Rome
periods.summary: A town huddled in the Tiber bend and Trastevere inside walls built for a million: tower-houses of the Orsini and Colonna, brick churches with bell-towers, ancient marble burned for lime, two-thirds of the walled area vineyards and ruins. Ruled contentiously by pope, barons and commune; Boniface VIII's Jubilee of 1300 floods the streets with pilgrims.
periods.feel: Pilgrims, cows in the Forum, baronial towers, and the marvels of the Mirabilia half-buried among the vines.

periods.label: Renaissance Rome
periods.summary: The papal capital rebuilt: straight new streets (Via Giulia, Coronari), palaces of travertine and stucco, St Peter's dome rising, aqueducts being repaired, Michelangelo's Capitol under way. Recovering from the Sack of 1527 under Pius IV, with the Inquisition, the Index, the Ghetto (1555) and the Council of Trent: a city of clerics, bankers, courtesans and pilgrims.
periods.feel: Carriages and cardinals on new streets, printers, lime-kilns and Pasquino's wit beneath the unfinished dome.

landmarks.name: Roman Forum

kingdom-600bce.note: A freshly drained, gravel-paved open space ringed by huts and the first shrines (Vesta, the Regia). The Cloaca Maxima, still an open channel, runs through it to the Tiber.

republic-200bce.note: Stone temples of Saturn, Castor and Concord, the Comitium and Rostra, and shops along both long sides. The first basilicas (Porcia 184, Aemilia 179, Sempronia 170 BCE) rise within this period.

republic-50bce.note: Sulla's repaving of the 80s BCE and Caesar's projects: the Basilica Julia replacing the Sempronia, a new Rostra, the Curia Julia begun. Caesar's body will be burned here in 44 BCE.

empire-100ce.note: Augustus's marble Forum: the Temple of Divine Julius at the east end, the rebuilt Basilicas Aemilia and Julia, the Temple of Vespasian. Domitian's equestrian statue (c. 91 CE) fell after his murder in 96.

empire-215ce.note: The Arch of Septimius Severus (203 CE) dominates the west end. The square is crammed with honorific columns and statues; Julia Domna rebuilt Vesta's temple after the fire of 191 CE.

late-400ce.note: Still kept up: Diocletian's rebuilt Curia and Basilica Julia, seven honorific columns before the Basilica Julia, restored statues. Temples were closed by law in 391 CE but the buildings stand intact.

medieval-1300.name: Campo Vaccino (the Forum)
medieval-1300.note: The 'cow field': cattle graze among half-buried columns. Churches occupy the Curia (Sant'Adriano), the Temple of Antoninus (San Lorenzo in Miranda) and the Temple of Romulus; the Frangipane fortify the arches.

renaissance-1560.name: Campo Vaccino (the Forum)
renaissance-1560.note: A pasture and marble quarry. Columns of Saturn, Vespasian and Castor stand half-buried; popes strip blocks for St Peter's. Antiquarians like Pirro Ligorio sketch and dig among the ruins.

landmarks.summary: The valley between the Capitoline and Palatine hills, drained around 600 BCE and for a thousand years the political, religious and commercial heart of Rome.
details: Marshy ground was drained by the Cloaca Maxima and paved around 600 BCE. Through the Republic it filled with temples (Saturn, Castor, Concord), basilicas (Aemilia, Sempronia), the Comitium and Rostra. Caesar and Augustus rebuilt it in marble; later emperors added arches and the Temple of Vespasian. After the 7th century CE it sank under silt and rubble and became pasture, the Campo Vaccino, until excavations began in 1803.

The miniature shows the open paved square with its principal buildings massed around it, scaled down and simplified. Exact facades of Republican buildings are largely conjectural; the imperial state follows the usual reconstructions based on surviving foundations, the Severan Marble Plan and coin images. The statues, columns and honorific monuments that crowded the real square are reduced to a few representative pieces.
landmarks.built: Drained and paved c. 600 BCE; continuously rebuilt to the 4th century CE
landmarks.function: Civic square: assemblies, law courts, temples, markets

landmarks.name: Temple of Saturn

kingdom-600bce.note: Not yet built. An altar of Saturn is said to have stood here at the foot of the Capitoline; the temple was vowed and begun around the end of the monarchy.

republic-200bce.note: The early Republican temple, probably Tuscan in style with a wooden roof and terracotta ornament. Inside the podium the quaestors keep the treasury, the legions' standards and the bronze tablets of laws.

republic-50bce.note: Still the old building; Plancus's complete rebuilding in travertine on a new high podium (42 BCE) is a few years away. The Saturnalia procession starts here each December.

empire-100ce.note: Plancus's temple: probably six Ionic columns across the front, a high podium with the treasury vaults inside, and the long stair up from the Forum. The Clivus Capitolinus climbs past its flank.

empire-215ce.note: Unchanged in form; the treasury remains here in name even though real money sits in the imperial fiscus. Its bulk closes the west end of the Forum below the Capitoline.

late-400ce.name: Temple of Saturn (restored)
late-400ce.note: Rebuilt after a fire (probably that of 360 CE) with second-hand granite columns and clumsily cut Ionic capitals; the architrave records the Senate's restoration. One of the last pagan temples maintained by Rome's senators.

medieval-1300.name: Ruins of the Temple of Saturn
medieval-1300.note: The cella is gone; the porch, six columns across and two deep, stands half-buried at the edge of the Campo Vaccino. The podium is quarried for marble and lime; a lane passes under the columns.

renaissance-1560.name: Ruins of the Temple of Saturn
renaissance-1560.note: Eight columns and architrave stand in the cattle field, drawn by artists like Heemskerck and du Pérac. Antiquarians still debate whether this is the Temple of Saturn or of Concord.

landmarks.summary: Among the oldest temples of the Forum, dedicated c. 497 BCE and housing the state treasury; its eight surviving granite columns belong to a rebuilding after a fire, probably in 360 CE.
details: Tradition dates the dedication to 497 BCE. Lucius Munatius Plancus rebuilt it in 42 BCE on a high podium that still survives. After a fire, probably in 360 CE, the front was patched together from reused columns of grey and pink granite with ill-matching Ionic capitals; the architrave inscription records that 'the Senate and People of Rome restored what fire had consumed'.

The miniature shows the Plancus temple: a hexastyle Ionic front on a tall podium with steps rising from the Forum side, the treasury vaults inside the podium. For the Republic the earlier form is conjectural; for 400 CE the model reuses the same mass with the patched columns of the restoration. Medieval and Renaissance periods show the stripped front standing in the field, as in 16th-century drawings.
landmarks.built: Dedicated c. 497 BCE; rebuilt 42 BCE; restored after fire, late 4th century CE
landmarks.function: Temple of Saturn and state treasury (aerarium Saturni)

landmarks.name: Curia Julia

kingdom-600bce.name: Curia Hostilia
kingdom-600bce.note: The senate meets in the hall King Tullus Hostilius is said to have built on the north side of the Comitium. Its early form is unknown; a simple gabled hall is assumed.

republic-200bce.name: Curia Hostilia
republic-200bce.note: The Curia Hostilia, its side wall painted with Messalla's victory of 263 BCE over the Carthaginians, faces the circular Comitium and the speakers' platform, the Rostra, at the Forum's northwest corner.

republic-50bce.name: Curia Hostilia / Curia Cornelia
republic-50bce.note: Sulla's enlarged Curia Cornelia burned in 52 BCE when the mob cremated Clodius inside. Faustus Sulla's rebuilding is barely finished before Caesar demolishes it for his Curia Julia, begun 44 BCE.

empire-100ce.note: Augustus's Curia Julia (29 BCE): a tall brick-and-concrete hall faced with marble below and stucco above, bronze doors, the altar and statue of Victory inside, and the Chalcidicum portico beside it.

empire-215ce.note: Unchanged in form, with the Augustan facade. Senators of diminished power gather here while the army makes emperors; decrees still issue from it. A fire in 283 CE will gut it.

late-400ce.name: Curia (Diocletian's rebuilding)
late-400ce.note: Diocletian's rebuilding (c. 303 CE): the surviving hall, about 21 m high, with opus sectile floor and three tiers of seats. The Altar of Victory, removed in 382 CE, caused the last great pagan-Christian dispute.

medieval-1300.name: Sant'Adriano al Foro
medieval-1300.note: Sant'Adriano, consecrated by Honorius I in 630 CE. The Roman hall is intact under a church roof, with an apse added and the bronze doors in place; the ground outside has risen several metres.

renaissance-1560.name: Sant'Adriano al Foro
renaissance-1560.note: Still Sant'Adriano, a parish church of the Campo Vaccino with a campanile. The ancient brick walls are untouched; a Baroque remodelling and the removal of the bronze doors to the Lateran (1660) lie ahead.

landmarks.summary: The Senate House of Rome: the Curia Hostilia of the kings, rebuilt by Sulla, replaced by Caesar's Curia Julia (29 BCE), rebuilt by Diocletian, and preserved as the church of Sant'Adriano.
details: The Curia Hostilia, attributed to King Tullus Hostilius, stood on the north side of the Comitium. Sulla enlarged it (Curia Cornelia) c. 80 BCE; it burned in 52 BCE at Clodius's funeral. Caesar started the Curia Julia on a new alignment in 44 BCE; Augustus dedicated it in 29 BCE. After the fire of 283 CE Diocletian rebuilt it, and that brick hall survives, converted into Sant'Adriano in 630 CE.

The imperial miniature follows the standing building: a plain brick box about 21 m high with a gabled roof, a tall door and three windows over a marble-faced lower facade. The Curia Hostilia is far less certain, resting on excavations under the Comitium and later descriptions, so that model is an interpretation. The church keeps the shell, with a bell tower and a floor raised above the Forum silt.
landmarks.built: Curia Hostilia 7th century BCE (traditional); Curia Julia 44–29 BCE; rebuilt by Diocletian after 283 CE
landmarks.function: Senate house; church from 630 CE

landmarks.name: Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus

kingdom-600bce.name: Temple of Jupiter (under construction)
kingdom-600bce.note: Under construction on a vast podium under Tarquinius Priscus and Superbus; the hill-top is being levelled and the Etruscan sculptor Vulca of Veii will supply the terracotta cult statue. Dedicated 509 BCE.

republic-200bce.note: The archaic temple: timber beams, painted terracotta revetments, Vulca's clay Jupiter, and the Ogulnii's bronze Jupiter in a four-horse chariot (296 BCE) on the roof. Triumphs end on its steps.

republic-50bce.note: Catulus's rebuilding, dedicated 69 BCE after the fire of 83 BCE: the old plan with marble columns Sulla took from the Olympieion at Athens and a gilded ceiling. The Sibylline Books were replaced.

empire-100ce.note: Domitian's temple (after 80 CE): Corinthian columns of Pentelic marble, doors plated with gold, roof tiles of gilded bronze. Plutarch says the gilding alone cost 12,000 talents. The most expensive building in Rome.

empire-215ce.note: Domitian's gleaming temple unchanged, visible from the whole city. Caracalla and his successors still climb the Clivus Capitolinus for the annual vows and triumphs; the Capitoline Games continue.

late-400ce.note: Still standing, still gilded, admired by Ammianus in 357 CE, but closed to sacrifice after 391 CE. Zosimus says Stilicho stripped gold from its doors (c. 408); the Vandals take the gilded tiles in 455.

medieval-1300.note: Gone, quarried away. The southern summit is Monte Caprino, 'goat hill', with houses and vegetable plots; the podium's tufa blocks survive only in cellars and will be found under Palazzo Caffarelli.

landmarks.summary: The great temple on the Capitoline, Rome's chief sanctuary, vowed by the Tarquin kings and dedicated in 509 BCE: the largest Etruscan-style temple in Italy, rebuilt in marble after fires in 83 BCE, 69 CE and 80 CE.
details: Begun by the Tarquin kings and dedicated in 509 BCE, it stood on a podium about 53 by 62 m, still partly visible under Palazzo Caffarelli. Three cellae housed Jupiter, Juno and Minerva behind a deep triple colonnade, under a terracotta roof. It burned in 83 BCE, was rededicated by Catulus in 69 BCE, burned again in 69 and 80 CE, and Domitian rebuilt it in marble with gilded tiles.

The miniature reconstructs the plan from the podium and from coins: a wide low temple with six columns across the front, three deep, and a broad gable. Elevation and decoration are debated; the archaic version with terracotta acroteria and a four-horse chariot on the roof follows Pliny and Livy. The site has been built over since the Middle Ages, so nothing of the superstructure is shown for 1300 or 1560.
landmarks.built: Dedicated 509 BCE; rebuilt 69 BCE, 75 CE (Vespasian) and after 80 CE (Domitian)
landmarks.function: State temple of Jupiter, Juno and Minerva; goal of triumphal processions

landmarks.name: Colosseum

republic-50bce.note: A low valley between the Esquiline, Caelian and Palatine with houses and a stream. After the fire of 64 CE Nero will flood it as the ornamental lake of his Golden House.

empire-100ce.note: Brand new: three tiers of arches, travertine gleaming white, gilded shields on the attic, statues in the arcades. The hypogeum below the arena is finished; Domitian's and Trajan's games draw the city.

empire-215ce.note: Still complete and in full use under Caracalla, who, Dio says, killed beasts in the arena himself. In 217 CE lightning will set the upper timber seating ablaze; repairs continue to 240 CE.

late-400ce.note: Gladiatorial combat is fading (last mentioned c. 435 CE); beast hunts go on. After an earthquake, probably in 443, city prefects repair it, as surviving inscriptions record.

medieval-1300.name: Colosseum (Frangipane fortress)
medieval-1300.note: The Frangipane family holds the shell as a fortress (from the 12th century); houses, workshops and a chapel fill the arcades. The southern outer ring still stands; its fall waits for the earthquake of 1349.

renaissance-1560.name: Colosseum (ruin)
renaissance-1560.note: A roofless ruin, half its outer ring fallen; the city quarries travertine for Palazzo Venezia and St Peter's. Until 1539 the Gonfalone confraternity stages Passion plays inside; the arena is overgrown.

landmarks.summary: The Flavian Amphitheatre, inaugurated in 80 CE with 100 days of games: the largest amphitheatre ever built, seating some 50,000 spectators for gladiatorial combat and beast hunts.
details: Vespasian began it c. 72 CE on the drained lake of Nero's Golden House, probably paid for with Jerusalem's spoils; Titus inaugurated it in 80 CE and Domitian added the top storey and the hypogeum. The travertine ellipse, 189 by 156 m, rose 48 m in three arcaded storeys and an attic. A lightning fire in 217 CE was repaired under Alexander Severus; earthquakes damaged it in the 5th century.

The miniature shows the complete exterior with its 80 arches per storey, statues in the upper arcades and the masts of the velarium awning; the hypogeum is not modelled. The Frangipane fortress of 1300 and the ruined state of 1560, after the southern outer ring collapsed in the earthquake of 1349, are schematic. The arena floor and the Meta Sudans fountain outside are simplified.
landmarks.built: c. 72–80 CE; top storey and hypogeum under Domitian; repaired 217–240s CE
landmarks.function: Amphitheatre for gladiatorial games and beast hunts; later fortress and quarry

landmarks.name: Circus Maximus

kingdom-600bce.note: A flat valley with a stream, where Tarquinius Priscus is said to have marked out the track and given senators and knights wooden stands. Races run around the shrine of Murcia and a few posts.

republic-200bce.note: Still mostly timber: the starting gates of 329 BCE, stone turning posts and the seven bronze egg lap-counters set up by the censors in 174 BCE. Seating burns and is rebuilt repeatedly.

republic-50bce.note: Caesar extends the track and seating, digging a water channel around the arena to protect spectators from wild beasts. Stone seats for senators, wood above; the spina gains its first shrines.

empire-100ce.note: Trajan's rebuilding after the collapse of 103 CE: stone and brick arcaded seating, marble lower tiers, the imperial box on the Palatine side, Augustus's obelisk on the spina. Perhaps 150,000 can watch.

empire-215ce.note: Trajan's stone circus unchanged; it is the city's main entertainment while fire shuts the Colosseum after 217 CE. Crowds roar for the Blues and Greens.

late-400ce.note: Still racing: Constantius II added a second obelisk in 357 CE, the tallest in Rome. Seats are repaired; chariot factions and star drivers draw crowds that Christian bishops deplore. Races continue until 549 CE.

medieval-1300.note: An empty, marshy valley of fields and water mills on the stream; the Frangipane tower (Torre della Moletta) stands near the curved end. Both obelisks lie buried in mud until 1587.

landmarks.summary: Rome's oldest and largest racetrack, in the valley between the Aventine and Palatine: a 600-metre stadium for chariot races that held perhaps 150,000 spectators and was rebuilt by Caesar, Augustus and Trajan.
details: Tradition credits Tarquinius Priscus with the first wooden seats in the Murcia valley. Starting gates came in 329 BCE, the central barrier with turning posts later. Caesar enlarged it; Augustus placed an obelisk on the spina and built the imperial box. After the fire of 64 CE and a collapse in 103 CE Trajan rebuilt the seating in stone and brick, the form seen on the Marble Plan.

The miniature shows Trajan's circus: a track 621 by 118 m with stone seating in three tiers, the curved end with the triumphal arch of Titus (81 CE), the starting gates at the flat end and the spina with obelisk and turning posts. Earlier wooden phases are reconstructions. Only the lower seating foundations survive at the southeast end, so the superstructure follows coins and the Marble Plan.
landmarks.built: Timber seating 6th century BCE (traditional); starting gates 329 BCE; stone rebuilding by Trajan c. 103 CE
landmarks.function: Chariot racing and games; route of triumphs

landmarks.name: Arch of Titus

republic-50bce.note: Open ground on the Velia, the saddle between Palatine and Esquiline, where the Sacred Way crests among aristocratic houses; Cicero's house stood nearby on the Palatine slope.

empire-100ce.note: Less than twenty years old, white Pentelic marble about 15 m high, probably crowned by a bronze group. Travellers coming up the Sacred Way pass beneath the menorah relief.

empire-215ce.note: Unchanged, now framed by Hadrian's Temple of Venus and Roma to the east and the Colosseum below; its inscription looks down the Sacred Way toward the Forum.

late-400ce.note: Still intact on the Via Sacra, among senatorial restorations. The reliefs are weathered; Christians now read the menorah procession as proof of the Temple's fall.

medieval-1300.note: Built into the Frangipane family's fortress on the Velia with the Turris Chartularia nearby; the passage serves as a fortified gate. The inscription stays visible.

renaissance-1560.note: Still sunk in fortifications and houses; the outer piers are gone but the inscription and reliefs show. Artists sketch it; by tradition Rome's Jews refuse to walk beneath it.

landmarks.summary: A single-bay marble arch at the top of the Sacred Way, erected by Domitian c. 82 CE to honour the deified Titus and his capture of Jerusalem in 70 CE, famous for its relief of the menorah carried in triumph.
details: Built after Titus's death in 81 CE on the Velia, at the highest point of the Via Sacra. The attic inscription reads 'The Senate and People of Rome to the deified Titus'. Inside the passage two reliefs show the triumphal procession of 71 CE with the spoils of the Jerusalem Temple, and Titus in his chariot; the vault shows his apotheosis. Pentelic marble, about 15 m high, with Composite capitals.

The miniature shows the arch as rebuilt: Valadier's 1821–23 restoration replaced the lost flanks in travertine and removed the medieval Frangipane additions, so the ancient outer piers are conjectural. The crowning group on the attic, presumably a bronze quadriga, is lost and conjectural. In the medieval model the arch is embedded in the Frangipane fortifications; the real wall buildings are simplified.
landmarks.built: c. 81–85 CE, under Domitian
landmarks.function: Triumphal arch commemorating Titus and the sack of Jerusalem

landmarks.name: Pantheon

republic-50bce.note: Open meadows of the Campus Martius, used for military exercise and voting; Agrippa will drain and build here after 33 BCE, with his baths, the Saepta and the Pantheon.

empire-100ce.name: Pantheon of Agrippa
empire-100ce.note: Agrippa's Pantheon, restored by Domitian after the fire of 80 CE: with caryatids by Diogenes of Athens (Pliny). Its plan and orientation are debated. It will burn again in 110 CE.

empire-215ce.note: Hadrian's rotunda, repaired by Severus and Caracalla in 202 CE (their inscription is on the architrave): gilded bronze roof tiles, bronze doors, the dome lit by the oculus, statues of the gods in the niches.

late-400ce.note: Intact though closed as a temple; its bronze roof and marble veneer survive. Ammianus records Constantius II's wonder at it in 357 CE; in 609 CE the emperor Phocas will give it to the pope.

medieval-1300.name: Santa Maria ad Martyres (the Pantheon)
medieval-1300.note: Santa Maria ad Martyres, consecrated 609 CE; the bronze roof tiles went to Constantinople in 663 CE. The forecourt is buried under houses and a market; a small campanile rises over the porch.

renaissance-1560.name: Santa Maria Rotonda (the Pantheon)
renaissance-1560.note: Santa Maria Rotonda, surrounded by the fish and vegetable market of Piazza della Rotonda. Raphael was buried inside in 1520; Eugenius IV had cleared the porch of stalls. The bronze porch trusses survive until 1625.

landmarks.summary: Hadrian's temple to all the gods (c. 118–128 CE), replacing Agrippa's of 27 BCE: a concrete rotunda whose 43.3 m dome remains the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world, preserved as a church since 609 CE.
details: Agrippa's Pantheon of 27–25 BCE burned in 80 CE and again in 110 CE. Hadrian rebuilt it, keeping Agrippa's name on the frieze: a 16-column granite porch leads through bronze doors into a rotunda 43.3 m wide and high, with a coffered dome and 9 m oculus. Septimius Severus and Caracalla repaired it in 202 CE. Pope Boniface IV consecrated it as Santa Maria ad Martyres in 609 CE.

The miniature shows Hadrian's building with its forecourt and colonnades; the roof is simplified, and the bronze tiles and bronze porch trusses, removed by Constans II in 663 CE and Urban VIII in 1625, are shown intact in antiquity. Agrippa's building for 100 CE is a reconstruction: older studies made it a temple facing south, newer ones a rotunda facing north. The 1560 model omits later bell towers.
landmarks.built: 27–25 BCE (Agrippa); rebuilt c. 118–128 CE (Hadrian); repaired 202 CE
landmarks.function: Temple to all the gods; church of Santa Maria ad Martyres since 609 CE

landmarks.name: Theatre of Marcellus

republic-50bce.note: Caesar has begun clearing houses and the Temple of Pietas in the Forum Holitorium for a theatre to rival Pompey's. Only foundations are in hand at his death in 44 BCE.

empire-100ce.note: Augustus's theatre complete: 41 arches a storey, Doric below and Ionic above, a marble stage front, awnings against the sun. Plays and part of Augustus's Secular Games of 17 BCE were held here.

empire-215ce.note: Vespasian restored its stage and held games for the rededication; Alexander Severus is said to have planned another restoration. Plays and pantomime continue.

late-400ce.note: Listed in the 4th-century regionary catalogues, but decaying: its travertine is reportedly reused for the Pons Cestius rebuilding of 370 CE, and performances have largely ceased.

medieval-1300.name: Theatre of Marcellus (Savelli fortress)
medieval-1300.note: A fortress of the Pierleoni and, from the 13th century, the Savelli: the cavea filled with houses and rubble (the mound of Monte Savello), the arcades walled up.

renaissance-1560.name: Palazzo Savelli (Theatre of Marcellus)
renaissance-1560.note: Palazzo Savelli, built by Baldassare Peruzzi in the 1520s on top of the ancient arcades; the ground-floor arches house shops and the square is Monte Savello. Half-buried arches show the Doric order.

landmarks.summary: One of Rome's three permanent stone theatres, begun by Caesar and dedicated by Augustus in 13 or 11 BCE in memory of his nephew Marcellus; its arcaded outer wall survives as the base of Palazzo Savelli-Orsini.
details: Caesar cleared the site near the Forum Holitorium, demolishing the Temple of Pietas; Augustus completed it and dedicated it in the name of Marcellus, who died in 23 BCE. The cavea, about 111 m across, seated perhaps 11,000–20,000 and rose in three storeys of travertine arcades with Doric and Ionic half-columns. The stage building backed onto the Tiber; the Temples of Apollo Sosianus and Bellona stood beside it.

The miniature reconstructs the full semicircle with its stage building, following the surviving arcades and the Marble Plan. The stage, the upper attic storey and the awning masts are conjectural. For 1300 the model shows the Pierleoni and Savelli fortress on the shell, and for 1560 Baldassare Peruzzi's palazzo (1523–27) rising from the upper tier, with houses crammed in the arcades.
landmarks.built: Begun under Caesar; dedicated 13 or 11 BCE
landmarks.function: Theatre for plays and games; later fortress and palace

landmarks.name: Theatre of Pompey

republic-200bce.note: Open fields of the southern Campus Martius near the Circus Flaminius; temporary wooden theatres are put up and torn down for festivals, since the Senate forbids a permanent one.

republic-50bce.note: Just dedicated (55 BCE) with games that killed hundreds of lions and twenty elephants: a marble cavea topped by the temple of Venus Victrix, and the portico gardens with plane trees and Pompey's statue.

empire-100ce.note: Rebuilt by Tiberius after the fire of 21 CE and by Domitian after 80 CE. The Curia of Pompey, where Caesar fell, was walled up by Augustus; the portico gardens are a fashionable promenade.

empire-215ce.note: Fully in use for plays and pantomime, the largest theatre in the city. The Severan Marble Plan of c. 210 CE records it in detail: the arcaded cavea, the Venus temple and the great portico.

late-400ce.note: Restored by Diocletian after a fire, and again under Arcadius and Honorius (c. 395–402 CE) with an inscription praising its beauty; Theoderic will still repair it in the 6th century.

medieval-1300.note: The cavea's vaults are quarried and inhabited; the Orsini hold a fortress on the ruins and the curve of the seats survives in Via di Grotta Pinta. Campo de' Fiori is a meadow.

landmarks.summary: Rome's first permanent stone theatre, dedicated by Pompey in 55 BCE with a temple of Venus Victrix atop the seating and a vast garden portico behind, where Caesar was assassinated in 44 BCE.
details: Pompey evaded the ban on permanent theatres by presenting the cavea as a stairway to the Temple of Venus Victrix. The semicircle, about 150 m across, seated perhaps 17,000 (Pliny says 40,000). Behind the stage a portico of 180 by 135 m enclosed gardens and the Curia of Pompey, where the Senate met on the Ides of March 44 BCE. Fires in 21 and 80 CE brought rebuildings.

The miniature combines the Marble Plan with the surviving substructures under Via di Grotta Pinta and Campo de' Fiori. The temple on the cavea's crown and the stage building are conjectural, as is the portico's garden layout. The cavea's curve still shapes the streets today, which is what the medieval note describes: houses and palaces (later Palazzo Orsini-Pio) built into the vaults.
landmarks.built: Dedicated 55 BCE; restored after fires of 21 CE and 80 CE; repaired 4th and 6th centuries
landmarks.function: Theatre, temple of Venus Victrix, garden portico and senate meeting place

landmarks.name: Forum of Caesar

republic-50bce.name: Forum of Caesar (under construction)
republic-50bce.note: Under construction: Caesar's agents Cicero and Oppius have bought and demolished a block of houses behind the Curia; the podium of Venus Genetrix rises. Dedicated hastily in 46 BCE with the temple unfinished.

empire-100ce.note: Augustus completed the square: porticoes on three sides, Caesar's bronze equestrian statue (on a horse with toe-like hooves, Suetonius says) and the Venus Genetrix temple with Cleopatra's gilded statue inside.

empire-215ce.note: Trajan's rebuilding (113 CE): a new, taller Venus temple with eight marble columns, double porticoes, the Basilica Argentaria for bankers on the west, and shops; the Severan Marble Plan records this layout.

late-400ce.note: Still intact and used; Diocletian repaired it after the fire of 283 CE together with the Curia. The temple is closed but the square serves as a thoroughfare to the Forum of Trajan.

medieval-1300.note: Buried under metres of debris with houses and gardens on top; the temple columns lie fallen until the excavations of 1932. The Via Alessandrina quarter will be built over it in the 1580s.

landmarks.summary: The first of the Imperial Fora, begun by Caesar in 54 BCE and dedicated in 46 BCE: a colonnaded square beside the Roman Forum dominated by the Temple of Venus Genetrix, ancestress of the Julian family.
details: Caesar paid 60 million sesterces for the land by 54 BCE (Cicero), 100 million in all (Suetonius). The piazza, about 75 by 160 m, had porticoes on three sides and the Temple of Venus Genetrix at its northwest end, dedicated in 46 BCE after Pharsalus. Augustus completed it. Trajan rebuilt the temple and added the Basilica Argentaria after cutting back the Capitoline saddle; it was rededicated in 113 CE.

The miniature shows the Trajanic form that survives today: the temple front on its high podium, the double porticoes and the paved square. For 50 BCE it shows the site under construction, with houses cleared and the podium rising; the equestrian statue of Caesar in front is restored from the sources. The tabernae and the Basilica Argentaria are simplified.
landmarks.built: 54–46 BCE; completed by Augustus; rebuilt by Trajan, rededicated 113 CE
landmarks.function: Civic square and law courts; temple of Venus Genetrix

landmarks.name: Forum of Augustus

republic-50bce.note: A crowded residential block on the lower slopes toward the Subura, with the Argiletum running past. Augustus will buy up house after house here, paying with the spoils of war.

empire-100ce.note: Complete and gleaming: Mars Ultor in white Carrara marble with the recovered Parthian standards inside, coloured marble paving, statue galleries, the Hall of the Colossus. Here the Senate debates war and governors take leave.

empire-215ce.note: Unchanged in form; the Severan Marble Plan records it. Hadrian had restored it, and the square connects to the Forum of Nerva and Trajan's complex through gates in the firewall.

late-400ce.note: Standing but little used after the temples closed in 391 CE; the porticoes and statues are maintained by the prefects. Serious quarrying begins only in the 6th century.

medieval-1300.note: Three columns of Mars Ultor rise above gardens; the Knights of St John hold a priory on the portico. Houses cover the rest; the firewall gate is the Arco dei Pantani.

landmarks.summary: Augustus's forum, dedicated in 2 BCE on land bought from private owners: a colonnaded square with the Temple of Mars Ultor, avenger of Caesar, galleries of statues of Rome's heroes, and a 33 m firewall behind.
details: Vowed at Philippi in 42 BCE, dedicated in 2 BCE. The temple of Mars Ultor, eight Corinthian columns across and 17.7 m high, held the standards recovered from Parthia. Two porticoes with exedrae were lined with statues of the summi viri, and of Aeneas and Romulus. The peperino firewall at the back, up to 33 m high, still stands; Augustus never completed the land purchase, so the plan is skewed.

The miniature shows the temple on its high podium against the firewall, the porticoes with attic caryatids and the two semicircular exedrae. The Hall of the Colossus and the full statue programme are simplified. The ancient street level is restored from excavations; the Via Alessandrina quarter that later covered the square (and was demolished in 1932) is not shown.
landmarks.built: Vowed 42 BCE; dedicated 2 BCE
landmarks.function: Civic square, law courts and military ceremonies; temple of Mars Ultor

landmarks.name: Forum of Trajan

republic-50bce.note: A saddle of ground joins the Capitoline to the Quirinal here, covered in houses and streets; the Clivus Argentarius runs along the Capitoline foot. Trajan's engineers will cut this hill away.

empire-100ce.name: Forum of Trajan (under construction)
empire-100ce.note: Shown a few years early: Domitian may have begun clearing, but the main works follow the Dacian War of 106 CE, when Apollodorus's crews cut back the Quirinal. Dedication 112 CE.

empire-215ce.note: Complete and dazzling: Trajan's ashes rest in the Column's base, Hadrian's Temple of Divine Trajan stands north of it, the Basilica Ulpia's gilded roof shines. Marcus Aurelius auctioned palace treasures here in 169 CE.

late-400ce.note: Ammianus describes Constantius II's awe before it in 357 CE: a construction unique under heaven. Statues of senators, generals and poets still accumulate in its porticoes and basilica.

medieval-1300.name: Trajan's Column
medieval-1300.note: The Column stands alone amid ruins, with the small church of San Nicola de Columna against its base; houses and gardens cover the Basilica. A Senate decree of 1162 forbids anyone to damage it.

renaissance-1560.name: Trajan's Column
renaissance-1560.note: The Column rises from a hollow of ruins among houses; Paul III cleared its base and the church in 1536 for Charles V's entry. In 1587 Sixtus V will set St Peter's statue on top.

landmarks.summary: The last and grandest of the Imperial Fora, dedicated in 112 CE: a 300-metre complex of piazza, Basilica Ulpia, libraries and Trajan's Column, cut into the Quirinal slope by the architect Apollodorus of Damascus.
details: Dacian booty paid. Builders removed a saddle of the Quirinal as high as the column, about 35 m with its base, as its inscription says. The piazza, flanked by exedrae, led to the Basilica Ulpia with its gilded bronze roof, then the Column (dedicated 113 CE) flanked by Greek and Latin libraries, and later the temple of Divine Trajan. Trajan's Markets rise in brick tiers on the hillside behind.

The miniature follows the excavated plan; the 1998–2000 digs overturned older reconstructions of the south entrance, which remains debated, as does the place of Trajan's equestrian statue. The Column is shown with its spiral relief, perhaps once painted, and the bronze statue of Trajan on top (replaced by St Peter in 1587). For 100 CE the model shows the site being cut back and the first foundations.
landmarks.built: c. 106–112 CE; Column dedicated 113 CE; Temple of Divine Trajan c. 125–138 CE
landmarks.function: Civic square, law courts, libraries, imperial commemoration

landmarks.name: Imperial Palace (Domus Flavia and Domus Augustana)

republic-50bce.note: The Palatine is the best address in Rome: houses of Cicero, Clodius, Hortensius and Catulus stand here among old shrines. Octavian buys Hortensius's house in the 40s BCE as his own.

empire-100ce.note: Domitian's new palace, finished c. 92 CE: a marble-lined audience hall, a dining room flanked by fountain courts, the private wing stepping down toward the Circus Maximus, and the garden stadium. Trajan rules from here.

empire-215ce.note: Enlarged by Septimius Severus: a new wing on arched substructures projects over the Circus end, and the Septizodium, a three-storey fountain facade, greets travellers from the Appian Way. Elagabalus will add his sun temple.

late-400ce.note: Emperors rule from Milan, Trier or Ravenna, but prefects maintain the palace for rare visits, such as Constantius II's in 357 CE and Honorius's triumph of 404 CE. Still called the Palatium, root of 'palace'.

medieval-1300.note: Ruined vaults and gardens; the Frangipane fortify the northeast corner, and the church of San Sebastiano al Palatino occupies the temple terrace above the Flavian halls. Vineyards cover the Domus Augustana.

renaissance-1560.name: Orti Farnesiani (Farnese Gardens)
renaissance-1560.note: Cardinal Alessandro Farnese has begun the Orti Farnesiani (1550s) over the Domus Tiberiana; the terraces and aviaries come later. The Flavian halls are vineyards dug for statues.

landmarks.summary: Domitian's palace on the Palatine (c. 81–92 CE, architect Rabirius): the official Domus Flavia with audience hall and banqueting room, the private Domus Augustana and the sunken garden 'stadium', seat of emperors for three centuries.
details: Augustus lived modestly beside the Temple of Apollo; Tiberius and Nero built larger houses. Domitian levelled the hilltop and built a palace in three parts: the Domus Flavia (Aula Regia, basilica, peristyle, triclinium), the two-storey Domus Augustana around a sunken court, and a garden 160 m long shaped like a stadium. Septimius Severus extended it southward on huge arches with the Septizodium facade facing the Appian Way.

The miniature shows the Flavian plan as excavated, with roofs restored over the great halls; heights, the Aula Regia's vault or timber roof, and the facades are all debated. The Severan extension and Septizodium are included for 215 and 400 CE in simplified form. For 1560 the model shows the Farnese Gardens laid out by Vignola over the Domus Tiberiana, with the Flavian ruins as vineyards.
landmarks.built: c. 81–92 CE under Domitian; extended by Septimius Severus c. 200 CE
landmarks.function: Imperial residence and seat of government

landmarks.name: Baths of Caracalla

empire-100ce.note: A suburban quarter of houses, gardens and tombs along the first stretch of the Appian Way outside the Porta Capena; houses of Hadrian's day, later found under the baths, stand here.

empire-215ce.note: Almost finished: Caracalla will open the central block in 216 CE. Thousands of workers lay the vaults; the Aqua Antoniniana aqueduct arrives on a new arcade; the outer enclosure is still bare ground.

late-400ce.note: In use, restored by Aurelian and later emperors; one of the eleven great baths of the regionary catalogues. The Farnese Hercules probably stands in one of its halls. Cutting the aqueduct in 537 ends bathing.

medieval-1300.name: Ruins of the Baths of Caracalla
medieval-1300.note: Roofless since the 6th century, the vaults still largely standing; vineyards inside the enclosure and lime kilns at the edges. Pilgrims to San Sebastiano on the Appian Way pass its hulk.

renaissance-1560.name: Ruins of the Baths of Caracalla
renaissance-1560.note: Pope Paul III's Farnese excavations (from 1545) have pulled the Farnese Hercules, Bull and Flora from the rubble; the walls stand as a vast ruin among vines, drawn by Palladio and du Pérac.

landmarks.summary: The Antonine Baths, built 212–216 CE: a vast bathing complex on the edge of the Aventine whose concrete halls, inside an enclosure 337 by 328 m, remain among the best-preserved imperial ruins in Rome.
details: Begun in 212 CE and inaugurated by Caracalla in 216 CE; the enclosure with libraries, gardens and stadium was finished under Elagabalus and Alexander Severus. The central block, 214 by 110 m, held a frigidarium 58 by 24 m under three cross vaults and a domed caldarium 35 m across. Some 1,600 could bathe at once, supplied by a branch of the Aqua Marcia, the Aqua Antoniniana.

The miniature shows the full enclosure with the central block as reconstructed from the standing walls, vaults restored; the marble veneer, mosaics and the Farnese sculptures (Hercules, Bull) are not represented. The hidden service levels and mills under the floors are omitted. For 1300 and 1560 the model shows the roofless block, stripped by lime burners and, from 1545, by the Farnese excavators.
landmarks.built: 212–216 CE; enclosure completed by c. 235 CE
landmarks.function: Public baths, libraries and gardens

landmarks.name: Baths of Diocletian

empire-215ce.note: A crowded quarter on the Viminal slopes near the Vicus Patricius, with houses, workshops and a few mansions; Diocletian will clear it all in 298 CE for the largest baths in the empire.

late-400ce.note: Newly complete, the biggest baths in the empire: marble halls, the cross-vaulted frigidarium with granite columns about 14 m high, the open pool, gardens and libraries, taking about 3,000 bathers. The Aqua Marcia feeds it.

medieval-1300.name: Ruins of the Baths of Diocletian
medieval-1300.note: The vast roofless shell stands in vineyards and fields on the edge of the inhabited city; the aqueducts have been cut since 537 CE. Lime burners work the marble; vaults shelter shepherds and their flocks.

renaissance-1560.name: Santa Maria degli Angeli (Baths of Diocletian)
renaissance-1560.note: Soon Pius IV will grant it to the Carthusians (1561) and Michelangelo will design Santa Maria degli Angeli (from 1563) inside the frigidarium, its vaults becoming the church. Villas and vineyards surround.

landmarks.summary: The largest baths of Rome, built 298–306 CE on the Viminal for perhaps 3,000 bathers; its cold hall became the church of Santa Maria degli Angeli to Michelangelo's design, from 1563.
details: Begun by Maximian in Diocletian's name in 298 and dedicated after their abdication in 305–306, the complex covered 13 hectares: an enclosure about 380 by 370 m with exedrae and libraries, and a central block on the Caracalla model with a frigidarium 90 m long under three cross vaults, a domed caldarium and a huge open pool (natatio). The bathing halls were lined with marble and granite columns.

The miniature reconstructs the whole enclosure from Marble Plan fragments, Palladio's drawings and the surviving halls (the church, the Aula Ottagona, the exedra of Piazza della Repubblica). For 1300 the vaulted shell stands roofless in open country; for 1560 the model anticipates Michelangelo's conversion of the frigidarium (begun 1563, finished after his death in 1564) and the Carthusian monastery.
landmarks.built: 298–306 CE; church of Santa Maria degli Angeli from 1561
landmarks.function: Public baths; church and monastery from the 16th century

landmarks.name: Baths of Trajan

republic-50bce.note: Houses and gardens on the Oppian spur of the Esquiline, above the Subura; part of the old Esquiline burial ground lies to the east. Nero's Golden House will cover the slope after 64 CE.

empire-100ce.name: Baths of Trajan (under construction)
empire-100ce.note: Shown a few years early: after a fire in 104 CE the Esquiline wing of Nero's Golden House will be filled with rubble as foundations. The baths open in 109 CE.

empire-215ce.note: In use for a century: the grand frigidarium, the sunlit caldarium facing southwest, gardens and exedrae for lecturing, the smaller Baths of Titus next door. The Marble Plan of this period records its layout.

late-400ce.note: Still functioning and listed in the 4th-century regionary catalogues, fed by the Sette Sale cistern. Decline comes with the cutting of the aqueducts in 537 CE.

medieval-1300.note: Ruined vaults and exedrae stand in vineyards and orchards on the Oppian hill; locals call them the Baths of Titus, a confusion lasting into the 19th century. San Pietro in Vincoli sits at the edge.

landmarks.summary: The first of the great imperial bath complexes, opened in 109 CE on the Oppian Hill over the buried wing of Nero's Golden House, probably designed by Apollodorus of Damascus and the model for later imperial baths.
details: Trajan built the baths on a platform about 330 by 340 m over Nero's Domus Aurea, which was filled in to serve as foundation after the fire of 104 CE damaged the hill. Dedicated 22 June 109 CE. The central block with its huge frigidarium, cross-vaulted halls and southwest-facing caldarium was surrounded by a garden enclosure with exedrae, libraries and lecture rooms, and fed by the Sette Sale cistern.

Only fragments stand in the Parco di Colle Oppio, so the miniature follows the Marble Plan, Palladio's 16th-century drawings and comparison with Caracalla's baths. Hall heights are reconstructed. The 100 CE model shows the Golden House being filled in and the platform under construction. In the medieval note the hill is vineyards; the surviving exedrae were long attributed to Titus.
landmarks.built: c. 104–109 CE; dedicated 22 June 109 CE
landmarks.function: Public baths with gardens, libraries and meeting halls

landmarks.name: Mausoleum of Augustus

republic-50bce.note: Open ground of the northern Campus Martius between the Via Flaminia and the river bend, used for burials and exercise; Octavian will choose it for his tomb in 28 BCE.

empire-100ce.note: Full of imperial ashes, sealed after Nerva's burial in 98 CE; the cypress-planted mound rises above the Ara Pacis and Augustus's sundial, among groves open to the public.

empire-215ce.note: Unchanged, a landmark of the Campus Martius; emperors are now buried in Hadrian's tomb across the river. The groves and the Ustrinum, the cremation enclosure, are still visible beside it.

late-400ce.note: Still standing, obelisks in place; the bronze Res Gestae tablets and crowning statue will be lost at an unknown date, perhaps in the sack of 410 CE. The groves have given way to building.

medieval-1300.name: Mausoleum of Augustus (Colonna fortress)
medieval-1300.note: The Colonna fortified it in the 12th century; after Rome's defeat by Tusculum in 1167 they were banished and the fortress dismantled. The obelisks lie broken and buried; the quarter is called the Augusta.

renaissance-1560.name: Mausoleum of Augustus (Soderini garden)
renaissance-1560.note: The Soderini family, owners from the mid-16th century, have made the drum a hanging garden with statues in the niches. The obelisks lie nearby, broken, until their re-erection in 1587 and 1786.

landmarks.summary: The dynastic tomb Augustus built in 28 BCE in the Campus Martius: a round earth-topped mound about 90 m across, planted with cypresses, that held the ashes of Augustus, his family, several Julio-Claudian emperors and Nerva.
details: Built on his return from Egypt, before the title Augustus: concentric concrete walls faced in travertine, 87–90 m in diameter, with a tumulus of earth and cypress trees above and a bronze statue of Augustus on top. Two obelisks flanked the entrance, with the bronze Res Gestae tablets. It held Marcellus (23 BCE), Agrippa, Drusus, Augustus himself in 14 CE, Livia, Tiberius, Claudius and Nerva, the last in 98 CE.

The miniature follows the usual reconstruction: a stepped drum with tree-planted terraces and a crowning statue; the number of terraces and the top are debated, and some restore a tall central tower. The Colonna fortress of 1300 and the 16th-century garden of the Soderini (hanging gardens with statues) are shown schematically. The obelisks now stand at Santa Maria Maggiore and the Quirinal.
landmarks.built: 28 BCE
landmarks.function: Imperial tomb; later fortress, garden, bullring and concert hall

landmarks.name: Mausoleum of Hadrian

empire-100ce.note: The Gardens of Domitia on the right bank, with fields and tombs along the Via Cornelia. Hadrian will take the gardens for his tomb, begun c. 123 CE, and the Pons Aelius to reach it.

empire-215ce.note: Complete: the marble-clad drum topped by a garden and a gilded quadriga, approached over the Pons Aelius (134 CE) lined with statues. Septimius Severus's ashes lie inside; Caracalla's will be the last.

late-400ce.name: Mausoleum of Hadrian (fortified)
late-400ce.note: Since 401 CE a bastion of Honorius's wall: battlements on the drum, the bridge gate fortified, statues still standing. The tomb's bronze doors and marble remain; imperial burials have ceased.

medieval-1300.name: Castel Sant'Angelo
medieval-1300.note: Castel Sant'Angelo, named for Gregory the Great's vision of 590 CE, with a chapel of St Michael on top. Held by the Crescentii, then Orsini; Nicholas III's Passetto (1277) now links it to the Vatican.

renaissance-1560.name: Castel Sant'Angelo
renaissance-1560.note: The papal fortress: Renaissance bastions, Paul III's frescoed apartments, Raffaello da Montelupo's marble angel (1544) on top. Clement VII sheltered here in the Sack of 1527; Cellini claims he manned its guns.

landmarks.summary: Hadrian's tomb across the Tiber, finished by Antoninus Pius in 139 CE and reached by the Pons Aelius: a 64 m drum on a square base, later Rome's river citadel, papal fortress and prison, Castel Sant'Angelo.
details: Begun c. 123 CE, completed 139 CE: a square base 89 m a side, a drum 64 m across faced in travertine and marble, an earth mound with cypresses, and a quadriga on top. The emperors from Hadrian to Caracalla were buried here. In 401 CE Honorius made it a bastion of the city wall; it withstood the Goths in 537 CE, when defenders hurled statues down on them.

The miniature shows the standard reconstruction of the tomb (mound and crowning quadriga are debated), then the fortified mausoleum of c. 400 with the bridge, the medieval castle with its angel chapel, and the Renaissance castle: bastions of Alexander VI and his successors, the Passetto to the Vatican, and the papal apartments of Paul III. The angel statue on top is simplified.
landmarks.built: c. 123–139 CE; fortified 401 CE; papal castle rebuilt 14th–16th centuries
landmarks.function: Imperial tomb; later fortress, papal refuge and prison

landmarks.name: Ara Pacis Augustae

republic-50bce.note: Flat meadow beside the Via Flaminia in the northern Campus Martius, outside the city proper and prone to Tiber floods; the voting pens and exercise grounds lie further south.

empire-100ce.note: Dedicated 9 BCE beside the Via Flaminia, with the Mausoleum to the north and Augustus's obelisk sundial (10 BCE) nearby; a debated theory has its shadow touch the altar on his birthday.

empire-215ce.note: Still standing, though the yearly sacrifice may have lapsed. A brick wall was built round it in the 2nd century to hold back floods and rising ground; the Campus is built up.

late-400ce.note: Sinking into Tiber silt behind its protective wall, the reliefs still visible but sacrifices ended by law in 391 CE. The altar will lie under 4 m of mud by the Middle Ages.

medieval-1300.note: Buried under silt beneath houses of the Campo Marzio near the Via Lata. The first fragments will reappear in 1568 under Palazzo Peretti (later Fiano) and go to the Medici and other collections.

landmarks.summary: The Altar of Augustan Peace, voted in 13 BCE and dedicated 30 January 9 BCE in the Campus Martius: a marble enclosure carved with the imperial procession and allegories of peace, the masterpiece of Augustan sculpture.
details: The Senate voted it when Augustus returned from Spain and Gaul in 13 BCE; it was dedicated on Livia's birthday, 9 BCE. A marble screen 11.6 by 10.6 m encloses the altar on a podium; outside, friezes show the procession of the imperial family, priests and senators, panels with Aeneas, Romulus, Roma and a peaceful goddess, and acanthus scrolls below. It stood beside the Via Flaminia, near Augustus's sundial obelisk.

The miniature shows the altar at its original site, a few hundred metres south-east of the present museum, under Palazzo Fiano by the Via Flaminia, where fragments were found in 1568 and 1859 and excavated under Palazzo Fiano in 1903 and 1937–38. The painted colours of the reliefs are not shown. In antiquity Tiber floods and rising ground slowly buried it; by 400 CE it may already have been half-sunk.
landmarks.built: Voted 13 BCE; dedicated 30 January 9 BCE
landmarks.function: State altar for annual sacrifices to Pax Augusta

landmarks.name: Stadium of Domitian

republic-50bce.note: Open fields of the central Campus Martius, where temporary wooden stadia for Greek athletics were raised by Caesar in 46 BCE and will be again by Augustus in 28 BCE.

empire-100ce.note: Newly built with travertine arcades and statues, seating perhaps 20,000–30,000; Greek athletes compete every four years in Domitian's Capitoline Games, with music in the Odeon next door.

empire-215ce.note: Still staging foot races, boxing and wrestling; after the Colosseum fire of 217 CE gladiators fight here too. Alexander Severus repairs it. St Agnes's legend places her martyrdom in a brothel under its arches.

late-400ce.note: Listed in the regionary catalogues (one gives 30,088 places); athletics are dying out with the end of pagan festivals. Christians venerate the spot of Agnes's martyrdom (c. 304 CE) in the arcades.

medieval-1300.name: Piazza in Agone (Stadium of Domitian)
medieval-1300.note: The arena is the Campus Agonis, an open space in the inhabited Campo Marzio with the small church of Sant'Agnese in Agone built over the arcades. Houses and towers rise on the cavea.

renaissance-1560.name: Piazza Navona
renaissance-1560.note: Piazza Navona: the city's main market since 1477, surrounded by houses and small palaces and the Spanish church of San Giacomo. The medieval Sant'Agnese still stands; Bernini's fountain and Borromini's church are a century off.

landmarks.summary: A stadium for Greek-style athletics, built by Domitian c. 86 CE in the Campus Martius for his Capitoline Games; its 275 m track survives as the shape of Piazza Navona.
details: Domitian built it in brick-faced concrete and travertine for the Capitoline Games of 86 CE, the first permanent athletics stadium in Rome. The track, about 275 by 106 m, had a curved north end and seating for around 30,000 in two storeys of arcades. It served foot races, boxing and wrestling, and gladiators when the Colosseum burned (217 CE). The cult of St Agnes placed her martyrdom in its arcades.

The miniature reconstructs the arcaded exterior from the surviving travertine piers under Piazza di Tor Sanguigna and Sant'Agnese, by analogy with the Colosseum; the attic is conjectural. For 1300 it shows the arena as the open Campus Agonis with houses built into the cavea; for 1560 Piazza Navona with the market and palazzi, before Bernini's fountain of 1651.
landmarks.built: c. 86 CE
landmarks.function: Athletics stadium; later market square (Piazza Navona)

landmarks.name: Temple of Portunus

kingdom-600bce.note: The river landing of early Rome, with huts and a ferry; an archaic shrine or altar of Portunus may already stand here, though no trace is known. The Forum Boarium cattle market begins nearby.

republic-200bce.note: An earlier temple on a tufa podium, probably Italic in style with a wooden roof and terracotta decoration, facing the busy river port where grain and salt are unloaded. Its form is a guess.

republic-50bce.note: The present temple, rebuilt c. 120–80 BCE: Ionic, with travertine for the free-standing columns and stuccoed tufa elsewhere, a frieze of garlands and candelabra. Harbour traffic unloads below it.

empire-100ce.note: Unchanged; the river port has moved mostly downstream to the Emporium, but the Forum Boarium bustles. The nearby round Temple of Hercules, the Ara Maxima and the Pons Aemilius frame it.

empire-215ce.note: Still standing and in use; the Severan Marble Plan records the Forum Boarium around it, and the Arch of the Argentarii (204 CE) is new beside the Velabrum.

late-400ce.note: The temple survives among the warehouses and markets of the Forum Boarium; the four-way Arch of Janus (4th century) stands near. Christian use is not yet attested, but its small size will save it.

medieval-1300.name: Santa Maria Egiziaca (Temple of Portunus)
medieval-1300.note: The church of Santa Maria de Secundicerio (consecrated 872 CE), later renamed Santa Maria Egiziaca: columns walled in, a bell-cote, 9th-century frescoes inside. Across the lane stands the Casa dei Crescenzi.

renaissance-1560.name: Santa Maria Egiziaca (Temple of Portunus)
renaissance-1560.note: Santa Maria Egiziaca, a small parish church; the temple's Ionic order is admired and drawn by Palladio. In 1571 Pius V will give it to the Armenian community, who keep it until 1921.

landmarks.summary: A small Ionic temple of the late 2nd or early 1st century BCE beside the river harbour, dedicated to Portunus, god of harbours and doors, perfectly preserved as the church of Santa Maria Egiziaca.
details: A temple stood here by the 3rd century BCE (dedicated 17 August, the Portunalia); the present building, in travertine and tufa coated with stucco, dates to c. 120–80 BCE. It is pseudoperipteral: a porch four Ionic columns wide and two deep, with half-columns engaged in the cella walls, on a podium about 11 by 19 m. It overlooked the Portus Tiberinus, the old river port of the Forum Boarium.

The miniature shows the temple as it stands, with stucco restored to a white finish and a terracotta-tiled roof. The Republican version for 200 BCE is a guess, modelled on the earlier podium found beneath. From 872 CE it was a church, with the colonnade walled up, a bell-cote and frescoes inside, which the model shows for 1300 and 1560.
landmarks.built: c. 120–80 BCE on an earlier 3rd-century BCE podium; church from 872 CE
landmarks.function: Temple of the harbour god Portunus; church

landmarks.name: Temple of Hercules Victor

republic-200bce.note: Open ground of the Forum Boarium between the river port and the Ara Maxima of Hercules, where cattle dealers and oil merchants trade; the Greek-style round temple is a few decades off.

republic-50bce.note: Some decades old, in Pentelic marble from Athens: 20 Corinthian columns round a circular cella. The pure Greek style is a showpiece amid Rome's tufa and stucco.

empire-100ce.note: Restored by Tiberius in 15 CE after flood damage: several columns and capitals replaced in Luna marble. Oil merchants trade nearby, and the Ara Maxima's feast of Hercules passes it on 12 August.

empire-215ce.note: Unchanged, one of the Forum Boarium's two surviving temples beside Portunus; the new Arch of the Argentarii (204 CE) honours the Severan family at the entrance to the Velabrum.

late-400ce.note: Still standing; its small size and solid marble will carry it through the Middle Ages intact. The cattle market and river port continue; the 4th-century Arch of Janus stands uphill.

medieval-1300.name: Santo Stefano alle Carrozze (Temple of Hercules)
medieval-1300.note: Santo Stefano alle Carrozze, a church since 1132, its columns walled in and an altar inside; antiquarians call it the Temple of Vesta. The origin of the name is unclear.

renaissance-1560.name: Santo Stefano alle Carrozze (Temple of Hercules)
renaissance-1560.note: Still Santo Stefano alle Carrozze; the original entablature is already lost and the low tiled roof sits straight on the capitals. In the 17th century it is rededicated to Santa Maria del Sole.

landmarks.summary: The round marble temple in the Forum Boarium, c. 120 BCE, the oldest surviving marble building in Rome: twenty Corinthian columns of Pentelic marble around a cella, probably dedicated to Hercules Victor, perhaps the 'Olivarius' of the oil merchants.
details: Perhaps the Temple of Hercules Victor that Marcus Octavius Herrenus, a merchant, dedicated in the late 2nd century BCE; a Greek architect (perhaps Hermodorus of Salamis) built it in Pentelic marble, its 20 columns 10.6 m high on a stepped base 14.8 m across. Tiberius restored it in 15 CE after Tiber floods, replacing some columns in Luna marble. It was long called the Temple of Vesta.

The miniature shows the temple with its original tall entablature and conical tiled roof restored; the present roof is a later low tiled cone. The attribution to Hercules Olivarius rests on an inscription found nearby and remains uncertain, as does the identity of its donor. For 1300 and 1560 it appears as Santo Stefano alle Carrozze, with the spaces between the columns walled.
landmarks.built: c. 120 BCE; restored 15 CE
landmarks.function: Temple of Hercules (probably Hercules Olivarius)

landmarks.name: Temple of Aesculapius (Tiber Island)

kingdom-600bce.note: A low willow-grown island in the river, reachable by ford or boat; legend says it formed from the grain of the expelled Tarquins thrown into the Tiber in 509 BCE. No buildings yet.

republic-200bce.note: The temple of Aesculapius (289 BCE) stands at the south end with a portico and spring; sick pilgrims sleep in the precinct for healing dreams. Shrines of Faunus (194 BCE) and Jupiter share the island.

republic-50bce.note: The island is probably being faced as a ship, with a travertine prow (the obelisk 'mast' may be later); the Pons Fabricius (62 BCE) and soon the Pons Cestius link it to both banks.

empire-100ce.note: Busy with the sick; Claudius ruled that sick slaves abandoned here are free if they recover. The temple of Aesculapius with its spring, the portico lodgings and the Faunus temple fill the island.

empire-215ce.note: Unchanged: a healing sanctuary with dream incubation and a famous spring, inscriptions recording cures, the two stone bridges busy with traffic from the Trastevere market gardens.

late-400ce.note: The pagan cult ends after 391 CE, the buildings still standing; the island keeps its sick and its spring. Nothing certain is known of its 5th-century fate; silt covers the pavements.

medieval-1300.name: San Bartolomeo all'Isola
medieval-1300.note: San Bartolomeo, built c. 1000 CE by Otto III over the temple for the relics of St Bartholomew and St Adalbert; a well in the chancel marks the old spring. Mills turn in the river.

renaissance-1560.name: San Bartolomeo all'Isola
