renaissance-1560.note: San Bartolomeo with its 12th-century campanile, damaged by the flood of 1557; the Fatebenefratelli hospital of St John of God will open on the north side in 1585. The travertine prow is half-buried.

landmarks.summary: Temple of Aesculapius, founded 291 BCE after a plague, when the god's sacred snake was brought from Epidaurus; the island was later shaped like a ship, and its healing role lives on in San Bartolomeo and the Fatebenefratelli hospital.
details: Livy and Ovid say the snake swam ashore here in 291 BCE; the temple, dedicated in 289 BCE, probably lay at the downstream end under San Bartolomeo. In the 1st century BCE the island's tip was faced in travertine as a ship's prow and stern and later an obelisk as mast; the carved prow with Aesculapius's staff survives. Sick slaves were abandoned there, and Claudius freed those who recovered.

The miniature shows the temple on its platform at the downstream end, flanked by the ship-shaped embankments and the two bridges; the temple's elevation is a reconstruction, nothing standing. Other island shrines (Faunus, Jupiter Jurarius, Tiberinus) are omitted. For 1300 and 1560 the model shows Otto III's church of San Bartolomeo (c. 1000 CE), rebuilt after floods, with its Romanesque campanile.
landmarks.built: Temple 291–289 BCE; travertine 'ship' 1st century BCE; San Bartolomeo c. 1000 CE
landmarks.function: Healing sanctuary; church and hospital island

landmarks.name: Pons Fabricius

republic-200bce.note: A wooden bridge probably crossed here to the island, serving the temple of Aesculapius after 289 BCE; nothing certain is known of it. The bank is lined with the Forum Holitorium vegetable market.

republic-50bce.note: Brand new (62 BCE): two travertine-faced arches with a small relief arch over the pier; Fabricius's name cut four times. In 21 BCE the consuls will inspect it after a great flood.

empire-100ce.note: In daily use, leading from the Theatre of Marcellus quarter across to the healing island. Travertine still bright, the parapets simple. Fishermen and pilgrims to Aesculapius cross all day.

empire-215ce.note: Unchanged, the oldest intact bridge in the city; crowds cross to the island sanctuary, and from it over the Pons Cestius to Trastevere. The Marble Plan shows it with the island as a ship.

late-400ce.note: Still sound while the neighbouring Pons Cestius was entirely rebuilt in 370 CE. Traffic to the island continues; nothing of the ancient fabric has changed.

medieval-1300.name: Ponte dei Quattro Capi (Pons Fabricius)
medieval-1300.note: Called Pons Judaeorum, the Jews' bridge, for the Jewish quarter on the near bank, and later Ponte dei Quattro Capi for the four-faced herms on its parapet. Mills and fishing boats moor beneath its arches.

renaissance-1560.name: Ponte dei Quattro Capi (Pons Fabricius)
renaissance-1560.note: Ponte dei Quattro Capi, the daily link between the fish market at Sant'Angelo in Pescheria, the new Ghetto (1555) and the island. Still wholly ancient; Innocent XI's brick refacing comes in 1679.

landmarks.summary: The oldest Roman bridge still in use, built in 62 BCE by Lucius Fabricius, curator of roads, linking the Campus Martius to Tiber Island with two 24.5 m arches, as its inscription proudly repeats four times.
details: Built in 62 BCE of tufa and peperino faced with travertine, 62 m long and 5.5 m wide, with two arches and a small flood arch over the pier. Inscriptions on both faces read 'L. Fabricius, curator of roads, saw to its making'; another records the consuls of 21 BCE approving it after a flood. Two four-headed herms on the parapet give the name Ponte dei Quattro Capi.

The miniature shows the bridge essentially as it stands: the brick facing seen today came in 1679 under Innocent XI, so the ancient travertine finish is restored. The approach from the Campus Martius ran past the Theatre of Marcellus; medieval houses on the bank are simplified. The four-faced herms that give the medieval name probably came from the nearby church of San Gregorio, at a disputed date.
landmarks.built: 62 BCE; repaired 21 BCE; brick refacing 1679
landmarks.function: Bridge between the Campus Martius and Tiber Island

landmarks.name: Pons Aemilius

kingdom-600bce.note: No stone bridge yet. The Pons Sublicius, the city's only bridge, a wooden span on piles usually placed a little downstream, is the one Horatius Cocles famously defended. The cattle market's ford lies nearby.

republic-200bce.note: The stone piers of 179 BCE carry a timber roadway; the stone arches of 142 BCE are the next step. Carts from the Forum Boarium and the salt road to Etruria cross here.

republic-50bce.note: A complete six-arch stone bridge, Rome's first, linking the Forum Boarium to Trastevere and the Via Aurelia, with heavy traffic of grain and produce; the Pons Sublicius still stands nearby for ritual.

empire-100ce.note: Probably restored under Augustus with travertine facing; the bridge is the main crossing for the Forum Boarium markets and the road toward the coast. The Emporium quays lie downstream.

empire-215ce.note: Unchanged; the Marble Plan records it as the Pons Aemilius with the Forum Boarium markets at its head. Barges unload on both banks beneath its arches.

late-400ce.note: Still intact; the regionary catalogues count it among the city's eight bridges. The Tiber's floods wear the piers; Trastevere's mills and the cattle market still depend on it.

medieval-1300.name: Ponte Santa Maria (Pons Aemilius)
medieval-1300.note: Called Pons Senatorum or Ponte Santa Maria, it collapsed in the flood of 1230 and was rebuilt under Gregory IX; it carries pilgrims from Trastevere toward the Forum Boarium and the Velabrum.

renaissance-1560.name: Ponte Santa Maria (Pons Aemilius)
renaissance-1560.note: Ponte Santa Maria, battered by the flood of 1557 and half-ruined; Gregory XIII will rebuild it in 1575 (Michelangelo had been consulted earlier), only for the flood of 1598 to leave the Ponte Rotto arch.

landmarks.summary: Rome's first stone bridge, with piers of 179 BCE and arches of 142 BCE, carrying the road from the Forum Boarium to Trastevere; broken by floods and abandoned in 1598, it survives as the single arch of the Ponte Rotto.
details: The censors Marcus Fulvius Nobilior and Marcus Aemilius Lepidus built the stone piers in 179 BCE; Publius Scipio Aemilianus and Lucius Mummius added the arches in 142 BCE. Six arches crossed about 140 m of river just below the Tiber Island. It was probably restored under Augustus; it collapsed repeatedly in floods (1230, 1422, 1557) and after 1598 was left as the Ponte Rotto, the 'broken bridge'.

The miniature shows the six-arch bridge in travertine with its roadway and parapets, the usual reconstruction from the surviving pier, Renaissance drawings and the Marble Plan. Its exact alignment and the number of arches are debated. The medieval Ponte Santa Maria, repaired after the collapse of 1230, is shown entire; Gregory XIII's rebuilding of 1575 fell in 1598, after our last period.
landmarks.built: Piers 179 BCE; arches 142 BCE; restored under Augustus; rebuilt 1575; broken 1598
landmarks.function: Road bridge from the Forum Boarium to Trastevere

landmarks.name: Porticus Octaviae

republic-200bce.name: Porticus Metelli
republic-200bce.note: By the end of this period (146 BCE) Metellus has enclosed the temple of Juno Regina (179 BCE) and Hermodorus's all-marble Jupiter Stator in a portico holding Lysippus's bronze horsemen of the Granicus.

republic-50bce.name: Porticus Metelli
republic-50bce.note: The Porticus Metelli: a colonnade around Juno Regina and the marble Jupiter Stator; Pliny tells of the cult statues of Juno and Jupiter accidentally set up in each other's temples.

empire-100ce.note: Augustus's rebuilding (c. 27–23 BCE), named for Octavia: new porticoes, Greek and Latin libraries, a curia, schools, and Greek sculptures praised by Pliny. A fashionable gallery for strolling.

empire-215ce.note: Restored by Severus and Caracalla in 203 CE after a fire, probably that of 191: the surviving propylon, with its Corinthian columns and inscription, dates from this restoration.

late-400ce.note: The complex is listed in the regionary catalogues; the temples are closed, the libraries' fate unknown. The propylon still carries the Severan inscription; the quarter is turning to housing.

medieval-1300.name: Sant'Angelo in Pescheria (fish market)
medieval-1300.note: Sant'Angelo in Pescheria, a church of 755 CE built into the propylon, gives its name to the fish market: fishmongers' slabs lean on the columns. The Jewish community lives in the streets around.

renaissance-1560.name: The Ghetto and the fish market
renaissance-1560.note: The Ghetto, walled by Paul IV in 1555, adjoins the fish market under the propylon; a plaque reserves the largest fish heads for the Conservators. From 1584 Jews are forced to hear sermons at Sant'Angelo.

landmarks.summary: Colonnaded enclosure around the temples of Jupiter Stator and Juno Regina, built by Metellus in 146 BCE and rebuilt by Augustus in his sister Octavia's name c. 27 BCE; its propylon later housed the fish market.
details: Metellus Macedonicus, celebrating his triumph of 146 BCE, enclosed the two temples with a portico and placed Lysippus's bronze group of Alexander's companions inside; the first all-marble temple in Rome (Jupiter Stator by Hermodorus) stood here. Augustus rebuilt it from Dalmatian spoils with libraries, a curia and schools; Septimius Severus and Caracalla restored it after a fire, dedicating the surviving propylon in 203 CE.

The miniature shows the Augustan-Severan complex: a rectangle about 130 by 120 m of double colonnades, the propylon on the south side with its gable, and the two temples inside; the Republican Porticus Metelli is similar in plan but without the propylon, by conjecture. The 1300 and 1560 models show the propylon as the arcade of the fish market with the church of Sant'Angelo in Pescheria behind.
landmarks.built: 146 BCE (Porticus Metelli); rebuilt c. 27–23 BCE; restored 203 CE
landmarks.function: Monumental portico with temples, libraries and art; later fish market

landmarks.name: Basilica of Maxentius

empire-215ce.note: Not yet built. The site held the Horrea Piperataria, Domitian's spice and pepper warehouses, which burned in the fire of 283 CE and were cleared for the basilica.

late-400ce.note: Complete. Constantine finished Maxentius's hall after 312 CE, adding a south entrance on the Via Sacra and a north apse; his colossal seated statue filled the west apse.

medieval-1300.name: Ruins of the Basilica of Maxentius
medieval-1300.note: The nave vaults have fallen, probably in the earthquake of 847 CE. Only the three barrel vaults of the north aisle stand; people call the ruin the Templum Pacis.

renaissance-1560.name: Ruins of the Basilica of Maxentius
renaissance-1560.note: The same three north-aisle vaults, now studied by Bramante and other architects as a model for St Peter's. The last standing nave column still rises amid vineyards.

landmarks.summary: The largest vaulted hall of ancient Rome, begun by Maxentius around 308 CE and finished by Constantine, whose concrete vaults later taught Renaissance architects how to build St Peter's.
details: Maxentius began the basilica around 308 CE on the site of Domitian's spice warehouses; Constantine completed it after 312 CE, turning the entrance to the Via Sacra and adding a second apse. The nave, 80 by 25 metres, rose 35 metres under three coffered cross-vaults carried on eight marble columns; the side aisles had barrel vaults. Marble veneer and a colossal statue of Constantine filled the interior.

The miniature shows the full building in 400 CE and the three surviving north-aisle vaults for 1300 and 1560. The nave vaults probably fell in the earthquake of 847 CE, though some scholars prefer a later date. The roofing of the nave, in gilt bronze tiles or lead, and the exact form of the south porch are reconstructed.
landmarks.built: Begun c. 308 CE by Maxentius; completed after 312 CE by Constantine
landmarks.function: Law courts and civic hall

landmarks.name: Arch of Septimius Severus

empire-100ce.note: Not yet built. This corner of the Forum, between the Rostra and the Senate house, was open paving around the Umbilicus Urbi, the symbolic navel of the city.

empire-215ce.note: Dedicated in 203 CE for Severus's Parthian victories. Since 212 CE Geta's name has been chiselled from the inscription on Caracalla's orders; a bronze six-horse chariot crowns the attic.

late-400ce.note: Intact, though the bronze chariot group on top is probably gone by now. The relief panels of Parthian cities under siege are still crisp; the Forum around it is still paved and used.

medieval-1300.note: Half buried in silt and rubble. The small church of Santi Sergio e Bacco leans against one side and a tower of the Cimini family sits on the other; the central passage is choked.

renaissance-1560.note: Still buried to the springing of the side arches, with the Forum now the Campo Vaccino cattle market. Artists sketch and measure it; full excavation comes only in 1803.

landmarks.summary: Triple triumphal arch dedicated in 203 CE at the foot of the Capitol to celebrate Septimius Severus's Parthian wars, its inscription famously altered after the murder of Geta.
details: The Senate dedicated the arch in 203 CE to Severus and his sons for the Parthian victories of 195–198 CE. Of travertine and brick faced with marble, it is 23 metres high and 25 wide, with three passages, four large relief panels of sieges and campaigns, and a bronze chariot on the attic. After Caracalla murdered Geta in December 211 CE his name was erased from the dedication.

The miniature shows the arch at full height with its lost bronze crowning group for the imperial periods, then progressively buried in the medieval and Renaissance scenes. The exact form of the chariot group is known only from coins; the medieval church and tower attached to the arch are placed approximately.
landmarks.built: Dedicated 203 CE
landmarks.function: Triumphal arch

landmarks.name: Arch of Constantine

empire-215ce.note: Not yet built. The spot lay on the triumphal route between the Palatine and the Caelian, beside the Meta Sudans fountain and the Colossus; some scholars suspect an earlier arch stood here.

late-400ce.note: Dedicated in 315 CE for Constantine's ten-year jubilee and his victory at the Milvian Bridge. Its panels are largely recut from monuments of Trajan, Hadrian and Marcus Aurelius.

medieval-1300.note: Standing, but embedded in the Frangipane family's fortifications that stretch from the Colosseum to the Palatine. The arch doubles as a gate tower; the ground has risen around its base.

renaissance-1560.note: Freed from most fortifications, it stands on the road to the Lateran used by papal processions. In 1534 Lorenzino de' Medici knocked the heads off some of its statues.

landmarks.summary: The largest surviving Roman triumphal arch, dedicated in 315 CE for Constantine's victory over Maxentius and assembled largely from sculpture taken off second-century monuments.
details: The Senate dedicated the arch in 315 CE, three years after Constantine's victory at the Milvian Bridge. It is 21 metres high and 26 wide, with three passages. Most of its sculpture is reused: Trajanic battle friezes, Hadrianic hunting roundels and Marcus Aurelius's panels, with the emperors' heads recut. New work includes the narrow frieze of Constantine's campaign, the inscription, the pedestal reliefs and the spandrel Victories.

The miniature shows the arch complete, with its attic statues of Dacian prisoners. Whether Constantine's builders adapted an existing Hadrianic arch or built from the foundations up is still disputed. The medieval Frangipane walls that joined it to the Colosseum are shown schematically.
landmarks.built: Dedicated 315 CE
landmarks.function: Triumphal arch

landmarks.name: Temple of Venus and Roma

empire-100ce.note: Not yet built. The vestibule of Nero's Golden House stood here with his 30-metre bronze Colossus; Hadrian will have the statue dragged aside by 24 elephants to clear the site.

empire-215ce.note: Hadrian's temple, dedicated in 135 CE, stands on its vast terrace: ten columns across the front, two cellas back to back, Venus facing the Colosseum and Roma facing the Forum.

late-400ce.note: Rebuilt by Maxentius after a fire in 307 CE with coffered brick-vaulted apses and porphyry columns inside. Closed as a temple by the edicts of 391 CE, it still dominates the Velia.

medieval-1300.name: Santa Maria Nova (Temple of Venus and Roma)
medieval-1300.note: The gilt bronze roof tiles went to St Peter's in 625 CE. The church of Santa Maria Nova, founded in the 9th century, occupies the Roma end; its Romanesque bell tower dates from the 1160s.

renaissance-1560.name: Santa Maria Nova (Temple of Venus and Roma)
renaissance-1560.note: Santa Maria Nova, where Francesca Romana was buried in 1440; canonised in 1608, she will give the church its later name. Beyond its apse the two temple cellas stand roofless amid gardens and vines.

landmarks.summary: Hadrian's double temple of 135 CE, the largest in Rome, whose western cella later became the church of Santa Maria Nova, today Santa Francesca Romana.
details: Hadrian designed the temple himself, begun in 121 CE and dedicated in 135 CE. A terrace 145 by 100 metres, ringed with grey granite colonnades, carried a building of ten by twenty Proconnesian marble columns with two cellas set back to back. Cassius Dio says Apollodorus mocked the seated cult statues as too big for their rooms. Fire in 307 CE led Maxentius to rebuild the cellas with coffered vaults.

The miniature shows the temple in its Maxentian form, then the medieval church inserted into the Roma cella with its campanile. The height of the columns and the pediment sculpture are reconstructed; the ancient roof and the exact layout of the 9th-century church before its 1615 remodelling are uncertain.
landmarks.built: Begun 121 CE, dedicated 135 CE; rebuilt c. 307 CE; church from the 9th century
landmarks.function: Temple of Venus Felix and Roma Aeterna; later a church

landmarks.name: Column of Marcus Aurelius

empire-100ce.note: Not yet built. In 100 CE this was open ground in the northern Campus Martius along the Via Flaminia; the Antonine temples and the column come two generations later.

empire-215ce.note: Finished by 193 CE. The 100-foot marble shaft, carved with a spiral of Marcus's wars on the Danube, carries a bronze statue of the emperor; his temple probably stood nearby.

late-400ce.note: Intact, with its bronze statue still on top. The spiral reliefs, including the 'rain miracle' scene of 172 CE, remain the showpiece of the square.

medieval-1300.note: Standing, but the bronze emperor is long gone and houses crowd its base. The monks of San Silvestro in Capite own it and charge visitors a fee to climb the internal stair.

renaissance-1560.note: Weathered but complete, its base partly buried. In 1589 Sixtus V will restore the pedestal and set a bronze St Paul on top; in 1560 the summit is still empty.

landmarks.summary: A 100-foot marble column completed in 193 CE, carved with a spiral of Marcus Aurelius's Danube wars in imitation of Trajan's Column, and still standing in Piazza Colonna.
details: Begun after Marcus's death in 180 CE and finished by 193 CE, the column copies Trajan's: a Carrara marble shaft of 100 Roman feet on a tall pedestal, hollowed by a spiral stair, with reliefs of the Marcomannic and Sarmatian wars of 172 to 175 CE. The carving is deeper and harsher than Trajan's, and the scene of a rain god saving a Roman army became famous.

The miniature shows the column with its original bronze statue of the emperor and the pedestal reliefs, both lost. The surrounding Antonine square and temple are only partly known from excavation, and the ground level has risen about four metres since antiquity.
landmarks.built: Completed by 193 CE
landmarks.function: Commemorative column

landmarks.name: Old St Peter's Basilica

empire-215ce.note: Not yet built. The Vatican slope is a roadside cemetery beside the Circus of Gaius and Nero; a small shrine of about 160 CE marks what Christians hold to be Peter's grave.

late-400ce.note: Constantine's basilica, begun around 320 CE over the necropolis: five aisles on 88 columns, a transept over the shrine, an apse, and a great colonnaded atrium entered from the east.

medieval-1300.note: The same basilica, now with a bell tower, a mosaic façade of the 1220s, the Leonine Walls around the Borgo, and Giotto's Navicella mosaic in the atrium, made about this time.

renaissance-1560.name: New St Peter's (under construction)
renaissance-1560.note: Bramante's four piers and arches stand at the west end and Michelangelo, architect since 1547, is raising the drum. Sangallo's wall of 1538 cuts off the old nave, which is still in use.

landmarks.summary: The church over the tomb of St Peter: Constantine's great fourth-century basilica, which stood for twelve centuries before being replaced by the domed Renaissance church.
details: Constantine began the basilica around 320 CE on the Vatican slope, levelling a pagan cemetery to centre the church on a modest second-century shrine identified as Peter's grave. Roughly 110 metres long with five aisles, a transept and an apse, fronted by a colonnaded atrium, it became the chief pilgrimage church of the West. In 1506 Julius II had Bramante start demolishing it; the old nave survived until about 1610.

The miniature shows Constantine's church for 400 CE, its medieval additions for 1300, and in 1560 the new crossing piers, Michelangelo's rising drum and the dividing wall with the old nave behind. Details of the fourth-century façade, the medieval bell tower and the state of the building site in exactly 1560 are reconstructed from drawings and engravings.
landmarks.built: Old basilica c. 320–360 CE; new basilica begun 1506, dome completed 1590, nave 1614
landmarks.function: Pilgrimage basilica over the tomb of St Peter

landmarks.name: Lateran Basilica

empire-215ce.note: Not yet built. Septimius Severus has just built the Castra Nova here, a brick fort for the Equites Singulares, the emperor's horse guard, beside the old houses of the Laterani family.

late-400ce.note: The Basilica of the Saviour, founded by Constantine about 313 CE on the razed fort of the disbanded horse guard: five aisles, an apse with a silver fastigium, and the octagonal baptistery nearby.

medieval-1300.name: The Lateran (basilica and papal palace)
medieval-1300.note: The cathedral of Rome with the sprawling papal palace: Leo III's banqueting hall, bell towers, the bronze Marcus Aurelius outside and Boniface VIII's new loggia painted by Giotto for the 1300 Jubilee.

renaissance-1560.note: The basilica, rebuilt after fires in 1308 and 1361 with a Gothic altar canopy; the medieval palace beside it is half derelict since the popes moved to the Vatican. Sixtus V razes it in 1586.

landmarks.summary: Rome's cathedral and the first great Christian basilica, founded by Constantine around 313 CE on the site of his rival's cavalry barracks, with the popes' palace beside it for a thousand years.
details: After the Milvian Bridge Constantine disbanded Maxentius's horse guard, demolished their fort and gave the ground to the bishop of Rome. The basilica, about 100 by 55 metres with five aisles, was dedicated to the Saviour and later to the two Johns. The adjoining palace, the Patriarchium, housed the popes until the exile to Avignon in 1309; fires in 1308 and 1361 gutted the church.

The miniature shows the Constantinian basilica with its baptistery, then the medieval complex of basilica, palace, towers and loggia. The fourth-century roof and façade are reconstructed from the Liber Pontificalis and later views; the medieval palace is known mainly from sixteenth-century drawings made shortly before Sixtus V demolished it.
landmarks.built: Basilica founded c. 313 CE; baptistery 432–440 CE; palace enlarged c. 800; rebuilt after 1308 and 1361
landmarks.function: Cathedral of Rome and papal residence

landmarks.name: Santa Maria Maggiore

late-400ce.note: Not yet built. In 400 CE the Esquiline summit held aristocratic houses and a market hall; tradition says Pope Liberius founded a church here after a miraculous August snowfall, but nothing of it is known.

medieval-1300.note: Sixtus III's basilica of the 430s, with its forty-column nave and fifth-century mosaics, newly extended by Nicholas IV: a transept and Torriti's apse mosaic of 1295, and a mosaic façade by Rusuti.

renaissance-1560.note: Dominated by its 75-metre bell tower of the 1370s, the tallest in Rome. Inside, a gilded coffered ceiling of the 1490s, said to use the first gold from the Americas. Fontana's Sistine chapel comes later.

landmarks.summary: The great fifth-century basilica of the Virgin on the Esquiline, built by Sixtus III after the Council of Ephesus and still carrying its original nave mosaics and Rome's tallest medieval bell tower.
details: Sixtus III built the basilica in 432 to 440 CE, soon after the Council of Ephesus proclaimed Mary Mother of God. The nave, flanked by forty Ionic columns, keeps its mosaic panels of Old Testament scenes and a mosaic triumphal arch. Nicholas IV added the transept and Jacopo Torriti's apse mosaic in the 1290s; the campanile dates from the 1370s and the coffered ceiling from the 1490s.

The miniature shows the medieval church with its mosaic façade and campanile; the eighteenth-century façade and the two Baroque domes are absent. The legend of the snow and Pope Liberius's earlier church is unverified; excavations found only Roman houses under the nave.
landmarks.built: 432–440 CE; transept and apse 1290s; campanile 1370s
landmarks.function: Papal basilica dedicated to the Virgin

landmarks.name: Santa Maria in Aracoeli

late-400ce.note: Not yet built. The Arx, the Capitol's northern summit, still carries the Temple of Juno Moneta of 344 BCE and the old mint, closed as a sanctuary after 391 CE.

medieval-1300.note: The Franciscans' new church, rebuilt from the 1250s in brick with a plain unfinished façade and a nave on 22 ancient columns; the Roman commune holds its assemblies here.

renaissance-1560.note: Reached by the 124-step marble stair of 1348, built in thanks for the plague's end. Pinturicchio's Bernardino chapel of the 1480s is inside; Michelangelo's planned ramp to the Campidoglio is not yet built.

landmarks.summary: The Franciscan church on the Capitol's northern summit, rebuilt from the 1250s over an older monastery and the ancient citadel, and the civic church of medieval Rome.
details: A monastery of Santa Maria de Capitolio is recorded on the Arx by the 9th century; the legend of an altar raised by Augustus after the Sibyl's prophecy gave it the name Aracoeli. Innocent IV gave the church to the Franciscans in 1249 or 1250, who rebuilt it in Romanesque-Gothic form by about 1300, reusing 22 ancient columns. The great stair was added in 1348.

The miniature shows the brick church, the stair and the convent beside it, with the Capitol's Roman substructures below. Whether the Temple of Juno Moneta lay exactly under the church or further south under the Vittoriano is disputed; the medieval convent, demolished in the 1880s, is shown schematically.
landmarks.built: Monastery by the 9th century; rebuilt 1250s–c. 1300; stair 1348
landmarks.function: Franciscan church and civic church of the Roman commune

landmarks.name: Torre delle Milizie

late-400ce.note: Not yet built. The upper terrace of Trajan's Markets rose here on the slope of the Quirinal, its brick halls and shops still in use.

medieval-1300.note: A three-tiered brick tower about 50 metres high, built in the early 1200s on Roman foundations. In 1301 Boniface VIII's nephew Pietro Caetani buys it from the Annibaldi to dominate the quarter.

renaissance-1560.note: Reduced to two tiers and leaning: the earthquake of 1348 brought down the top storey and tilted the rest. Held by the Conti family, the old fortress now stands among gardens and convents.

landmarks.summary: The tallest surviving medieval tower in Rome, raised in the early 1200s on the Quirinal slope above Trajan's Markets, later linked by legend to Nero watching the fire.
details: The tower was built in the first decades of the 13th century, probably under Gregory IX, on foundations of Trajan's Markets, as the fortified heart of a baronial compound. Originally about 50 metres in three receding brick tiers, it passed from the Annibaldi to the Caetani in 1301 and later to the Conti. The earthquake of 1348 toppled the top storey and left the rest leaning.

The miniature shows the full three tiers in 1300 and the truncated, slightly tilted tower in 1560. The exact builder and date are not certain, and the surrounding curtain walls and lesser towers of the compound are reconstructed from medieval descriptions.
landmarks.built: Early 13th century; top storey lost 1348
landmarks.function: Baronial fortress tower

landmarks.name: Santa Maria in Cosmedin

late-400ce.note: Not yet a church. A colonnaded hall of the Statio Annonae, the grain-supply office, stands here in the Forum Boarium, probably beside the old Great Altar of Hercules.

medieval-1300.note: The church rebuilt in the 1120s after the Norman sack: nave on reused columns, a schola cantorum, Cosmatesque floor, a porch, and the seven-storey brick bell tower that still marks the Forum Boarium.

renaissance-1560.note: Unchanged in essentials, still called the church of the Greeks for the community it once served. The Bocca della Verità, an ancient drain cover, does not move into the porch until 1632.

landmarks.summary: A small medieval church in the Forum Boarium built into a Roman grain-office hall, famous for its twelfth-century bell tower and, later, the Bocca della Verità in its porch.
details: A welfare station, or diaconia, was set up here in the 6th century inside the hall of the Roman Statio Annonae, whose columns remain embedded in the walls. Hadrian I enlarged it around 780 for Greek refugees, hence 'in Cosmedin', from the Greek for ornament. After the Normans wrecked it in 1084, Gelasius II and Callixtus II rebuilt the church in 1118 to 1124 with its campanile and marble furnishings.

The miniature shows the twelfth-century church with its porch and campanile, as it looked before the Baroque façade of 1718, itself removed in the 1890s. The Roman podium under the church is usually identified as the Ara Maxima of Hercules, but this is not proven.
landmarks.built: Diaconia 6th century; enlarged c. 780; rebuilt 1118–1124
landmarks.function: Church of the Greek community and papal diaconia

landmarks.name: Tabularium

republic-200bce.note: Not yet built. The saddle between the two Capitoline summits held the Asylum and, from 192 BCE, the small Temple of Veiovis, later buried in the Tabularium's foundations.

republic-50bce.note: Built in 78 BCE by Quintus Lutatius Catulus after the fire of 83 BCE: a massive substructure of peperino and travertine with an arcaded gallery that closes the Forum's west end.

empire-100ce.note: The arcade now peers over the new Temple of Vespasian and the rebuilt Concord at its foot; upper storeys, probably of brick, carry offices above the gallery.

empire-215ce.note: Much as in 100 CE. The Severan restoration of the Forum temples below leaves the Tabularium as the austere backdrop to the Arch of Septimius Severus.

late-400ce.note: Still standing and presumably still housing records and offices, though the Capitoline temples around it are closed. The upper storeys are the least known part of the building.

medieval-1300.name: Palazzo Senatorio (on the Tabularium)
medieval-1300.note: The commune's Senator rules from a fortified palace on the Roman vaults since 1143, with corner towers and a loggia; the ground floor is a salt store, the Forum side a cliff of arches.

renaissance-1560.name: Campidoglio (Michelangelo's piazza, in progress)
renaissance-1560.note: Michelangelo's scheme of 1538 is half built: the Marcus Aurelius statue stands on its new base and the Senatorio's double stair is done, but the palace façades and the oval paving are still to come.

landmarks.summary: The Republican record office of 78 BCE whose arcaded substructure still closes the Forum, later the base of the medieval Senator's palace and of Michelangelo's Campidoglio.
details: Catulus built the Tabularium in 78 BCE to tie the two summits of the Capitol together and to store state archives, as an inscription records. A gallery of eleven arches with Doric half-columns runs 73 metres along the Forum side above a blind wall; the upper floors are lost. In 1143 the new Roman commune installed its Senate on top, and the palace grew towers and a loggia.

The miniature shows the Republican substructure with a reconstructed upper storey, the medieval palace for 1300, and for 1560 the piazza mid-construction. The Roman superstructure, the name of the building and the medieval palace's shape before Michelangelo are all partly conjectural; Giacomo della Porta's façade and the twin side palaces came after 1560.
landmarks.built: 78 BCE; Senator's palace from 1143; Michelangelo's piazza begun 1538
landmarks.function: State archive; later the seat of Rome's civic government

landmarks.name: Palazzo Farnese

medieval-1300.note: Not yet built. In 1300 this is the Regola quarter near the river: lanes of ropemakers, tanners and small houses which the Farnese will buy up from 1495 to clear a site.

renaissance-1560.note: The grandest palace in Rome, its façade finished by Michelangelo's cornice of 1547 and his central balcony. The rear loggia is still open at the back; the Farnese Hercules stands in the courtyard.

landmarks.summary: The greatest of Rome's Renaissance palaces, begun in 1517 by Antonio da Sangallo for Cardinal Alessandro Farnese and crowned by Michelangelo's cornice after Alessandro became Pope Paul III.
details: Sangallo began the palace in 1517 and enlarged it after 1534, when Alessandro Farnese became Paul III. When Sangallo died in 1546, Michelangelo added the massive cornice, the central window and the third storey of the courtyard. Vignola and then Giacomo della Porta finished the garden front by 1589. The courtyard displayed the colossal Hercules and the Farnese Bull dug from the Baths of Caracalla.

The miniature shows the palace as it stood in 1560: the façade of 56 metres with its cornice complete, the courtyard largely done, the rear wing still unfinished. The piazza's twin granite basins arrived only in 1626 and the Carracci gallery frescoes after 1597, so neither appears.
landmarks.built: Begun 1517; enlarged from 1534; cornice 1547; completed 1589
landmarks.function: Palace of the Farnese family

landmarks.name: Villa Farnesina

medieval-1300.note: Not yet built. Vineyards and gardens line the riverbank below the Janiculum, outside Trastevere's built-up core; the buried Roman villa of around 20 BCE under them will be found in 1879.

renaissance-1560.note: Agostino Chigi's suburban villa of 1506 to 1510, with Raphael's Galatea and Cupid and Psyche loggia. The Chigi heirs neglect it; soldiers' graffiti from the Sack of 1527 scar the frescoes.

landmarks.summary: The banker Agostino Chigi's riverside villa, built by Peruzzi in 1506 to 1510 and frescoed by Raphael and his circle, the model Renaissance pleasure house in Rome.
details: Baldassare Peruzzi designed the villa for the Sienese banker Agostino Chigi between 1506 and 1510 as a U-shaped block with a garden loggia. Raphael painted the Galatea around 1512 and designed the Loggia of Cupid and Psyche in 1517 to 1518; Sebastiano del Piombo, Sodoma and Peruzzi worked beside him. Chigi died in 1520; Cardinal Alessandro Farnese bought the villa in 1579 (some say 1577), giving it its name.

The miniature shows the villa with its garden, Raphael's stables (demolished in 1808) and the riverside loggia, lost to the Tiber embankments in the 1880s. The layout of the gardens and the river front is reconstructed from sixteenth-century plans and views.
landmarks.function: Suburban villa of Agostino Chigi

landmarks.name: Santa Maria in Trastevere

empire-215ce.note: A crowded Trastevere street of houses and workshops. Tradition says Pope Callixtus I won this plot, a tavern or veterans' hostel, for Christian use around 220 CE; nothing of it is visible.

late-400ce.name: Titulus Callisti (Santa Maria in Trastevere)
late-400ce.note: A fourth-century basilica attributed to Pope Julius I, the titulus Callisti or Iulii. Its plan is unknown; the model gives a plain aisled hall of the kind built in Rome around 350 CE.

medieval-1300.note: Innocent II's church of 1140–43, on 22 granite columns said to come from the Baths of Caracalla, with his apse mosaic, a campanile, and Cavallini's new mosaics of the Virgin's life, dated 1291.

renaissance-1560.note: Essentially the twelfth-century basilica with its mosaic façade and medieval porch. Domenichino's gilded ceiling of 1617 and Carlo Fontana's porch of 1702 lie in the future.

landmarks.summary: Perhaps the oldest church of the Virgin in Rome, a titulus of the third or fourth century rebuilt in the 1140s with reused columns and mosaics that still glow across the main square of Trastevere.
details: The Liber Pontificalis credits Callixtus I with founding a Christian meeting place here and Julius I with building a basilica in the 340s; a legend says oil welled from the ground on the site in 38 BCE. Innocent II rebuilt the church in 1140 to 1143 with ancient columns and Ionic capitals, traditionally from the Baths of Caracalla, a mosaic apse and a campanile. Pietro Cavallini added mosaics in 1291.

The miniature shows a conjectural fourth-century hall, then Innocent II's basilica, which survives little changed. Nothing of the early church has been excavated, so its size and orientation are guesses; the twelfth-century façade mosaic and porch are shown as recorded before Fontana's rebuilding.
landmarks.built: Titulus by the 4th century; rebuilt 1140–1143
landmarks.function: Titular church of Trastevere

landmarks.name: San Clemente

empire-215ce.note: No church yet. A brick apartment block and a large warehouse-like building stand here; in the block's courtyard a Mithraeum has just been fitted out for worshippers of the Persian god.

late-400ce.name: Titulus Clementis (San Clemente)
late-400ce.note: A basilica built in the late 4th century over the earlier buildings, mentioned by Jerome in 392 CE. Three aisles with an apse; the plan of this lower church was excavated in 1857.

medieval-1300.note: The upper church, rebuilt around 1100 to 1120 on fill above the old basilica wrecked by the Normans in 1084, with its Tree of Life apse mosaic, Cosmatesque floor and sixth-century choir screens.

renaissance-1560.note: Little changed since 1120 apart from Masolino's frescoed chapel of St Catherine of about 1430. The lower church is forgotten and entirely buried beneath the floor.

landmarks.summary: A church built three times on one spot: a Roman apartment block with a Mithraeum, a fourth-century basilica over it, and the twelfth-century church with its famous apse mosaic above that.
details: The lowest level holds first-century buildings and a Mithraeum of c. 200 CE. A basilica dedicated to Pope Clement, the titulus Clementis, was built above them in the late 4th century and frescoed until the 11th century, including one of the earliest inscriptions in Italian. After Robert Guiscard's Normans burned the quarter in 1084, Paschal II's clergy filled the old church and built the present one by about 1120.

The miniature shows the fourth-century basilica and then the twelfth-century church with its forecourt and porch. The upper storeys of the Roman insula and the roof of the early basilica are reconstructed; the forecourt is shown as rebuilt in the 1700s, which may differ slightly from its medieval form.
landmarks.built: Mithraeum c. 200 CE; basilica late 4th century; rebuilt c. 1100–1120
landmarks.function: Titular church

landmarks.name: Pyramid of Cestius

republic-50bce.note: Not yet built. The Via Ostiensis runs through tombs and market gardens outside the Servian Wall; the pyramid goes up here about 18 to 12 BCE, after Rome's conquest of Egypt.

empire-100ce.note: A gleaming marble-faced pyramid 36 metres high, the tomb of the magistrate Gaius Cestius, standing among roadside tombs with bronze statues of the dead man at its corners.

empire-215ce.note: Unchanged, though the Egyptian fashion that produced it has passed. Travellers on the Via Ostiensis pass it a kilometre outside the gates.

late-400ce.note: Since the 270s CE the pyramid is built into the Aurelian Walls beside the Porta Ostiensis, serving as a bastion; its marble facing is intact.

medieval-1300.name: Pyramid of Cestius ("tomb of Remus")
medieval-1300.note: Pilgrims' guides call it the tomb of Remus, twin to the 'tomb of Romulus', a pyramid near the Vatican. Its inscription is hidden by soil and ivy; the gate beside it is Porta San Paolo.

renaissance-1560.note: Still called Meta Remi, though scholars have begun to read Cestius's name. Half buried, with vegetation on its slopes; Alexander VII's clearing and restoration come in 1660 to 1662.

landmarks.summary: The marble tomb of Gaius Cestius, a 36-metre pyramid built about 18 to 12 BCE in the Egyptian craze after Actium, and later built into the Aurelian Walls.
details: The inscription names Gaius Cestius, praetor, tribune and member of the priestly college of the Epulones, and says the tomb was finished in 330 days; since his heir Agrippa died in 12 BCE it dates from about 18 to 12 BCE. The pyramid is brick-faced concrete clad in Carrara marble, 29.6 metres square and 36.4 high, with a small frescoed burial chamber. Aurelian's wall-builders incorporated it in the 270s CE.

The miniature shows the pyramid with its marble facing clean and the bronze statues of Cestius on their columns, known from the inscribed bases found in 1660. In the medieval and Renaissance scenes the lower courses are buried and the walls and gate beside it are shown in their later form.
landmarks.built: c. 18–12 BCE; incorporated into the Aurelian Walls 271–275 CE
landmarks.function: Tomb

landmarks.name: Porta Maggiore

republic-50bce.note: No gate yet. The Via Praenestina and Via Labicana fork here among tombs outside the city; the baker Eurysaces is building his odd tomb shaped like a stack of dough mixers.

empire-100ce.name: Aqua Claudia arches (Porta Maggiore)
empire-100ce.note: Claudius's double arch of 52 CE carries the Aqua Claudia and Anio Novus over the two roads in rough-hewn travertine; inscriptions of Vespasian and Titus record repairs of 71 and 81 CE.

empire-215ce.name: Aqua Claudia arches (Porta Maggiore)
empire-215ce.note: Still a free-standing aqueduct crossing, not a gate. Beyond it the twin arcades of the Claudia and Marcia stride across the countryside; the roads pass under its two arches.

late-400ce.note: Now a city gate: Aurelian used the arch in his wall of the 270s, and Honorius (c. 401–405 CE) added towers and a forward bastion, burying the baker's tomb inside one of them.

medieval-1300.note: Called Porta Maggiore after the road to Santa Maria Maggiore. The aqueduct channels above are dry; the Honorian towers still guard a largely empty, vineyard-filled corner of the city.

renaissance-1560.note: Little changed. Travellers entering from Palestrina pass under Claudius's arch between Honorius's towers; Gregory XVI removes the towers and reveals the baker's tomb only in 1838.

landmarks.summary: Claudius's monumental aqueduct arch of 52 CE over the Praenestine and Labican roads, later turned into a gate of the Aurelian Walls, with the famous baker's tomb beside it.
details: Claudius finished the Aqua Claudia and Anio Novus in 52 CE and marked their crossing of two roads with a double arch of deliberately rough travertine blocks, 32 metres wide, carrying both channels. Aurelian incorporated it into his wall in 271 to 275 CE, and Honorius in the early 400s added towers and a bastion that enclosed the tomb of the baker Eurysaces, built about 30 BCE.

The miniature shows the arch with its aqueduct channels, then the gate with Honorius's towers, which were demolished in 1838. The inscriptions and attic are well preserved; the form of the Honorian bastion and the medieval buildings against the gate are reconstructed from early drawings.
landmarks.built: 52 CE; made a gate 271–275 CE; towers early 5th century
landmarks.function: Aqueduct crossing, later city gate

landmarks.name: Porta Appia

empire-215ce.note: No gate: Rome has no walls here. The Via Appia leaves the city between tombs, passing under the new arch carrying Caracalla's aqueduct to his baths, later called the Arch of Drusus.

late-400ce.note: Aurelian's gate of the 270s, rebuilt about 401 to 403 CE under Honorius: a single arch between two tall towers faced below in marble, with an upper gallery and portcullis.

medieval-1300.name: Porta San Sebastiano (Porta Appia)
medieval-1300.note: Named for San Sebastiano on the Appian Way. The towers are garrisoned; in 1327 Romans beat back King Robert of Naples's troops here, as an archangel and inscription carved in the passage record.

renaissance-1560.name: Porta San Sebastiano (Porta Appia)
renaissance-1560.note: The largest and best-kept gate in the walls, still the ceremonial entrance from the south. Charles V entered here in 1536; Marcantonio Colonna's triumph after Lepanto will pass through it in 1571.

landmarks.summary: The gate of the Appian Way in the Aurelian Walls, rebuilt under Honorius around 401 to 403 CE and the largest and best-preserved of Rome's ancient gates.
details: Aurelian's wall of 271 to 275 CE crossed the Via Appia with a twin-arched gate between round towers. Around 401 to 403 CE Honorius's engineers rebuilt it with a single arch, marble-faced towers raised on square bases, and a fortified upper storey; later repairs raised the towers again. Just inside stands the so-called Arch of Drusus, really an arch of Caracalla's aqueduct.

The miniature shows the Honorian gate with its gallery and towers, which survive to full height. The exact appearance of Aurelian's original gate and the sequence of later heightenings are reconstructed from the brickwork; the inscription of the 1327 battle and later graffiti are not modelled.
landmarks.built: 271–275 CE; rebuilt c. 401–403 CE
landmarks.function: City gate on the Via Appia

landmarks.name: Castra Praetoria

republic-50bce.note: Not yet built. Fields and tombs stretch beyond the great earthen rampart of the Servian Wall on the Viminal; the Praetorians will be stationed here under Tiberius.

empire-100ce.note: Sejanus's fort of 21 to 23 CE: a brick-walled rectangle of 440 by 380 metres with four gates, holding nine cohorts of the Praetorian Guard in rows of barracks around a headquarters.

empire-215ce.note: Here in 193 CE the Guard auctioned the empire to Didius Julianus. Septimius Severus purged and refilled it with his Danube legionaries; the camp is the real power behind the Severan throne.

late-400ce.note: Dissolved. Constantine disbanded the Guard after 312 CE and razed the inner west wall; the other three sides survive only as part of Aurelian's city wall, enclosing empty ground.

landmarks.summary: The brick fortress of the Praetorian Guard, built by Sejanus in 21 to 23 CE on the north-east edge of Rome, where emperors were made and unmade until Constantine abolished the Guard.
details: Tiberius's prefect Sejanus concentrated the Praetorian cohorts in one camp of 440 by 380 metres, 17 hectares, in 21 to 23 CE. Its brick-faced concrete walls, under 5 metres high, with rounded corners and four gates, enclosed barracks for perhaps 10,000 men. Aurelian built the camp into his city wall in the 270s; Maxentius heightened it; Constantine razed the west side in 312 CE.

The miniature shows the walled camp with its gates and barrack rows; the internal plan is poorly known and follows the standard layout of a Roman fort. The three surviving sides, still part of the Aurelian Walls, stand much higher today after repeated raisings.
landmarks.built: 21–23 CE; walls raised 270s and c. 310 CE; west wall razed 312 CE
landmarks.function: Barracks of the Praetorian Guard

landmarks.name: Emporium and Horrea Galbae

kingdom-600bce.note: No port yet. A flood meadow below the Aventine, outside the settlement; boats still beach at the Forum Boarium upstream by the Tiber Island ford.

republic-200bce.note: Being laid out. The aediles of 193 BCE build the Emporium and the Porticus Aemilia, later a vaulted hall nearly 500 metres long; the censors pave the quay in 174 BCE.

republic-50bce.note: The city's working harbour: a travertine quay with mooring rings and ramps, the long portico behind it, and the new Horrea Galbae, a vast three-courtyard warehouse of the Sulpicii Galbae.

empire-100ce.note: At full stretch. Grain, oil and wine for perhaps a million people come up from Claudius's harbour at Portus, which Trajan is enlarging; broken oil amphorae are already being stacked into Monte Testaccio.

empire-215ce.note: The Severan grain and oil doles keep the quays busy; the amphora mound climbs ever higher. Rows of warehouses, many imperial property, cover the plain down to the river.

late-400ce.note: Still working but shrinking: dumping of Spanish and African oil jars at Testaccio stopped around 260 CE, and the Vandal seizure of Carthage in 439 CE will cut the grain fleet too.

medieval-1300.note: Gone. The plain is the Prati del Popolo Romano, pasture and vineyards where the commune holds its Carnival games below Monte Testaccio; marble is quarried from the old quay, the Marmorata.

landmarks.summary: Republican Rome's river port below the Aventine, with the Porticus Aemilia and the enormous Horrea Galbae warehouses, where the grain, oil and marble of the empire were landed for over six centuries.
details: Livy records the aediles Lepidus and Paullus building the Emporium and Porticus Aemilia in 193 BCE, and censors paving and rebuilding in 174 BCE; the vaulted hall measured 487 by 60 metres. The Horrea Galbae, warehouses founded by the Sulpicii Galbae, grew into courtyards covering more than 3 hectares. A travertine quay with ramps and mooring rings served the barges; discarded oil amphorae formed the 35-metre Monte Testaccio.

The miniature shows the quay, the portico and the warehouse courtyards in a simplified grid. The identification of the great vaulted building as the Porticus Aemilia has recently been challenged by scholars who see it as a shipyard; the internal plan of the Horrea Galbae is only partly excavated.
landmarks.built: Emporium and Porticus Aemilia 193 BCE, rebuilt 174 BCE; Horrea Galbae 2nd–1st century BCE
landmarks.function: River port and state warehouses

landmarks.name: Ludus Magnus

republic-50bce.note: Not yet built. Crowded housing fills the valley between the Caelian and the Esquiline; Nero's Golden House and then the Colosseum will clear it a century later.

empire-100ce.note: Domitian's new gladiator school, finished under Trajan: a small elliptical practice arena with seats for a few thousand, ringed by three storeys of cells, linked by tunnel to the Colosseum.

empire-215ce.note: The chief of four imperial gladiator barracks around the amphitheatre, run by an imperial procurator. Fighters train in the arena while spectators watch from the stands.

late-400ce.note: Still standing, but gladiatorial combat is dying out and ends in Rome in the early 5th century. The barracks are probably half empty and being put to other uses.

medieval-1300.note: Buried under rubble and vineyards beside the road to the Lateran. The ruins are rediscovered only in 1937 and excavated in 1957 to 1961.

landmarks.summary: The principal gladiator barracks of imperial Rome, built by Domitian beside the Colosseum with its own miniature arena and an underground passage into the amphitheatre.
details: Domitian began the Ludus Magnus in the 80s CE and Trajan completed it. A rectangular block of three-storey cells enclosed a courtyard with an elliptical training arena of 62 by 42 metres, surrounded by stands for about 3,000 spectators. A tunnel led directly to the Colosseum. Three other schools, the Ludus Dacicus, Gallicus and Matutinus, stood nearby.

The miniature shows the complete barracks block and arena, reconstructed from the excavated north-west half and the Severan marble plan of the city. The height of the cell blocks and the roofing of the stands are conjectural.
landmarks.built: Begun 80s CE under Domitian; completed under Trajan
landmarks.function: Gladiator training barracks

landmarks.name: Ospedale di Santo Spirito

late-400ce.note: Not yet built. The Via Cornelia runs here through the Vatican meadows between the river and St Peter's, past tombs and the fading remains of Nero's circus.

medieval-1300.note: Innocent III's hospital of 1198, run by the Order of the Holy Spirit on the site of the Saxon pilgrims' hostel founded about 727. Wards, a church and a foundling wheel serve the Borgo.

renaissance-1560.note: The Corsia Sistina, rebuilt by Sixtus IV in 1473 to 1478 after a fire: two wards 120 metres long under an octagonal lantern, frescoed with the pope's life. Sangallo's church of the 1540s adjoins it.

landmarks.summary: Rome's great medieval hospital in the Borgo, founded by Innocent III in 1198 on the site of the Saxon pilgrims' hostel and rebuilt by Sixtus IV as the vast Corsia Sistina.
details: King Ine of Wessex is said to have founded a hostel for English pilgrims here about 727, the Schola Saxonum. In 1198 Innocent III gave the site to Guy of Montpellier's Order of the Holy Spirit as a hospital for the sick and for abandoned infants, received through a wheel in the wall. After a fire, Sixtus IV rebuilt it in 1473 to 1478 as the Corsia Sistina.

The miniature shows the Corsia Sistina with its lantern and the adjoining church of Santo Spirito in Sassia; the medieval hospital of 1300 is reconstructed from scanty evidence. The Palazzo del Commendatore of the late 1560s and later wings are left out.
landmarks.built: Founded 1198; rebuilt 1473–1478; church 1538–1545
landmarks.function: Hospital and foundling home

landmarks.name: Pons Aelius

empire-100ce.note: Not yet built. The Campus Martius bank here is open ground; the only crossing to the Vatican is Nero's bridge a little downstream, which Hadrian's new bridge will replace.

empire-215ce.note: Hadrian's bridge of 134 CE leads straight to his mausoleum: three great arches of travertine over the river, with smaller arches and ramps on the banks.

late-400ce.note: Intact and busy with pilgrims to St Peter's. The mausoleum at its end is now a fortress built into the Aurelian Walls.

medieval-1300.name: Ponte Sant'Angelo
medieval-1300.note: The pilgrims' bridge to the Borgo, named for the angel seen over the castle in 590 CE, lined with stalls. In the Jubilee of 1300 traffic keeps to one side, as Dante notes.

renaissance-1560.name: Ponte Sant'Angelo
renaissance-1560.note: After the crush that killed some 170 pilgrims in the Jubilee of 1450, Nicholas V cleared the bridgehead. Statues of Peter and Paul of 1534 guard the entrance; Bernini's angels are a century away.

landmarks.summary: Hadrian's bridge of 134 CE to his mausoleum, the Ponte Sant'Angelo, which carried every pilgrim into the Borgo and St Peter's for fourteen centuries.
details: Hadrian built the Pons Aelius in 134 CE to link the Campus Martius with his mausoleum, the later Castel Sant'Angelo. Three central arches span the river, with smaller arches at each bank and long ramps, altogether about 135 metres. After the 1450 disaster Nicholas V rebuilt the approach and added two chapels, replaced in 1534 by statues of Peter and Paul.

The miniature shows the Roman bridge with its ramps and the bank arches, which were buried under the Renaissance approach and uncovered in 1892 when the embankments were built. The ancient parapet decoration is unknown; the medieval shops on the bridge are shown schematically.
landmarks.built: 134 CE; approaches rebuilt 1450s; statues 1534
landmarks.function: Bridge to Hadrian's mausoleum and the Vatican

landmarks.name: Ponte Sisto

empire-100ce.note: No bridge here. Agrippa's bridge of about 19 BCE crosses the Tiber some 160 metres upstream; its piers were found in 1887. Trastevere is reached from there or from the island bridges.

empire-215ce.name: Pons Aurelius
empire-215ce.note: A stone bridge, probably the Pons Aurelius or Antoninus built under Caracalla around 215 CE on the line of Agrippa's bridge, carrying the road from the Campus Martius into Trastevere.

late-400ce.name: Pons Aurelius
late-400ce.note: Restored by Valentinian and Valens about 366 CE and renamed after them in inscriptions found in the riverbed. Four or five arches of travertine over the river.

medieval-1300.note: Ruined: the Pons Fractus, broken since at least the 8th century, with only its piers standing. Trastevere is reached by the Ponte Santa Maria downstream.

renaissance-1560.note: Sixtus IV's bridge of 1473 to 1475, built for the Jubilee on the Roman piers: four travertine arches with a round opening, the occhialone, in the central pier to let floods through.

landmarks.summary: Sixtus IV's bridge of 1475 on the piers of a Roman bridge, the Pons Aurelius, reconnecting Trastevere with the Campus Martius after seven centuries of ruin.
details: A bridge was built here in the Antonine or Severan period, probably under Caracalla, replacing Agrippa's bridge upstream; Valentinian I restored it about 366 CE. It was broken by the 8th century and stayed the 'Pons Fractus' until Sixtus IV rebuilt it in 1473 to 1475 for the Jubilee, perhaps to Baccio Pontelli's design: four arches of travertine-faced tufa, 108 metres long, with the occhialone in the middle pier.

The miniature shows a conjectural Roman bridge, then its broken piers, then the Renaissance bridge. The name, date and arch count of the Roman bridge are debated; its relationship to the Pons Agrippae upstream is not fully resolved.
landmarks.built: Roman bridge c. 215 CE; restored c. 366 CE; rebuilt 1473–1475
landmarks.function: Bridge between the Campus Martius and Trastevere

spots.name: Cloaca Maxima outfall
spots.summary: Rome's great drain, begun under the Etruscan kings to dry the Forum marsh, vaulted in stone by the 2nd century BCE and still emptying into the Tiber below the Forum Boarium.
details: Livy credits the Tarquins with the first channel, an open ditch draining the valleys between the hills. It was vaulted over in stages; the stone outfall arch, about 5 m across, is late Republican. Pliny marvelled that it had carried floods and falling buildings for 700 years; Agrippa cleaned it in 33 BCE and, Dio says, sailed through it.

It never stopped working. Medieval and Renaissance Romans knew the mouth as a cave in the river bank beside the broken Ponte Rotto, and the drains of the inhabited quarter still fed it. The miniature shows the outfall arch and the embankment; the course beneath the Forum is simplified.

vignettes.text: After a night of rain the vaulted mouth roars brown into the Tiber; a public slave with a pole clears driftwood and a drowned dog from the grating.
Low summer water: the outfall is a dark cave breathing cold, sour air. Boys dare each other to wade in; boatmen tie up away from the current it makes.
The drain is quiet, a trickle under the arch. Lamps on the Trastevere bank; from the Forum above, cart wheels on the stones, now that carts are allowed.

spots.name: Temple of Vesta and the Regia
spots.summary: The round hearth-temple of Vesta, tended by six Vestal Virgins, and the Regia, the old 'king's house' used by the pontifex maximus: the religious centre of the Forum from the 7th century BCE.
details: The Regia, built over archaic huts around 600 BCE, kept its odd trapezoidal plan through every rebuilding; it held the spears of Mars and the pontifical archive. Vesta's round temple sheltered the state hearth that must never go out. The Regia was rebuilt in marble in 36 BCE, Vesta's temple by Julia Domna after 191 CE.

Beside the temple stood the House of the Vestals; a storeroom (penus) held the sacred objects. The miniature shows the imperial marble temple; the archaic version, probably thatched and wooden, is a reconstruction. The cult ended in 394 CE and the buildings fell into ruin.

vignettes.text: A Vestal in white, hair bound in six braids, feeds the hearth with dry wood; smoke rises through the roof opening. A lictor waits outside to walk her across the Forum.
On the Kalends the queen of sacred rites sacrifices to Juno in the Regia. Matrons bring offerings; on 9 June, the Vestalia, bakers' donkeys pass garlanded with loaves.
Dusk: the temple door is barred; the hearth glow shows through the lattice. Vestals walk back the few metres to their house under the Palatine, lictors ahead.

spots.name: Lacus Curtius
spots.summary: A walled pit in the middle of the Forum, the last trace of its marsh, named for a Curtius who, legend says, rode fully armed into a chasm to save the city.
details: Romans told three stories: the Sabine Mettius Curtius bogged in the marsh, the youth Marcus Curtius who leapt into a chasm in 362 BCE, and a consul who fenced a lightning-struck spot. The surviving paving and enclosure are Augustan; a relief (a copy stands in the Forum) shows the horseman.

Suetonius says that every year people of all ranks threw a coin into the Lacus for Augustus's health. In 69 CE the emperor Galba was cut down beside it. The miniature shows an altar and fenced enclosure; its exact form before the Augustan paving is uncertain.

vignettes.text: A shopkeeper crossing to the Tabernae Novae stops, drops a copper coin over the low wall and mutters a wish for the emperor's health, as Suetonius describes.
Guides tell visitors from the provinces the tale of the horseman; a fig, an olive and a vine planted beside the pit, as Pliny notes, throw a little shade.
Evening litter-bearers skirt the enclosure. The altar is bare except for yesterday's dried flowers; someone has scratched a name into the travertine.

spots.name: Carcer (Mamertine Prison)
spots.summary: The state prison at the foot of the Capitol: a round rock-cut cell below and a vaulted chamber above, where enemies of Rome were held before execution, later venerated as St Peter's prison.
details: The lower Tullianum, probably an old cistern cut in the tufa, is the oldest part; the upper chamber dates from the 2nd century BCE and carries a travertine front of 39–42 CE. Sallust described it: twelve feet down, dark, stinking and frightful. Jugurtha starved here; the Catilinarians and Vercingetorix were strangled here.

It was never a prison for sentences, only a holding place before execution. From the Middle Ages it was shown to pilgrims as the cell of Peter and Paul, with the spring the apostle used for baptisms. The church of San Giuseppe dei Falegnami above it was begun in 1597.

vignettes.text: The jailer, a public slave, lowers bread and water through the hole in the floor; the prisoner below cannot see it. A guard yawns at the door onto the Forum.
A crowd gathers by the steps beside the prison: a strangled body will be dragged out and shown before going to the river. Vendors sell chickpeas.
At night the only sounds are the Cloaca running beneath and the sentry's steps; in the Tullianum the damp is absolute, the darkness complete.

medieval-1300.name: San Pietro in Carcere
medieval-1300.note: A chapel of San Pietro in Carcere; the Mirabilia and pilgrim guides send visitors down to the cell of Peter and Paul and the spring that gushed for their baptisms.

renaissance-1560.name: San Pietro in Carcere
renaissance-1560.note: Still a pilgrim stop with a custodian and an altar in the lower cell; the carpenters' guild church of San Giuseppe above it is begun in 1597.

spots.name: Bankers' booths (Tabernae Novae)
spots.summary: Rows of shops flanking the Forum's long sides, taken over by money-changers (argentarii) from the 4th century BCE: Rome's first banking district, cramped booths with scales, coin-trays and ledgers.
details: The Tabernae Veteres on the south side and Tabernae Novae on the north began as butchers' shops; by 310 BCE Livy calls them argentariae, hung with captured Samnite shields. Bankers changed coin, tested silver, took deposits and bid at auctions. Plautus' Curculio places lenders and borrowers 'beneath the Old Shops' and warns against the men behind Castor's temple.

The northern row was rebuilt as the front of the Basilica Aemilia (14 BCE). Coins fused into its floor by the fire of 410 CE show business still going on at the sack. The miniature shows a row of narrow booths; interior fittings are reconstruction from Pompeii.

vignettes.text: Shutters come down from the booth fronts; an argentarius sets out his scales and touchstone. A slave carries the ledger. A litigant's friend waits to borrow for a court deposit.
An auction on the Forum side: the banker's clerk notes bids on wax, the crier calls. Coins from a dozen provinces are weighed and bitten, foreign silver taken at a discount.
Booths bolted, the strongbox carried off under guard. Dice rattle in a bar behind the Temple of Castor, among the men Plautus says you should not trust.

spots.name: Booksellers of the Argiletum
spots.summary: The busy street running from the Forum into the Subura, where booksellers like Atrectus and the Sosii pinned lists of titles to their door-posts; Martial sent his readers here to buy him.
details: The Argiletum was a street of shoemakers and booksellers (librarii), with scribes copying texts onto papyrus rolls in back rooms. Martial names Atrectus's shop 'opposite Caesar's Forum', its posts scribbled with titles, where a polished copy of his Epigrams cost five denarii; the Sosii brothers sold Horace. Books were cheap to copy, dear to buy finished.

In 97 CE the Forum Transitorium (Nerva's forum) was built over the lower Argiletum, and the trade shifted up the street toward the Subura. The miniature shows narrow shops with rolls in pigeon-holes and a copying bench; individual shop positions are reconstruction.

vignettes.text: Door-posts freshly pasted with titles; inside, two slaves copy from dictation, reed pens scratching. A customer unrolls a volume to check the hand before paying.
Martial's clients pass, and Juvenal's would-be poets. Someone reads aloud at the door from a new satire; the scent of cedar oil, used against bookworms, hangs over the shelves.
Lamps lit, the copyists keep going by contract until the oil runs out. The shoemakers next door hammer lasts; a drunk from the Subura shouts down the street.

spots.name: Barber's shop in the Subura
spots.summary: A tonstrina at the mouth of the Subura: stool, bronze mirror, razors and shears, and the gossip of the neighbourhood; Martial even mentions a woman barber working here.
details: Barbers reached Rome from Sicily in 300 BCE, Pliny says; by the Empire every street had one, and the tonstrina was the exchange of news, a bar without drink. Shaving with an iron razor and water, no soap, drew blood: Martial jokes that a man would rather face a surgeon than Antiochus the barber.

Martial places a tonstrix 'at the first jaws of the Subura, where the torturers' bloody whips hang' (2.17). Shops opened to the street; customers sat on a bench outside. The miniature follows Pompeian shop-fronts; the location is Martial's, not archaeology's.

vignettes.text: First customers at sunrise: a client on his way to the morning salutatio needs his cheeks scraped smooth. The barber strops the razor; a boy heats water on a brazier.
The bench outside is full of men who are not waiting for a shave. Talk of yesterday's chariot race, a divorce, the price of wheat. The mirror passes round.
Hair plucked, nails pared, the last customer dabbed with spider's web on a nick. Sweepings of hair go into the gutter; the whip-seller next door closes up.

spots.name: Insula (apartment block) in the Subura
spots.summary: A five-storey tenement in Rome's crowded valley: shops below, decent flats on the first floor, then ever cheaper rooms up rickety stairs, no water, no kitchen, and the constant fear of fire.
details: The Regionary Catalogues count some 46,000 insulae in the 4th-century city. Ground floors held tabernae with sleeping lofts; the upper storeys were brick-faced concrete under Augustus's height limit of 70 Roman feet. Juvenal's third satire gives the texture: cracked walls shored with props, a fire starting on the third floor, chamber pots falling from windows.

Tenants cooked on braziers, fetched water from the street fountain and used public latrines. Rents were high and paid yearly on 1 July. The miniature is based on the surviving insulae of Ostia (House of Diana) and the Aracoeli block; the Subura's own buildings are lost.

vignettes.text: Still dark. Bakers' ovens glow in the ground-floor shop; a schoolmaster next door is already shouting at pupils; the water-carrier climbs to the fourth floor with two buckets.
A woman sits in the doorway shelling beans; a child plays dice in the stairwell. From a balcony a wet rag drips on passers-by. The landlord's agent knocks for the rent.
Ox-carts, banned by day, grind over the stones all night. On the top floor a lamp burns beside a straw mattress; a smell of smoke sends everyone to the window.

spots.name: Bakery (pistrinum)
spots.summary: A combined mill and bakery: donkeys turning hourglass millstones, a kneading machine, a domed oven and a shop counter on the street, the pattern seen at Pompeii and on the baker Eurysaces' tomb.
details: Pliny says Rome had no professional bakers until 171 BCE; households ground their own grain. By the Empire a pistrinum did everything: milling, kneading in a basin turned by a slave or donkey, stamping and baking in a wood-fired oven. The baker Eurysaces built a tomb (c. 30 BCE) shaped like mixing bowls, carved with every stage of the work.

Mill-slaves and donkeys worked in misery; Apuleius describes them scarred and half-blind. From the 270s CE the state dole was free bread and the bakers' guild became hereditary. The miniature follows Pompeian bakeries; a Subura pistrinum of this kind is probable, not attested.

vignettes.text: Martial says bakers wake the city: before dawn the donkeys are already circling the mills, hooves on stone, and the first batch slides into the oven on long paddles.
Loaves stacked on the counter, round and scored in eight. A slave carries a basket to a house that has paid in advance; cheap bran bread is weighed out for a porter.
The oven is raked and banked; the donkeys are unhitched, blinkers off. Flour dust in every fold of skin. On the Vestalia in June the beasts will wear garlands instead of harness.

spots.name: Thermopolium (hot-food bar) on the Vicus Tuscus
spots.summary: A hot-food bar with a masonry counter set with jars: wine, chickpeas, lentils, cheese, eggs and warm spiced wine, eaten standing or on a bench, for people who had no kitchen.
details: The type is known from Pompeii, Herculaneum and Ostia: an L-shaped counter faced with marble scraps, dolia sunk into it for dry food, a stove, shelves of cups, often a back room and a painted shrine. Emperors repeatedly tried to limit what popinae could sell cooked; Suetonius says Claudius closed taverns and Nero allowed only boiled vegetables.

The Vicus Tuscus between Forum and Velabrum was a street of fine shops, silk and perfume sellers; a bar here served porters and shoppers. Juvenal lists the company of a popina: sailors, thieves, runaways, hangmen, coffin-makers. The miniature's counter copies the Ostia bar on the Via di Diana.

vignettes.text: Bread, cheese and watered wine for breakfast; the barman ladles chickpeas from a jar sunk in the counter. The marble top is already sticky.
Lunch rush: cups passed over heads, a pot of lentils with leek bubbling on the stove, a dice game in the back room despite the law. Hot honeyed wine for a shivering porter.
Lamps and loud talk. Juvenal's mixed crowd leans on the counter; a girl sings. The aedile's men might look in; the owner has a bribe ready and a shutter half closed.

spots.name: Oil and wine shops of the Velabrum
spots.summary: The low ground between Forum and river, a street of grocers: oil, wine, smoked cheese and pickled fish, with Agrippa's warehouse court behind. Martial praises Velabrum cheese.
details: The Velabrum was the old marsh drained by the Cloaca; once dry it became the natural market between the river wharves and the Forum. Plautus already puts bakers, butchers and soothsayers here. Martial and Pliny both mention cheese smoked in the Velabrum; oil came up from the Emporium in amphorae, wine in skins and jars.

Under Augustus the Horrea Agrippiana, a great warehouse court, was built behind the shops, its ground floor let as tabernae. The miniature shows a lane of open-fronted shops with amphorae and hanging cheeses; their precise layout is reconstruction.

vignettes.text: Carts and porters from the river bring amphorae before the daytime traffic ban; a shopman tips oil into a customer's jar through a funnel, measuring by the sextarius.
Smoke from the cheese-smoking sheds hangs in the lane; flies on the fish-sauce jars. A cook's slave bargains for Falernian and is sold something from the Sabine hills.
The shops shutter; a watchman from the warehouse does his round with a lantern among stacked amphorae. Rats, and the smell of rancid oil in the gutter.

spots.name: Cattle market (Forum Boarium)
spots.summary: The cattle market by the river landing, Rome's oldest trading ground, with the Ara Maxima of Hercules where merchants paid tithes, and a famous bronze bull.
details: Here the Tiber ford, the salt road and the roads from Etruria and Latium met below the Palatine. Greek and Phoenician traders were present by the 6th century BCE; the archaic temple at Sant'Omobono dates from the 6th century BCE. Livestock from Latium was sold on the hoof; the first gladiatorial games were held here in 264 BCE.

The temples of Portunus and Hercules Victor (the round one) survive from the 2nd–1st centuries BCE. In 228 and 216 BCE two Gauls and two Greeks were buried alive here on the Sibylline books' orders. The miniature shows pens and a bronze bull; the market's edges are approximate.

vignettes.text: Drovers who walked through the night rest beside their herds; lowing, dung, the first buyers from the butchers' row prodding ribs. The Tiber mist has not lifted.
Merchants sacrifice a tenth of their profit at the Ara Maxima, where women may not enter; the priests of Hercules will eat well. A money-changer sits under an awning.
Unsold beasts are driven out toward the bridge; the pavement is sluiced from the public fountain. In the Temple of Portunus a lamp is lit for the god of the harbour.

spots.name: Vegetable market (Forum Holitorium)
spots.summary: The vegetable and fruit market outside the Porta Carmentalis, between Capitol and river, crowded by three small temples and later overshadowed by the Theatre of Marcellus.
details: Market gardeners from the Campus Martius and the suburbs sold cabbage, leeks, onions, figs and herbs here; the name means 'market of garden produce'. Three temples of the 3rd–2nd centuries BCE (Janus, Juno Sospita, Spes) stood in a row; their columns survive in the walls of San Nicola in Carcere.

Festus records a Columna Lactaria in the Forum Holitorium where infants were brought to be nursed, perhaps abandoned ones. The Theatre of Marcellus (13 BCE) took part of the space. The miniature shows stalls between the temple steps: a reconstruction of position, not of excavated stalls.

vignettes.text: Carts from the gardens unload before sunrise: baskets of cabbages still wet, bunches of leeks, snails in nets. Women set up on cloths under the temple colonnade.
Shouted prices, a crier announcing lost property; a slave buying for a kitchen fills a basket with chickpeas and herbs. Beggars on the temple steps, a wet-nurse at the column.
Bruised fruit sold off cheap, rot swept into the gutter toward the river. Near the theatre a crowd pushes to get in; the stallholders fold their awnings.

spots.name: Macellum Magnum (Nero's market hall)
spots.summary: Nero's great provision market on the Caelian (59 CE): a colonnaded court with a two-storey domed pavilion, selling fish, meat and delicacies to Rome's richest tables.
details: The macellum was the up-market food hall, distinct from the open forum markets; Rome had two, Livia's on the Esquiline and Nero's on the Caelian. A coin of 63–64 CE shows the Macellum Magnum as a round two-storey tholos inside a portico. Fishmongers, butchers and poulterers sold from marble tables, meat hung from hooks.

It stood on the Caelian, probably near Santo Stefano Rotondo, though the church is not built on it. Juvenal mocks the gourmet who ruins himself at the macellum. The miniature follows the coin image and the excavated macella of Pompeii and Pozzuoli; the detail is reconstruction.

vignettes.text: Fish carried up from the Tiber port and the Ostia road is laid out on wet marble; a slave buyer from a senator's house gets first pick of the mullet.
Lamb carcasses on hooks, Lucanian sausages; a poulterer plucks thrushes. In the central pavilion money is weighed and the market inspectors check the standard measures.
Stalls are hosed down; dogs and the poor wait for scraps at the drain. Juvenal's gourmet goes home having paid a fortune for one fish.

spots.name: Porters on the Emporium quays
spots.summary: Rome's river port below the Aventine, built from 193 BCE: a long stone quay with mooring rings and ramps, warehouses behind, and gangs of porters carrying grain, oil and marble.
details: The aediles Aemilius Lepidus and Aemilius Paullus laid out the Emporium in 193 BCE with the vast vaulted Porticus Aemilia behind it; the quay was paved in 174 BCE. Barges (codicariae) towed upriver from Ostia, later Portus, by oxen or men unloaded here. The Horrea Galbana stored grain, oil and wine for the city.

Porters (saccarii) worked in guilds and were paid by the load. Travertine quay blocks with rings and stepped ramps survive on the Lungotevere Testaccio. The miniature shows the quay, a stretch of warehouse and barges; the warehouses are reduced in scale.

vignettes.text: Barges that came up overnight are tied to the rings; porters queue for the first sacks, a tally-man cutting notches. The smell of wet rope, grain and river mud.
Marble blocks from Luna are dragged up the ramp on rollers; a measurer checks a grain sample for the prefect of the annona. Oil amphorae go to be registered and emptied.
The towing-oxen are stabled, boatmen sleep on deck under sailcloth. Taverns on the slope above fill with porters paid by the sack; a flute somewhere.

spots.name: Monte Testaccio (amphora dump)
spots.summary: A 35-metre hill made entirely of broken olive-oil amphorae, stacked in order behind the Emporium over about 250 years: the rubbish tip of the imperial food supply.
details: Some 53 million amphorae, most of them the globular Dressel 20 from southern Spain, were smashed and laid in terraces with lime scattered to kill the stink. Painted labels (tituli picti) record weights, shippers and inspectors, dated from the 140s to the 250s CE. Oil jars could not be reused, hence the dump.

Medieval Romans called it Monte de' Cocci; it hosted Carnival games and the Good Friday Way of the Cross. The miniature shows a stepped, grassy mound with a working face on the Emporium side; its exact outline in each period is uncertain.
