vignettes.text: Carts of broken jars arrive from the quays; slaves climb with baskets of sherds and tip them along a line, then sprinkle lime. The hill grows by the cart-load.
Heat off the pottery; a clerk reads the painted labels on jars before they are broken, checking the shipper's name against the register. Lizards among the sherds.
Nobody here at night but dogs and a watchman at the warehouses. The mound looms pale against the Aventine; in later centuries vineyards will come right to its foot.

medieval-1300.note: Monte de' Cocci: pasture and Carnival ground; carts of pigs and bulls were run down its slopes for the Testaccio games (Ludus Testaccie) before Lent.

renaissance-1560.note: The Way of the Cross climbs it on Good Friday; vineyards all around, and cool caves are probably already being cut into its base for wine cellars.

spots.name: Boatmen and barges on the Tiber
spots.summary: The river was Rome's highway: barges towed up from the sea, rafts of timber and wine floated down from Umbria, ferrymen, fishermen and later floating mills, all crowded onto a muddy, flood-prone Tiber.
details: Ancient boatmen formed guilds: codicarii who towed grain barges, lenuncularii who ran lighters and ferries, the fishermen of the Tiber with their June games. Timber and stone came down from the upper river; everything from overseas came up 35 km against the current, hauled by oxen along tow-paths.

After antiquity the Ripa Grande in Trastevere handled sea-borne goods and the Ripetta landing the river trade that fed the city with firewood, wine and charcoal. Floods (1530, 1557) regularly wrecked boats and mills. The miniature shows barges, a ferry and tow-paths; the river's banks are stylised.

vignettes.text: Mist on the water; a towing gang harnesses oxen on the far bank. Fishermen haul nets below the island; a ferryman shouts the fare for Trastevere.
A raft of chestnut beams from the Sabine hills is poled in and broken up; wine-barrels rolled ashore; an official checks tolls. Washerwomen beat linen on the steps.
Lanterns on moored barges; the current loud under the bridge piers. A boatman sleeps on his cargo of wood, a dog chained beside him against thieves.

spots.name: Pons Sublicius (the wooden bridge)
spots.summary: Rome's oldest bridge, all wood and no iron, kept by the pontiffs as a sacred thing: the crossing Horatius held, from which straw puppets were thrown each May.
details: Tradition gives it to King Ancus Marcius (7th century BCE). Pliny says it could contain no iron, perhaps so it could be cut quickly, and the pontifices repaired it with rites. Horatius Cocles held it against Porsenna (508 BCE). On the Ides of May the Vestals threw rush puppets (the Argei, 27 by Varro's count) from it into the river.

It was carried away by floods again and again (23 BCE, 69 CE) and always rebuilt in wood; its exact site is debated, probably just below the Pons Aemilius near the Forum Boarium. The miniature shows a timber trestle bridge; piers and width are a reconstruction.

vignettes.text: Carts of produce from Trastevere's gardens rattle over the planks; the timbers smell of pitch. Fishermen's boats slide between the piles below.
The pontiffs' workmen replace a rotten beam with oak pegged, not nailed. Beggars line the parapet: a bridge is the oldest place to beg, as Juvenal's cripples know.
Lamps on the Trastevere side; a goatherd crosses with his flock, the last of the day's traffic. When the Tiber rises, the pontiffs will pray and the planks will groan.

spots.name: Temple of Ceres, Liber and Libera
spots.summary: The plebeians' temple on the Aventine slope above the Circus, vowed in 496 and dedicated in 493 BCE: shrine, archive of the plebeian aediles and place of asylum, with Greek-painted walls.
details: Built in Etruscan style by Spurius Cassius, with decoration by the Greek artists Damophilus and Gorgasus, Pliny records. The aediles kept their archive and copies of senate decrees here; grain was distributed from it in crises. Fire destroyed it in 31 BCE; Augustus rebuilt it and Tiberius dedicated it in 17 CE.

Its site is not securely found; the usual guess is near Santa Maria in Cosmedin, beside the Circus Maximus starting gates. The Cerialia (19 April) ended with foxes let loose in the Circus with torches tied to their tails. The miniature is a reconstruction of a Tuscan triple-cella temple.

vignettes.text: A woman in white brings the first ears of this year's grain; the aediles' clerk opens the archive room beside the cella. A pig is led in for sacrifice.
During the Cerialia the Circus below roars; a plebeian aedile hears a complaint from a market woman on the steps. Matrons keep the spring fast of Ceres.
Doors closed; a slave who ran here for asylum sleeps on the podium under the guard's eye. Smell of pine resin from the lamps and of the Circus stables below.

spots.name: Primary school under a portico
spots.summary: An elementary school with no building of its own: a master, a bench, wax tablets and an abacus under a portico or in a rented shop, curtained from the street, from before dawn.
details: Boys and some girls, from about seven, learned letters, syllables, reading aloud and counting; the master (ludi magister) was poorly paid, taking fees monthly and a gift at the Minerva festival in March. Horace remembers boys with satchel and tablet; Martial curses a schoolmaster whose shouting and cane wake the street before cockcrow.

Schools shut for the Saturnalia and the summer heat; a Pompeian painting shows a flogging in the forum colonnade. The miniature puts the school in a portico beside the Forum; schools are attested in such spaces but no specific Roman one can be located.

vignettes.text: Lamps hang from the portico while it is still dark; boys chant syllables after the master, a slave paedagogus waits outside with each child's lunch. The cane lies ready.
Midday break: the master dismisses them to the street; tablets are smoothed with the stylus end. The neighbours, Martial says, would pay him to be quiet.
Afternoon: counting on the abacus, pebbles clicking; a girl reads a line of verse haltingly. From midsummer the bench will stay empty until October.

spots.name: Fuller's workshop (laundry and dye-works)
spots.summary: The fullers cleaned new cloth and dirty togas: trodden in tubs of urine and fuller's earth, rinsed, bleached over sulphur and brushed; a noisy, stinking workshop vital to a toga-wearing city.
details: The process is known in detail from Pompeii (fullonica of Stephanus) and Ostia: men stamped cloth in small basins (the 'fuller's dance'), rinsed it in big tanks, hung it over a wicker cage with burning sulphur, carded it with teasels and pressed it. Urine was collected in jars at street corners; Vespasian taxed it.

A law of 217 BCE (the lex Metilia) already regulated fulling in Rome. Fullers formed one of the city's largest trade guilds. The miniature shows an open court with tanks and treading stalls; this particular fullonica near the Velabrum is a plausible placement, not an excavated one.

vignettes.text: Jars from the street corner are collected, slopping; workers climb into the stalls and begin treading, ankle-deep in urine and clay. The smell reaches the next street.
Togas hang white in the court; a boy fans a sulphur pot under the cage, coughing. A client's slave argues that his master's cloak came back shrunk.
Cloth is folded into the screw press; water from the tanks runs into the drain. Fullers go home smelling of it: Martial's cruellest comparison is to a fuller's jar.

spots.name: Neighbourhood bath-house (balneum)
spots.summary: A small private bath-house of the kind every neighbourhood had: a quadrans to enter, a warm room, a hot room, a cold plunge, shouting, massage and snack-sellers, open from early afternoon.
details: The 4th-century Regionary Catalogues list 856 balnea besides the great imperial thermae. They were commercial, often cramped, heated by hypocaust from a stokehole; a bell rang at the eighth hour, about two o'clock. Seneca, living over one, lists the sounds: grunting weight-lifters, the masseur's slap, the hair-plucker's shriek, cake and sausage sellers.

Men and women bathed at different hours or in separate wings; mixed bathing was banned by Hadrian. Entry cost a quadrans, the smallest coin. The miniature uses the plan of small Pompeian and Ostian baths; a bath here in the Subura is probable, not attested.

vignettes.text: The furnace-man stokes before anyone comes; smoke from the stokehole drifts up the alley. Women's hours in the morning; attendants wipe down the benches.
The bell rings; men arrive with slaves carrying oil flask, strigil and towel. Ball games in the court, a weight-lifter grunting, a seller shouting sausages. Steam and shouted greetings.
Last bathers dry off and go to dinner; the water in the hot pool is grey. Someone's cloak is missing, the bath-thief of Catullus's poems. Lamps lit for the late crowd.

spots.name: Saepta Julia (voting hall, later a luxury market)
spots.summary: Agrippa's marble-colonnaded enclosure in the Campus Martius (26 BCE) for citizens to vote, soon better known as Rome's most fashionable shopping arcade, where Martial's Mamurra browsed all day.
details: Caesar planned a marble voting pen to replace the wooden Ovile; Agrippa finished it, 310 by 120 m, with the Diribitorium beside it for counting. Voting mattered less after Augustus, and the long porticoes filled with dealers in ivory, bronzes, silver, slaves and tortoiseshell. Augustus staged gladiatorial games here.

Martial has Mamurra handle the best boys and tables, price a vase and buy two cheap cups. Hadrian restored it after fires. Stretches of its walls survive just east of the Pantheon. The miniature shows the enclosure with shops in the colonnades; the interior courtyard is simplified.

vignettes.text: Dealers unroll silks and set bronzes on tables between the columns; a slave-dealer's stock stands on a platform with chalked feet. The voting lanes are long gone.
Mamurra's hour: the idle connoisseur turns every cup, asks the price of a Corinthian bronze, buys nothing. Money-changers at the entrance; shade, murmur, scent of cedar.
Shutters, strongboxes carried off; a few old citizens recall when the comitia met here. Across the way the Baths of Agrippa are emptying; torches are lit on the Pantheon steps.

republic-50bce.note: Caesar's marble Saepta is only a project (Cicero mentions it in 54 BCE); the site is still the Ovile, a wooden sheep-fold of voting lanes.

spots.name: Campus Martius exercise grounds
spots.summary: The flat flood-plain outside the old city, public land where the army mustered, the census was taken, elections were held and young men ran, rode, wrestled and swam in the Tiber.
details: After the kings' expulsion the Tarquins' fields became the Field of Mars (Livy). It lay outside the pomerium, so armed citizens could gather; the comitia centuriata met in the Ovile, the censors used the Villa Publica (435 BCE). The Equirria horse-races (27 February, 14 March) and the October Horse were run here.

Horace sends his young Roman to the Campus for riding and javelin and then into the Tiber; Strabo describes grass, ball-games and hoops among the first temples and porticoes. The miniature shows open meadow with a few monuments; by 50 BCE Pompey's theatre had begun to crowd it.

vignettes.text: Young men exercise before it is hot: javelin at a post, wrestling in the dust, then a swim across to the Trastevere bank. Oxen graze where the voters will stand.
Census year: citizens file by century past the Villa Publica to declare property and sons. Election day: lines of men in togas in the roped lanes of the Ovile.
Dusk; the meadow empties, dust settles, frogs start up from the Tarentum marsh. Sheep are driven in from the river. A trumpet somewhere near the altar of Mars.

spots.name: Meta Sudans fountain
spots.summary: A tall conical fountain 'sweating' water from its top beside the Colosseum, marking the meeting of four regions and the turn of triumphal processions; demolished in 1936 for Mussolini's road.
details: The brick-and-concrete cone, about 17 m high and faced with marble, was built under the Flavians (c. 80–96 CE) over an Augustan predecessor found in excavations in the 1980s. Water welled from the top and ran down the cone into a round basin. It appears on coins of Titus beside the Colosseum.

Tradition says gladiators washed here after the games. Nearby stood the Colossus of Nero, which gave the amphitheatre its name. The stump survived until 1936. The miniature shows the cone and basin; the rest of the square, with its arches, is simplified.

vignettes.text: Water-sellers fill jars at the basin to hawk by the amphitheatre gates; a street-sweeper clears last night's straw. The cone drips in the first sun.
Games day: the crowd funnels past the fountain to the numbered arches, sausage-sellers, programme hawkers. A mule-driver waters his beast. Spray cools the shaded side.
The amphitheatre dark and huge; the fountain's splash the loudest sound. A few bearers wait for a late litter; a watchman's torch passes along the Via Sacra.

spots.name: Spring of Juturna
spots.summary: The Forum's own spring, pooled in a marble basin beside the Temple of Castor, with a shrine to the nymph Juturna: water for sacrifices and for the sick, and later the aqueduct office.
details: The spring at the foot of the Palatine was one reason for settling the valley. Legend has Castor and Pollux watering their horses here after Lake Regillus (496 BCE). The basin, 5 m square with a central altar, was given marble steps in the 2nd century BCE and restored under Trajan; a small shrine and a well stand beside it.

Water from Juturna was used for sacrifices and thought to heal, Frontinus says. In the 4th century the Statio Aquarum, the water administration, moved here. The miniature shows the basin, altar and shrine; in 600 BCE it was an open spring at the marsh edge, a reconstruction.

vignettes.text: A temple slave draws water for the morning sacrifices in a bronze jug; someone has left a wax leg on the altar, thanks for a cure. Mist off the pool.
In August the basin is low and green; a sick child is washed in it. Clerks of the water office argue with a pipe-fitter about an unlicensed tap.
The lamps of Castor's temple reflect in the water. A drunk dips his head, a night-watchman shoos him; the frogs begin.

spots.name: Comitium (the assembly ground)
spots.summary: The round, stepped assembly ground before the Senate house, with the Rostra of ship-beaks, the black stone of the Vulcanal and Rome's oldest Latin inscription: the heart of Republican politics.
details: The Comitium was laid out and paved as early as the 7th century BCE; under the black marble pavement (Lapis Niger) lies a 6th-century cippus inscribed in archaic Latin and mentioning a rex. In 338 BCE the speakers' platform was decorated with the prows (rostra) of ships captured at Antium. Assemblies, trials and funeral orations happened here.

Caesar levelled it in 44 BCE, moving the Rostra and rebuilding the Curia; the area became ordinary Forum pavement. The miniature shows circular steps and the Rostra as reconstructed by Coarelli; that circular form is a well-supported interpretation, not a surviving structure.

vignettes.text: The augur takes his seat as the sun rises to watch for birds; if the omens are bad no assembly will meet today. Slaves sweep the steps.
A tribune on the Rostra, the crowd below shouting; clerks by the Curia door take the vote by tribe. In the shade a lawyer rehearses his speech.
Empty but for a ritual: a priest at the Vulcanal pours wine on the old stone. Workmen hang torches for tomorrow's funeral oration for a former consul.

spots.name: Mithraeum beneath San Clemente
spots.summary: A cave-like chapel of the god Mithras, fitted around 200 CE into the courtyard of a 1st-century house, with benches for the initiates' meal and the bull-slaying altar; now three storeys below San Clemente.
details: The brick house of the 1st century CE had a central court; about 200 CE its vault was studded with pumice to resemble a cave, benches were built along the sides and a marble altar with Mithras killing the bull set at the end. A schoolroom for initiates adjoins. The all-male worshippers rose through seven grades.

Mithraism was popular with soldiers and freedmen; this shrine fell out of use when pagan cults were banned in the 390s, and the Christian basilica above was enlarged. The miniature shows the vaulted room with benches and altar; ritual is reconstructed from painted mithraea at Ostia and Capua.

vignettes.text: Street level: a bakery and shops in the same block; nothing shows that below a flight of steps a god is carved killing a bull. A Raven, the lowest grade, sweeps the stairs.
Afternoon: the Father of the community meets a candidate; the room is cold, oil-lamps on the altar shelf, the spring in the next room trickling.
The initiates recline on the benches in the dark, lamps on the altar, incense and roast meat; the Lions serve the cups. Outside, the street is deaf to it.

spots.name: Terminus of the Aqua Virgo (the future Trevi)
spots.summary: Agrippa's aqueduct of 19 BCE ends in the Campus Martius; the distribution basin at the 'trivium' of three streets became the Trevi, Rome's one aqueduct that never quite stopped flowing.
details: The Aqua Virgo runs about 20 km, almost all underground, from springs near Salone; Frontinus tells the story of the girl who showed soldiers the spring. It fed Agrippa's baths and the Campus Martius fountains. In 1453 Nicholas V rebuilt the mouth as a plain wall with three spouts and a basin.

Through the Middle Ages the Virgo trickled on, patched by Hadrian I in the 8th century; the Trevi quarter was the only part of the city with running aqueduct water. Water-sellers (acquaroli) carried it from here in barrels. Salvi's fountain of 1732–62 replaced everything the miniature shows.

vignettes.text: Water-carriers load barrels on donkeys for the streets without pipes; a laundress is already at the trough. Horses are watered on the way out of town.
Children splash, a water-seller argues with a rival over his place at the spout. Heat, and the cool smell of running water in the dust of the three streets.
The spouts run on in the dark, the loudest thing in the quarter. A patrol pauses to drink. On the hill above, a cricket in a vineyard answers the water.

medieval-1300.name: Fontana di Trevi (medieval basin)
medieval-1300.note: A modest basin at the end of the aqueduct's half-ruined channel, fed by what still flows; washerwomen, water-carriers and horses share it.

renaissance-1560.name: Fontana di Trevi (old basin)
renaissance-1560.note: The basin of Nicholas V (1453): three spouts and a rectangular tank in a plain wall; Pius V's engineers are about to restore the channel.

spots.name: Huts on the Palatine (the Hut of Romulus)
spots.summary: Oval huts of wattle, daub and thatch on the south-west Palatine, the Rome of the 8th–7th centuries BCE; one was kept as the 'Hut of Romulus' into the Empire.
details: Excavations in the 1940s found post-holes cut in the tufa for huts about 5 by 4 m, with a central hearth, a drainage channel around and a porch; the earliest date to the 8th century BCE. By 600 BCE such huts were giving way to houses on stone footings with tiled roofs.

The Casa Romuli was repeatedly burned and rebuilt in the same materials; Dionysius saw it in the 1st century BCE, tended by state slaves. The miniature shows a cluster of thatched huts with a fenced yard; their number and arrangement are reconstruction.

vignettes.text: Smoke leaks through the thatch; a woman grinds emmer on a saddle quern at the door while goats are let out. The hill is still wet with dew.
Men return from fields by the river with a lamb; a potter fires jars in a pit. In a bigger house down the slope, new terracotta roof-tiles catch the sun.
Fire banked, the family sleeps on skins around the hearth; a dog by the door. From the Forum marsh below, frogs; from the Capitol, the sound of a lyre.

spots.name: Salt traders at the river ford
spots.summary: Where the Tiber ford met the salt road, salt from the pans at the river mouth changed hands with Sabine shepherds and inland traders: one of the reasons a city grew here.
details: The Via Salaria, the 'salt road', ran from the Tiber mouth up to the Sabine hills; Livy says Ancus Marcius seized the salt pans and that salt became a state monopoly in 508 BCE. Salt was carried by mule and sold by the measure near the Forum Boarium, just above the ford by Tiber Island.

Soldiers' pay (salarium) was supposedly a salt allowance. The ford's exact place is reconstruction; the island gave the shallowest crossing. The miniature shows mules, sacks and a shelter on the river bank; in 200 BCE the trade ran through the same site behind the new stone quays.

vignettes.text: Mule-trains from the salt-pans cross the ford at low water, sacks dripping; a Sabine shepherd waits with cheeses and wool to barter. Smoke from a fire on the bank.
Salt is measured out by the modius under the eye of the king's man, later the censors' contractor; a load goes up the valley toward Reate. Flies on the mule-dung.
The last buyers gone; the salt stacked under hides against the dew. Shepherds light a fire on the shore and sing; the river turns bronze under the Janiculum.

spots.name: Etruscan craftsmen's quarter (Vicus Tuscus)
spots.summary: The street of Etruscans below the Palatine, named for settlers from Etruria: craftsmen in bronze, terracotta and pottery who gave early Rome its temple roof-statues and its first luxury shops.
details: Livy and Varro explain the name differently (refugees after Porsenna's war; followers of Caelius Vibenna). Etruscan artists certainly worked in Rome: Pliny names Vulca of Veii, who made the terracotta Jupiter for the Capitoline temple about 509 BCE. The street ran from Forum to Velabrum and carried the Circus procession.

A statue of the Etruscan god Vertumnus stood here. By 200 BCE the Vicus Tuscus was a street of shops with a doubtful reputation (Plautus); later a street of silks and incense. The miniature shows workshops with open fronts and kilns behind; it is a reconstruction.

vignettes.text: A bronze-smith's furnace is lit; a boy works the bellows. Next door a coroplast presses clay into a mould, a gorgon's face for a temple roof.
A craftsman from Veii bargains in Etruscan with a Roman noble over a painted terracotta for his family tomb. Clay dust, charcoal, the smell of hot wax from the casting shop.
Kilns banked for the night; a seller of Greek cups from Caere stows his stock. Someone pours wine at the foot of Vertumnus's statue, the god who changes shape.

spots.name: Esquiline necropolis
spots.summary: The burial ground outside the earliest city on the Esquiline: Iron Age graves, then chamber tombs of noble families, and the pits (puticuli) where the poor and the executed were thrown.
details: Graves from the 10th to the 6th centuries BCE have been found on the Esquiline, cremations in urns and inhumations in trenches with pottery and bronze. Later, painted tombs of the Fabii and other families stood here. Varro explains the puticuli as pits where corpses rotted; the Campus Esquilinus was also the place of execution.

Horace's eighth satire remembers it: bones left by slaves, witches digging, a Priapus guarding the gardens Maecenas laid over the old graveyard around 35 BCE. The miniature shows mounds, cippi and a mass pit outside the agger; the layout is a reconstruction.

vignettes.text: A family carries a child wrapped in cloth to a trench grave at sunrise, with a cup and a fibula; the hired mourners have gone home. Crows wait.
Corpse-bearers tip a slave's body into the pit with lime; a dog is chased off. Farther along, a mason cuts a name into a tufa cippus.
Nothing moves but wind in the reed-screens; according to Horace, witches come by moonlight to gather bones and herbs here. A guard dog barks from the agger.

spots.name: Campo de' Fiori
spots.summary: A meadow over the ruins of Pompey's theatre that became, after paving in 1456, the city's liveliest square: horse market, inns, booksellers, hangings and, at every corner, a tavern.
details: The name (field of flowers) describes it in 1300: pasture and gardens between the Orsini fortress built into the theatre's cavea and the river quarter. It was paved under Callixtus III in 1456; Sixtus IV's new streets made it the hub of Parione. Horse and hay markets met here.

Vannozza Cattanei, mother of the Borgia children, ran the Hostaria della Vacca on a corner. Executions were held here from the 15th century; Giordano Bruno was burned here in 1600. The miniature shows a paved square with inns, stalls and a gallows; stall positions are reconstruction.

vignettes.text: Hay-carts and horse-dealers from the Campagna take their places; a crier announces the day's prices. Innkeepers sweep out last night's straw.
A horse is trotted for a buyer, boys shout; a notary witnesses the sale on a tavern table. Pilgrims look at prints of the city's wonders on a bookstall.
Taverns loud with Spaniards and German students; a courtesan's lamp in a window; the sbirri walk through. On execution days the pillory stands bare in the dark.

medieval-1300.note: Still open ground, the campus floris: meadow, vegetable gardens and a few houses under the Orsini tower; the pilgrim road to St Peter's skirts it.

renaissance-1560.note: Paved since 1456; horse market, inns full of Germans and Spaniards, booksellers and print-sellers, and the gallows where the papal governor's sentences are carried out.

spots.name: Banchi (the bankers' street)
spots.summary: The street leading to Ponte Sant'Angelo where Florentine, Genoese and German bankers kept their counters (banchi), handling papal finance, pilgrims' bills of exchange and the mint next door.
details: The Canale di Ponte, the lane to the bridge, was lined with money-changers by the Jubilee of 1450. Julius II's Via dei Banchi (c. 1508) made the quarter the financial heart of Rome: Agostino Chigi's bank, the Strozzi, the Altoviti and the Fugger and Welser agents, with Sangallo's new Mint (Zecca) at the end.

Bankers lent to popes against the alum of Tolfa and the tax farms; a crisis came with each papal death. Mountebanks and notaries crowded the street too. The miniature shows palaces with ground-floor counters and the Zecca; the later Banco di Santo Spirito is not yet founded.

vignettes.text: Clerks open the counters and oil the scales; a courier from Lyon arrives with letters of exchange. The bridge beyond is already busy with pilgrims and mule-trains.
Rates are shouted between Genoese and Florentines; a cardinal's steward draws on his master's account; the Mint's hammers clink behind the Zecca's rusticated front.
Iron grilles down, ledgers locked. In a loggia the bankers dine on Tuscan wine and news of the Spanish treasury. Beggars settle under the arcades by the bridge-head.

spots.name: Rosary-sellers of Via dei Coronari
spots.summary: The straight pilgrims' street (the ancient Via Recta) from the Tiber bend toward Ponte Sant'Angelo, widened by Sixtus IV for 1475 and lined with sellers of rosaries (corone), medals and images.
details: The Via Recta of medieval Rome was the main road from the inhabited quarter to the Vatican bridge. For the Jubilee of 1475 Sixtus IV paved and straightened it; its new name came from the coronari, rosary and devotional-goods sellers who served the stream of pilgrims passing toward St Peter's.

Houses with ground-floor shops and painted façades were built along it by cardinals' households and prosperous artisans; the house of the courtesan Fiammetta stands nearby. The miniature shows a straight street of shop-fronts with hanging rosaries; the medieval version is narrower and partly unpaved.

vignettes.text: Shutters up; rosaries of wood, bone and coral hang in rows; a woman strings beads. The first pilgrims, Germans in grey, pass singing toward the bridge.
A seller shouts in three languages; a Dalmatian pilgrim buys a lead medal of the Veronica. Mule-drivers curse the crowd. A street madonna is cleaned for a procession.
Shops closed, hostel doors still open; a lantern under a street shrine. Pilgrims who missed vespers at St Peter's argue about tomorrow's route to the seven churches.

medieval-1300.name: Via Recta (the pilgrims' street)
medieval-1300.note: The Via Recta: an unpaved, crooked lane through gardens and low houses, the main pilgrim route to the bridge; inns and a few relic-sellers already.

spots.name: Pilgrims' hostels on Via del Pellegrino
spots.summary: Inns and national hospices along the pilgrims' way to St Peter's, named Via del Pellegrino when Sixtus IV straightened it in 1483: beds in rows, soup, relics for sale and fleas.
details: The Jubilee of 1300 brought, Villani says, 200,000 pilgrims; Dante describes the crowd control on Ponte Sant'Angelo. Hospices were founded by nations (the Saxons at Santo Spirito, the English in 1362 on today's Via di Monserrato, the Germans and Netherlanders at Santa Maria dell'Anima from 1350), and private inns packed the street.

Sixtus IV's Via Peregrinorum (1483) ran from Campo de' Fiori toward the bridge; goldsmiths, innkeepers and rosary-sellers lived along it in the 1526 census. The miniature shows an inn with a courtyard and a hospice with a dormitory; individual inns are not located.

vignettes.text: Pilgrims rise from straw in a shared room, pay the host, and set off for St Peter's with staff and scrip. The soup-pot is already on for the next arrivals.
A hospice warden checks letters of introduction and assigns beds; a shoemaker repairs a hundred boots. Hawkers sell the Mirabilia, the guide to the city's wonders.
Six to a bed, snoring in five languages; the host counts coins. A late party from Siena knocks; the fire's last light shows a painted St Christopher.

spots.name: Jacket-makers of Via dei Giubbonari
spots.summary: The street of jacket- and doublet-makers (giubboni) running out of Campo de' Fiori, a trade street in Regola where clothes were cut, stitched and sold from open shops.
details: Renaissance Roman streets took names from trades, and the 1526 census shows the clothing trades concentrated around Campo de' Fiori. The giubbonari made men's doublets and jackets and sold ready-made clothes; tailors, hosiers and second-hand dealers (rigattieri, many of them Jews) shared the quarter.

Workshops opened straight onto the street; the master cut, apprentices and women stitched. The tailors' guild (università) regulated prices and apprenticeships. The miniature shows a narrow street of shops with cloth hung outside; attribution of individual houses is reconstruction.

vignettes.text: Cloth bolts set out in the doorway; the master chalks a pattern on fustian, apprentices sit on the threshold sewing. A dyer's boy delivers a dripping bundle.
A Spanish soldier is measured for a doublet; a dealer sells a dead man's jacket cheap. Noise from the horse market, and the midday bell at San Lorenzo in Damaso.
Needles put away, lamps lit for a rush order from a cardinal's household; the shopkeeper closes the half-door. Smell of wool, wax and the Tiber.

spots.name: Hat-makers of Via dei Cappellari
spots.summary: A dark, narrow lane behind Campo de' Fiori where hatters made and sold caps, berets and felt hats, one of the trade streets of Renaissance Parione.
details: The cappellari felted wool and rabbit fur over wooden blocks, then dyed and trimmed: black velvet caps for clerks, broad felts for travellers, straw for summer. The street was built up with tall houses on both sides in the 15th–16th centuries, so narrow that the upper storeys almost touch.

Hatters, like the other clothing trades, lived above their shops; the 1526 census lists households by street with the head's trade. The miniature shows a lane with hats hung on poles; the trade's concentration here rests on the name, its workshops on analogy.

vignettes.text: Steam from the felting kettles already fills the lane; a journeyman stretches wet felt over a block. Light hardly reaches the ground between the overhanging houses.
A muleteer tries on a broad hat; a cardinal's page collects six red-trimmed caps. Hats bob on poles outside the shops like a crowd without faces.
Shops shut; the lane is black. From an upper window a hatter's wife empties a basin; two Spaniards with a lantern look for a tavern.

spots.name: Key-makers of Via dei Chiavari
spots.summary: The locksmiths' street, laid over the stage of Pompey's theatre: forges, keys, locks, strongbox fittings and the iron grilles that every Roman shop and palace wanted.
details: The chiavari (key-makers) worked iron at charcoal forges, filing keys for the locks of chests, doors and the new palaces; blacksmiths and ironmongers shared the street. It runs along the line of Pompey's theatre stage, whose vaults were used as cellars and workshops.

Ironworkers' guilds had their statutes confirmed by the city and prices for locks were regulated. The miniature shows forges with open fronts and smoke; the street name is 16th-century, the number of shops reconstruction.

vignettes.text: Bellows roar as forges are lit; a boy sorts blanks by size. The clink of hammers starts before the church bells.
A householder waits while a key is filed to fit his lock; a banker's clerk orders a strongbox with three locks. Sparks and the smell of quenched iron.
Fires banked, keys hung in bunches on the shutters; an apprentice sweeps iron filings. Under the floor, the vaults of Pompey's theatre hold wine and rubbish.

spots.name: Chair-makers of Via dei Sediari
spots.summary: A short street by Sant'Eustachio named for chair-makers and, by tradition, the bearers of the papal chair (sediari pontifici): rush-seated chairs and litters built and sold here.
details: Chairs were still a modest luxury in 1560; most houses had benches and chests. Sediari made rush-seated and turned-wood chairs, folding stools and the sedan chairs that carried the sick and the rich through the mud. The papal sediari, who carried the pope's portable throne, traditionally lodged in this quarter.

The street lies in Rione Sant'Eustachio near the university (the Studium Urbis). The miniature shows workshops with chairs stacked outside; the attribution rests on the street name and the usual pattern of trade streets.

vignettes.text: A turner's lathe hums; rushes soak in a tub for seats. Chairs stacked five high outside the shop; a servant from a prelate's household orders twelve.
Students from the Sapienza pass arguing; a sedan chair is tested with the apprentice inside. Sawdust on the cobbles, a dog asleep on a stool.
Rushes and tools put away; a chair-bearer in papal livery comes home and drinks with the chair-makers. Vespers at Sant'Eustachio, under the stag's head above the door.

spots.name: The Ghetto
spots.summary: Rome's Jews, perhaps 3,000, were walled into a few flood-prone streets by the Tiber in 1555 by Paul IV: gates locked at night, yellow hats, one synagogue building, trade limited to rags and second-hand goods.
details: The bull Cum nimis absurdum (14 July 1555) created the enclosure in Rione Sant'Angelo beside the Portico of Octavia, where most Jews already lived. The 1526 census counted about 1,750 Jews in Rome; by 1560 the Ghetto probably held closer to 3,000 in a few acres of low, damp houses that grew upward as space ran out.

Jews could deal in second-hand clothes (strazzaria) and rags, lend on pawn, and practise medicine with permits. Five congregations (the Cinque Scole) shared one building. Pius IV relaxed the rules slightly after 1559. The miniature shows the walled block with its gates; the interior streets are simplified.

vignettes.text: The gates are unlocked at dawn by the Christian gatekeeper, whose wages the Jews must pay; pedlars with bundles of old clothes go out into the Christian streets.
Piazza Giudea market: second-hand cloaks, mended shoes, pawned silver. A Jewish physician visits a Christian patient with his permit. Tiber mud still in the lower rooms from the last flood.
Gates locked after the Ave Maria; inside, lamps, five congregations' evening prayers under one roof, a wedding song. Outside, the sbirri check that nobody is late.

spots.name: Tor di Nona prison
spots.summary: A medieval river-tower of the Orsini at the bridge-head, turned into the papal governor's prison: cramped cells, questioning by the rope, and the scaffold on the bank outside.
details: The tower (its name probably from the Annona, the grain office) guarded the Tiber above Ponte Sant'Angelo. From the 15th century it served as the prison of the Governor of Rome; prisoners were questioned with the strappado, and Beatrice Cenci and Giordano Bruno were later held here. Executions took place at Piazza di Ponte nearby.

In 1300 it was probably one of the Orsini strongholds controlling the bridge. The prison was demolished in the 17th century to make way for a theatre. The miniature shows a square tower on the embankment with a walled yard; the medieval form is reconstruction.

vignettes.text: Bread is handed through a grille; a notary arrives to take a deposition. Bells from across the river; the water slaps the tower's foot.
A debtor's family pleads at the gate; brothers of the confraternity of San Giovanni Decollato come to comfort a man condemned for tomorrow. Shouting from an upper cell.
Lanterns on the river stairs; the guard changes; from inside, a prisoner singing. In the morning the gallows will go up on the bank by the bridge.

spots.name: Pasquino, the talking statue
spots.summary: A battered Hellenistic marble group set up on a street corner in 1501, on which Romans pasted anonymous satires (pasquinades) against popes and cardinals: the city's unofficial newspaper.
details: Cardinal Oliviero Carafa placed the statue (Menelaus with the body of Patroclus) at the corner of his palace. Each 25 April, St Mark's day, it was dressed as a god and Latin verses were pinned to it by students; by the 1520s the verses had turned biting. Adrian VI wanted it thrown into the Tiber.

After Paul IV's death in 1559 the statue was covered with attacks on the Carafa, while the mob broke the pope's statue on the Capitol. Marforio, across the city, 'answered' Pasquino. The miniature shows the statue on its pedestal with papers; its exact mounting in 1560 is approximate.

vignettes.text: Before daylight someone pastes a sheet to the plinth and is gone; by sunrise a crowd reads, laughs, and one man copies it before the governor's men tear it down.
Booksellers' boys and clerks from the Cancelleria gather; a Spaniard reads aloud a sonnet against the Spanish. The statue is scarred, chipped and loved.
Dark corner; the night patrol passes. Someone tries a rhyme on his friends in a doorway: tomorrow it will hang on Pasquino, printed by a press that denies everything.

spots.name: Stationers and printers near Sant'Eustachio
spots.summary: Around the university at Sant'Eustachio, stationers, printers and print-sellers: Blado's papal press, Lafreri's maps and views of Rome, paper, ink and pens for students and the Curia's scribes.
details: Printing reached Rome in 1467. By the 1550s Antonio Blado printed for the Apostolic Camera, the Dorico brothers printed music, and Antonio Salamanca and Antonio Lafreri sold engraved views of ancient and modern Rome (later gathered as the Speculum Romanae Magnificentiae) from shops in Parione, near Sant'Eustachio and Piazza Navona.

Stationers (cartolari) sold paper, quires, ink and ready-ruled ledgers; scribes copied for the courts. Censorship tightened after the Index of 1559. The miniature shows a printing shop with a press visible and a print-seller's front; individual shop sites are approximate.

vignettes.text: Pressmen damp the paper; the compositor sets a papal bull in Blado's shop. A stationer trims quires for notaries. Students buy pens before lectures at the Sapienza.
An English traveller buys Lafreri's map of ancient Rome; the print-seller unrolls views of the Colosseum. Ink smell, paper dust, the thud of the press.
Proofs read by candle, a corrector marking errors. Outside, an Inquisition notary's visit is discussed; the Index of forbidden books is pinned to the door.

spots.name: Cattle grazing in the Forum (Campo Vaccino)
spots.summary: The Roman Forum under metres of silt and rubble, used as a cow field and cattle market: columns buried to their capitals, three churches, lime-kilns and grazing oxen.
details: After the 9th century the Forum's pavement vanished under flood-silt and debris. Churches occupied the Senate house (Sant'Adriano) and the temple of Antoninus and Faustina; the Frangipani fortified the arches. Pilgrims' guides pointed out the 'temple of Saturn' and the 'Temple of Peace'. Cattle grazed between the stumps of columns: hence Campo Vaccino.

In 1536 Paul III cleared houses and chapels for Charles V's triumphal entry along the ancient Via Sacra. Marble-robbers dug for building stone and lime. The miniature shows a sunken field with the three columns of Castor, the porch of Saturn and the arches; buried levels are approximate.

vignettes.text: Cowherds from the Campagna drive oxen in past the half-buried Arch of Septimius Severus; the field is wet. A monk at Santa Maria Nova rings for matins.
Cattle market in the shade of the three columns; a dealer counts beasts by the Arch of Titus, a lime-burner's cart picks over a marble cornice in the ditch.
Mist and the smell of cattle; an antiquary with a lantern measures a buried capital. In the Mamertine chapel, a lamp; bats under the Basilica of Maxentius.

spots.name: Lime-burners' quarter (Calcarario)
spots.summary: The lime-burners' quarter in the Campus Martius, where ancient marble, columns, statues and inscriptions alike, was fed into kilns to make mortar for the new city.
details: The Calcarario lay around the ruined Porticus Minucia and the temples of Largo Argentina; the church of Santa Lucia 'de Calcarario' took its name from the kilns. Marble burns to good lime, and for centuries the easiest quarry was the ancient city. Poggio Bracciolini in the 1430s and Raphael's letter to Leo X (1519) both lamented it.

Sixtus IV and later popes sold permits to dig; carts of fragments came from the Forum and the Campus. The miniature shows kilns, heaps of marble and smoke behind a row of houses; the number of kilns and their exact spots are reconstruction from Lanciani's records.

vignettes.text: Kilns lit before dawn; a cart tips a broken statue and lengths of column into the yard. Workers break them with sledgehammers, white dust on everything.
The kiln roars; a load of inscribed slabs waits, and a scholar copies one before it goes in. Lime is slaked in a pit: steam and a bite in the throat.
The fire is kept up all night; a watchman sleeps by the warm wall. Sacks of lime are loaded for a palace site on Via Giulia.

spots.name: Vineyards among the ruins (the disabitato)
spots.summary: Two-thirds of the walled city was countryside: vineyards, orchards, pasture and ruins between the Colosseum, the Lateran and the Caelian, worked by day and empty, feverish and lawless by night.
details: From the 9th century the population drew into the Tiber bend; the hills within the Aurelian Walls became the disabitato. Monasteries, fortified towers and great ruins stood among vines; aqueduct arches served as field walls. The 1526 census shows hardly any households here. Cardinals' vigne (villas with vineyards) spread over it after 1500.

Malaria haunted the low ground in summer; wolves were reported inside the walls. The miniature shows vines on terraces, a tower and ruins among olive and fig trees near San Clemente; field patterns are reconstruction from 16th-century maps such as Bufalini's of 1551.

vignettes.text: Vignaroli walk out from the city with hoes; a flock is driven past the Colosseum, whose arches shelter the sheep at night. Dew on the vines, a cuckoo in a ruin.
Hot and silent; a cardinal's gardener grafts a vine against an aqueduct pier. Lizards on a fallen cornice. The ox-driver drinks from a broken sarcophagus used as a trough.
Workers hurry back into the inhabited city before dark; a monastery bell at Santi Quattro Coronati. Fever-mist in the valley; owls in the Baths of Trajan.

spots.name: Floating mills on the Tiber
spots.summary: Grain mills on moored boats, their wheels turned by the river's current: a device born in the Gothic siege of 537, when the aqueducts were cut, and the city's millers ever after.
details: Procopius tells how Belisarius, with the aqueduct mills stopped, moored pairs of boats below a bridge with a wheel between them. For a thousand years the Tiber was lined with floating mills, chained to the banks near Tiber Island, Ponte Sisto and Ripa, owned by monasteries and families and worked by a millers' guild.

Floods swept them away; the great flood of 1557 destroyed many. They hindered boats and were a hazard at the bridges. The miniature shows two-hulled mills with a wheel between and a plank to the shore; their number and positions in each period are reconstruction.

vignettes.text: Millers row out to the moored hulls, sacks on their backs; the wheels creak into motion; flour dust blows off the water. Bakers' boys wait on the bank.
Full current, wheels thumping; a boat squeezes between two mills and the miller curses. A customs man checks sacks against the grain tax. Gulls on the hopper.
Chains groan, the river rising after rain upstream; millers sit up with lanterns, ready to cut loose and run for the bank. Somebody prays to St Christopher.

spots.name: Via Giulia (Bramante's new street)
spots.summary: A straight new street a kilometre long, cut by Julius II and Bramante from 1508 along the Tiber bend: palaces, the Florentine church, the unfinished Palace of the Tribunals, and the fashionable evening walk.
details: Julius II wanted to concentrate the law courts in one palace and give the Florentine bankers a straight road to the Vatican bridge. The Palazzo dei Tribunali was abandoned at its rusticated base (the 'sofas' of Via Giulia). San Giovanni dei Fiorentini was begun in 1519; Antonio da Sangallo the Younger built his own house here.

By 1560 Via Giulia was a street of bankers, courtesans and prelates, lined with palaces such as Sangallo's house, later Palazzo Sacchetti. The Farnese arch and the prisons came later. The miniature shows the straight street with palaces and a church under construction; façades are simplified.

vignettes.text: Masons on the scaffold of the Florentine church; a Florentine banker's mule passes; the rusticated blocks of the abandoned courts serve as a bench for idlers.
Litters of cardinals, a Spanish ambassador's coach, grooms shouting. A notary works in a ground-floor shop; a courtesan at a window ignores a poet.
The evening passeggiata: gentlemen on horseback, music from a palace loggia; by the river stairs, boatmen eat. Smell of the river and of jasmine over a garden wall.

spots.name: Osteria dell'Orso (inn)
spots.summary: A tall 15th-century inn near the river above Ponte Sant'Angelo, well placed for travellers arriving from the north: Montaigne took rooms here in 1580 before finding lodgings in the city.
details: The Hostaria dell'Orso, 'at the sign of the bear', occupies a house of about 1460 on the corner of Via dei Soldati and Via di Monte Brianzo, with a loggia and painted façade. Travellers coming down the Via Flaminia or by river from upstream found it early; it fed and stabled them, and charged accordingly.

Tradition adds Dante and Rabelais to the guest list; Montaigne's Journal is the sure witness. Inns were regulated by the city: posted prices, no gambling, no women of ill fame. The miniature shows the inn with its arcaded ground floor and stable yard; the yard is reconstruction.

vignettes.text: Ostlers water horses in the yard; a Flemish merchant's boxes come up from the Ripetta on a porter's back. Bread, cheese and wine on the trestle in the hall.
The host carves a kid for a table of French clerics; a courier from Venice eats standing. A scribe writes a letter for a guest; the painted façade needs retouching.
Boots in the corridor, a lute from the loggia; the host posts the bill on the door for the morning. Across the river, lights at Castel Sant'Angelo.

spots.name: Market stalls at the foot of the Aracoeli stairs
spots.summary: At the foot of the 124 marble steps built in 1348, stalls and criers of the old Capitoline market linger below the hill where Michelangelo's new piazza is being laid out.
details: The stairs were built in 1348, traditionally as thanks for surviving the Black Death; Cola di Rienzo was killed on the Capitol nearby in 1354. The Capitol was the city's market until Sixtus IV moved the market to Piazza Navona in 1477; fruit-sellers, criers and notaries stayed on at the foot.

From 1538 Michelangelo's design began to transform the hilltop; by 1560 the Senator's palace stairs were built, the cordonata ramp not yet. Public notices were cried here and criminals' sentences posted. The miniature shows stalls on a sloping piazza with the stairs behind; stall positions are reconstruction.

vignettes.text: Greengrocers from the disabitato set out figs and greens at the foot of the stairs; a Franciscan from the Aracoeli comes down to buy bread. Cattle lowing from the Forum behind.
The city crier reads a bando of the Conservators; a notary draws up a contract on a stall; children race up the 124 steps. Marble dust drifts from the works above.
Stalls folded; a beggar sleeps on the lowest step. Vespers from Santa Maria in Aracoeli drift down; a lantern climbs the old path toward the Senator's palace.

events.title: The Cloaca Maxima drains the Forum
events.text: Under the Tarquin kings the marshy valley between the Palatine and Capitoline was drained by a great channel, the Cloaca Maxima, running down to the Tiber. Livy says the kings set the common people to the work, which was hated for its hardship. Probably an open ditch at first, it was later vaulted in stone. Without it the Forum could never have become the city's centre.

events.title: Building Jupiter's temple on the Capitol
events.text: Tradition credits the Tarquins with levelling the Capitoline summit and raising the huge Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus, dedicated in 509 BCE, the first year of the Republic. Its podium, about 62 by 54 metres, is the largest known Etruscan-style temple base. Livy tells how workers digging the foundations found a human head, read as an omen that Rome would be head of the world.

events.title: First games in the Murcia valley
events.text: Livy places the first Circus games under Tarquinius Priscus, who marked out the valley between Palatine and Aventine and let senators and knights build their own wooden stands. Nothing permanent existed yet: the floor flooded, the turning posts were probably wooden, and most spectators stood on the slopes. Horse races for the god Consus were already held here, according to the legend of the Sabine women.

events.title: Scipio Africanus triumphs over Carthage
events.text: Returning from Zama, Scipio rode through the Forum and up to the Capitol in the most splendid triumph Rome had yet seen. Livy reports 123,000 pounds of silver carried in the procession and 400 asses paid to each soldier. The victory ended the Second Punic War; Livy notes he was the first general to be known by the name of a people he had conquered: Africanus.

events.title: Cato builds Rome's first basilica
events.text: As censor in 184 BCE, Cato the Elder bought houses and shops beside the Curia and built the Basilica Porcia, the first of Rome's great roofed halls for business and law. Plutarch says Cato built it in the teeth of opposition. The building, Greek in form, housed the tribunes' bench; it burned in 52 BCE together with the Curia during the riot at Clodius's funeral and was never rebuilt.

events.title: The Senate suppresses the Bacchanalia
events.text: In 186 BCE the consul Postumius addressed a public meeting in the Forum denouncing secret night-time rites of Bacchus as a conspiracy against the state. Livy says the gates were guarded, thousands were arrested across Italy and many executed. The Senate's decree, preserved on a bronze tablet found in Calabria, limited gatherings to five people without permission. A freedwoman informer, Hispala, was rewarded.

events.title: Praetor Marcius builds the Aqua Marcia
events.text: The praetor Quintus Marcius Rex was charged with repairing the old aqueducts and bringing in a new one, 91 kilometres from springs in the upper Anio valley. Its last stretch ran on long arcades, the first on such a scale at Rome, and it was the first to reach the Capitol, which the Sibylline Books had supposedly forbidden. Frontinus praised its cold, clear water. It cost 180 million sesterces.

events.title: Clodius's funeral pyre burns the Curia
events.text: After the gang leader Publius Clodius was killed on the Via Appia by Milo's men, his followers carried the corpse into the Forum. Urged on by two tribunes, the crowd built a pyre inside the Senate house from benches, tribunals and clerks' records. The Curia Hostilia burned to the ground with the Basilica Porcia beside it. Pompey was made sole consul to restore order; Cicero defended Milo and lost.

events.title: Pompey opens Rome's first stone theatre
events.text: Pompey dedicated his theatre in 55 BCE, during his second consulship, with games that Cicero, writing to a friend, found vulgar: six hundred mules in a tragedy, and elephants (twenty, says Pliny) slaughtered in the games, whose cries roused the crowd's pity rather than pleasure. A temple of Venus Victrix crowned the seating, letting Pompey call the whole theatre a temple and dodge the ban on permanent theatres.

events.title: Caesar buys land for a new forum
events.text: Cicero wrote to Atticus in 54 BCE that he and Caesar's agents had already spent sixty million sesterces buying private houses north of the old Forum to extend it. The result became the Forum of Caesar, dedicated unfinished in 46 BCE with a temple to Venus Genetrix, Caesar's claimed ancestress. It set the model every emperor followed: a forum bearing the builder's name, paid for with war booty from Gaul.

events.title: Cicero denounces Catiline in the Senate
events.text: On 8 November 63 BCE Cicero convened the Senate in the Temple of Jupiter Stator, at the foot of the Palatine, and delivered his First Catilinarian: "How long, Catiline, will you abuse our patience?" Senators moved away from Catiline's bench, leaving him alone. He left Rome that night. A month later five conspirators were strangled in the Tullianum beside the Forum, and Cicero told the crowd: "They have lived."

events.title: The Great Fire starts at the Circus
events.text: On the night of 18–19 July 64 CE fire broke out among the shops along the Circus Maximus, where flammable goods were stored, and raced through the valley driven by wind. Tacitus says it burned six days, then flared again; of fourteen regions only four escaped. Nero was at Antium when it began. He opened the Campus Martius to the homeless, then built his Golden House on the ashes.

events.title: Cutting the hill for Trajan's Forum
events.text: Spoils from the Dacian Wars paid for the largest imperial forum. Apollodorus of Damascus's workmen cut away a spur joining the Quirinal to the Capitoline; the inscription on Trajan's Column says its height, about 35 metres with the base, shows how much hill was removed. The complex, dedicated in 112, held a basilica, two libraries and a great colonnaded square with an equestrian statue of Trajan at the centre.

events.title: A day at the amphitheatre
events.text: A full programme began with wild beast hunts in the morning, executions of criminals at midday, and gladiators in the afternoon. Fifty thousand spectators sat by rank, senators at the front, women and the poor at the top beneath the awnings worked by sailors. Martial, who saw the opening games in 80 CE, describes a rhinoceros tossing a bull. Seneca found the midday executions dismal.

events.title: Buying Martial's epigrams in the Argiletum
events.text: Martial tells readers to seek his books in the Argiletum, opposite Caesar's Forum, where the bookseller Atrectus's shop has doorposts covered with advertisements for poets; a copy smoothed with pumice and dressed in purple costs five denarii. Scribes copy by hand in the back room. Every day customers browse, authors loiter hoping to be recognised, and the smell of papyrus and cedar oil drifts into the street.

events.title: The Tiber floods the lower city
events.text: In the spring of 69 CE, as Otho marched out against Vitellius, the Tiber rose over its banks and swamped the Campus Martius and the low ground of the Forum valley. Tacitus records collapsed tenements, people drowned in their shops and beds, food shortages, and the Via Flaminia, the army's route north, blocked by water. Romans read it as an omen.

events.title: The Baths of Caracalla open
events.text: Caracalla's enormous bathing complex south of the Aventine opened in 216, its main block alone covering over two hectares with pools, hot rooms, gymnasia and gardens for perhaps 1,600 bathers at once. A new branch of the Aqua Marcia, the Aqua Antoniniana, fed it. Entry was cheap or free, and crowds from the whole city came to see the vaulted halls, mosaics and colossal statues like the Farnese Hercules.

events.title: Caracalla murders his brother Geta
events.text: The two sons of Septimius Severus ruled jointly but hated each other, dividing the Palatine palace with separate entrances. In December 211 Caracalla arranged a reconciliation meeting in their mother Julia Domna's apartments and had centurions cut Geta down in her arms. Cassius Dio says Caracalla then had Geta's name chiselled from every monument and killed some 20,000 of his supporters; the erasure is still visible on the Severan Arch.

events.title: The Senate dedicates Severus's arch
events.text: In 203, marking ten years of his reign, the Senate dedicated a triple arch at the north-west corner of the Forum to Septimius Severus and his sons Caracalla and Geta, celebrating victories over the Parthians. The reliefs show sieges of Mesopotamian cities and chained captives. The inscription, once in bronze letters, named Geta; after 211 his line was recut to praise Caracalla instead, the old letter-holes still showing.

events.title: A marble map of the whole city
events.text: Between 203 and 211 the Severan government fixed a marble plan of Rome, about 18 by 13 metres, to a wall of the Temple of Peace, a wall that now belongs to the church of Santi Cosma e Damiano. At a scale of about 1:240 it shows every street, tenement, shop and staircase in ground plan. About a tenth survives, in some 1,186 fragments; scholars are still fitting them together.

events.title: Honorius strengthens the Aurelian Walls
events.text: With Alaric's Goths in Italy, the emperor Honorius and his general Stilicho ordered the Aurelian Walls restored and raised between 401 and 403. The curtain was heightened to roughly double, gates like the Porta Appia got new towers and portcullises, and inscriptions on several gates named the emperors Arcadius and Honorius. Builders used brick and whatever stone was at hand. The city soon needed them.

events.title: Symmachus pleads for the Altar of Victory
events.text: In 384 Symmachus, prefect of Rome and voice of the pagan senators, begged the young Valentinian II to restore the Altar of Victory, removed from the Senate house in 382. "We ask peace for the gods of our fathers," he wrote; "not by one road alone can we reach so great a mystery." Ambrose answered and won. Save a brief return under the usurper Eugenius (392–394), the altar was never restored.

events.title: Alaric's Goths enter the Porta Salaria
events.text: After three sieges, on 24 August 410 the Visigoths entered Rome through the Porta Salaria, probably opened from inside. For three days they looted houses and palaces; fires burned around the gate and the Gardens of Sallust. Alaric spared the churches of St Peter and St Paul as refuges. The first capture of Rome by a foreign enemy in 800 years shocked the empire; Jerome wrote that his voice failed.

events.title: Theodosius closes the temples
events.text: Laws of Theodosius in 391–392 forbade all sacrifice: no one might enter the temples or revere the images, and a later law banned even incense to the household gods. The great Temple of Jupiter on the Capitol, Rome's state sanctuary for 900 years, lost its priests and offerings. The Vandals stripped its gilded roof tiles in 455. Senators who had led the old religion quietly joined the churches.

events.title: Boniface VIII proclaims the first Jubilee
events.text: On 22 February 1300 Boniface VIII granted full forgiveness of sins to pilgrims who visited St Peter's and St Paul's on fifteen days during the year. The chronicler Giovanni Villani, who went, reckoned 200,000 foreigners in Rome at any moment and praised the city's handling of the crowds; Dante, in Inferno, describes the two-way lanes imposed on the Ponte Sant'Angelo. Innkeepers and money-changers grew rich.

events.title: Giotto's mosaic greets the pilgrims
events.text: Around 1300 (proposed dates run from about 1298 to 1310) Cardinal Jacopo Stefaneschi commissioned Giotto to make a vast mosaic of the Navicella, Christ walking on the water towards the apostles' storm-tossed boat, for the atrium of Old St Peter's. Every pilgrim crossing the courtyard passed beneath it: the ship was the Church, its pilot Peter. Only a heavily restored fragment survives in the new basilica's portico.

events.title: The Frangipane turn the Colosseum into a fortress
events.text: In the 12th century the Frangipane clan, who dominated the Forum valley, made the Colosseum a stronghold, walling up arches, raising towers on the vaults and controlling the roads to the Lateran. Houses, workshops and a chapel filled the arcades; the Annibaldi held it after them until Henry VII gave it to the Senate and people of Rome in 1312. Earthquakes and quarrying did the rest.

events.title: Cola di Rienzo seizes the Capitol
events.text: On Pentecost 1347 the notary Cola di Rienzo, after Mass at Sant'Angelo in Pescheria, marched in armour to the Capitol with a crowd and had new laws read out from the palace steps. The baronial senators fled; Cola took the title of Tribune and promised a reborn Roman republic. Petrarch cheered him. By December he had fled; in 1354 a mob killed him on the same hill.

events.title: Marble burns in the lime-kilns
events.text: Every working day the calcararii feed their kilns with broken statues, inscriptions and column drums from the ancient city. Burned for days, marble becomes lime for mortar. The quarter's name, Calcarario, survived in the church of Santa Lucia de Calcarario near Largo Argentina. Now and then someone copied an inscription before it burned, which is how some texts are known at all.

events.title: Michelangelo at work on St Peter's
events.text: At 85, Michelangelo, chief architect since 1547 and refusing any salary, was raising the drum of the great dome, having stripped Sangallo's over-elaborate plan back to a compact Greek cross. In 1560 Pius IV confirmed him in office and the drum's paired columns were going up. He had a large wooden model of the dome made in 1558–61 so work could follow his design after his death in 1564.

events.title: Paul IV walls in the Jews
events.text: With the bull Cum nimis absurdum of July 1555, Paul IV ordered Rome's Jews, long settled in Trastevere and the Sant'Angelo quarter, into a walled enclosure beside the Tiber, locked at night. They had to wear yellow hats, sell their property, keep one synagogue and trade only in rags and second-hand goods. Its opening words, calling it absurd for Jews to live among Christians, set the pattern for three centuries.

events.title: Michelangelo redesigns the Capitol
events.text: After Charles V's visit in 1536, Paul III moved the bronze Marcus Aurelius there in 1538 and asked Michelangelo to redesign it. He turned the square towards St Peter's, gave the Senators' Palace a double stair and planned twin palaces framing a trapezoid with an oval pavement. Work was slow: in 1560 only the Senators' stair was done; the Conservators' Palace followed from 1563 and the pavement waited until 1940.

events.title: Pasquino speaks again
events.text: Most mornings since about 1501 Romans have found verses pasted to the battered ancient statue at the corner of the Orsini palace (now Palazzo Braschi), mocking cardinals, popes and prices in Latin or Roman dialect. Adrian VI reportedly wanted the statue thrown in the Tiber; under Paul IV the pasquinades were savage. Crowds read and copy them before the police tear them down. Pasquino has rivals: Marforio, Madama Lucrezia.

events.title: The great Tiber flood of 1557
events.text: On 15 September 1557 the Tiber rose to nearly 19 metres on the Ripetta gauge, close to the record flood of 1530, drowning the Campo Marzio, the Ghetto and Trastevere. The floating mills moored by the Tiber Island broke loose and smashed against the bridges; bread ran short for days. Mud lay in the churches; a plaque at Santa Maria sopra Minerva marks the level. Embankments came only after 1870.

stories.title: The Triumph of Vespasian and Titus
stories.summary: Follow Vespasian and Titus through the city on the day in 71 CE when they celebrated the conquest of Judaea, as the eyewitness Josephus described it.

steps.title: The procession enters the city
steps.text: The emperors spent the night outside the walls by the Temple of Isis and at dawn took their seats at the Portico of Octavia, where the Senate and the army cheered them. Josephus says the parade was routed through the theatres so more people could see it; its way probably ran round the Circus Maximus. Crowds pack stands and rooftops; wagons of spoils roll past.

steps.title: The spoils of the Temple
steps.text: Here, where Domitian later raised this arch to his dead brother, the most striking spoils went by: the golden table, the seven-branched lampstand and the scroll of the Jewish Law, carried shoulder-high. The arch's relief shows exactly this moment, soldiers in laurel wreaths bearing the menorah. Josephus also describes towering floats, three or four storeys high, showing cities burning and fleets sinking.

steps.title: The prisoner dies in the Forum
steps.text: At the edge of the Forum the procession halted. By ancient custom the triumph waited while the chief captive, Simon bar Giora, who had led the defence of Jerusalem, was dragged with a noose round his neck to the Tullianum prison below the Capitol and executed. When the shout came that he was dead, the crowd cheered and the emperors moved on to sacrifice.

steps.title: Sacrifice on the Capitol
steps.text: Vespasian and Titus climbed the Clivus Capitolinus to the Temple of Jupiter and offered prayers and the customary sacrifices; then feasting began across the city. Josephus ends with the fate of the spoils: the golden vessels went into Vespasian's new Temple of Peace, while the Law and the purple curtains of the sanctuary were kept in the palace. Rome was celebrating a war that Josephus says cost a million lives.

stories.title: A Day in the Subura
stories.summary: An ordinary day around 100 CE in Rome's noisiest quarter, followed hour by hour through the complaints and jokes of Martial and Juvenal.

steps.title: Bakers before dawn
steps.text: Before first light the bakery's blindfolded mule is already turning the lava millstone, and the smell of bread climbs to the tenants above. Martial lists the baker's din among the things that keep a Roman from sleeping. Slaves knead dough at a long table; round loaves stamped with the baker's mark go into the domed oven. By the first hour the first batch is on the counter.

steps.title: Waking in the tenement
steps.text: Up five flights, the poor tenant has a single room: no kitchen, no water, a chamber pot emptied, or thrown, into the street. Juvenal notes that the tenant under the roof tiles, where the doves nest, burns last but has no way out. Below, the ground-floor shops take down their shutters. Clients hurry out in togas to their patron's morning greeting, hoping for the handout.

steps.title: At the barber's
steps.text: Second hour: men wait on stools for a shave. The barber works with an iron razor and water, no soap; Martial jokes about one so slow that the beard grows back on the first cheek before he finishes the second. Here you hear the quarter's gossip, the price of bread, who died in last night's fire.

steps.title: Lessons under the awning
steps.text: The schoolmaster has set up under a shop's awning, cane in hand; Martial complains that his shouting wakes the street before cockcrow. Boys and a few girls chant letters, scratch copies onto wax tablets and recite their reckoning tables. Fees are tiny, paid monthly. The children of freedmen sit beside slaves' children sent to learn enough to keep accounts.

steps.title: Lunch at the counter
steps.text: Sixth hour, midday: the quarter stops for a quick meal at the cookshop counter, where jars sunk in the masonry hold chickpeas, lentils, sausages and warm spiced wine. Juvenal sneers at the hot bars and the sweating cooks. With no kitchen upstairs, everyone eats here. Dice rattle at the back table, though gambling is illegal; the aedile seldom looks in.

steps.title: The afternoon bath
steps.text: Eighth hour: the baths open to men. A quadrans, the smallest coin, buys entry to a small neighbourhood balneum. Undress, oil, a ball game in the yard, then warm room, hot room and the cold plunge. Seneca once lodged above a bath and catalogued its noise: weightlifters grunting, the hair-plucker's victims shrieking, the sausage-seller and cake-seller each with his cry.

steps.title: Evening at the amphitheatre
steps.text: Towards evening the day's spectators pour out of the Colosseum and back up the Argiletum into the Subura. Those who stayed saw the afternoon's gladiators under the awning. Tonight dinner, for the lucky client, is at the patron's table; for the rest, bread and a cup at the bar. After dark the carts come in, since wheeled traffic is banned by day, and Juvenal's sleepless night begins.

stories.title: The Jubilee of 1300
stories.summary: Walk with the pilgrims of 1300, the first Holy Year, from the Tiber bridge to St Peter's and across the half-empty city to the Lateran.

steps.title: Crossing the bridge in lanes
steps.text: The old Pons Aelius is the only bridge to St Peter's. The crowd is so dense that the Romans have divided the roadway with a barrier: pilgrims going to the basilica keep one side, facing the castle, those returning keep the other, facing the Monte Giordano. Dante, who saw it, compares the sinners of Malebolge to this two-way traffic. Beggars and money-changers work both lanes.

steps.title: Fifteen visits for forgiveness
steps.text: The bull of February demands fifteen days of visits from foreigners, thirty from Romans. Inside the old Constantinian basilica, with its forest of columns, pilgrims shuffle past the confessio where Peter lies, wash at the bronze pine-cone fountain in the atrium, and leave coins. A chronicler from Asti saw two clerics at St Paul's raking in the offerings day and night.

steps.title: Where the pilgrims sleep
steps.text: Back in the Borgo the hostels of the nations, Saxon, Frisian and Lombard, are full; many sleep in the porticoes and in the fields. Villani praises the Romans for keeping bread, wine, meat, fish and oats plentiful, though hay and lodging went dear. Relic-sellers hawk little painted copies of the Veronica, the holy veil shown in St Peter's, for pilgrims to carry home.

steps.title: Through the lime-burners' lane
steps.text: Crossing the abitato, pilgrims pass the Calcarario, where kilns burn ancient marble into lime beneath the ruins of the Theatre of Pompey and the Circus Flaminius. Smoke, heat and the crack of splitting statues. The guidebook many carry, the Mirabilia Urbis Romae, points the way to the wonders of the ancients while workmen quietly turn them into mortar.

steps.title: The Senators' hill
steps.text: The Capitol is now the seat of the city's Senator, in a fortified palace on the Tabularium's ruins; the great stair up to Santa Maria in Aracoeli is not yet built. From the hill pilgrims look south over the Campo Vaccino, the cow pasture that was the Forum, to the Colosseum, now a baronial fortress. The Mirabilia still calls this the golden Capitol, head of the world.

steps.title: The pope's cathedral
steps.text: The walk ends at the Lateran, Rome's cathedral, where Boniface VIII has just built a loggia for blessings; a fresco attributed to Giotto shows him proclaiming the Jubilee from it. Pilgrims visit the Sancta Sanctorum chapel's relics and climb the holy stairs beside the palace. The indulgence is complete. Beyond the basilica, Rome is vineyards and ruins all the way to the walls.

stories.title: Building the New Rome
stories.summary: Rome in 1560 under Pius IV: markets, palaces, straight new streets, and Michelangelo, aged 85, directing the dome of St Peter's and the Capitol.

steps.title: Market in the morning
steps.text: Campo de' Fiori is the market: stalls of vegetables, fish and hay, horse-dealers, and inns round the square for pilgrims and papal couriers. Executions happen here too. Behind the houses the curve of Pompey's ancient theatre still shapes the lanes. Rome has grown back to perhaps 80,000 people since the Sack of 1527.

steps.title: The Farnese palace
steps.text: The largest private palace in Rome, begun by Sangallo for Cardinal Alessandro Farnese and finished, after he became Paul III, by Michelangelo, who added the great cornice and the window over the door. In 1560 Paul III's grandsons, Cardinals Alessandro and Ranuccio, keep building and filling it with antiquities from the Baths of Caracalla, the Farnese Bull and Hercules. The garden front is unfinished.

steps.title: Bramante's straight street
steps.text: Via Giulia runs a kilometre straight along the river, laid out for Julius II around 1508 for law courts that were never built; their rusticated blocks, the 'sofas', still jut from the pavement. Florentine bankers and churchmen have built palaces here, and San Giovanni dei Fiorentini is rising at its end. Carriages, newly fashionable, find it one of the few streets they fit through.

steps.title: The dome takes shape
steps.text: At St Peter's the old basilica's nave still stands, walled off from the new crossing, where Bramante's four great piers, thickened by Michelangelo, carry the rising drum. The architect, 85 and often too frail to ride out, sends instructions from his house and has a wooden model built so no one can alter his design. In 1560 Pius IV confirms his authority against critics among the works deputies.

steps.title: The Capitol remade
steps.text: On the Capitol the Marcus Aurelius sits on Michelangelo's base at the centre of a square still half built. The Senators' Palace has its double stair; the Conservators' Palace, with its giant pilasters, will be begun in 1563 and finished in the 1580s; the Dioscuri reach the balustrade in 1583. Senators and guilds meet here, in the shadow of the popes.

steps.title: The walled quarter at dusk
steps.text: The walk ends at the Ghetto gates, ordered by Paul IV five years ago. Pius IV would soon ease a few of the rules and let Jews trade more freely, but the walls stayed and the gates were locked each evening. Rag-dealers pack up their stalls; the river smell rises in the low streets. The new Rome of straight streets and domes is also a city of enclosure.
